questions.stem: About the organisation of the vascular system:

options.label: A
options.text: There are three circulations: pulmonary, systemic (caval) and portal

options.label: B
options.text: Blood leaving the heart passes through arteries, arterioles, then capillaries

options.label: C
options.text: The tunica intima consists of endothelium and an elastic lamina in connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: The tunica media is composed mainly of collagen

options.label: E
options.text: The endothelium is simple squamous epithelium lining all vessels

notes.A: The three circulations are pulmonary, systemic (caval) and portal.
notes.B: Blood passes from arteries to arterioles and then into capillaries.
notes.C: The intima is endothelium on connective tissue with an internal elastic lamina.
notes.D: The tunica media is mainly smooth muscle (plus elastic fibres in large arteries); collagen dominates the adventitia.
notes.E: Simple squamous endothelium lines every vessel and the heart.

questions.why: A vessel wall has three coats: intima (endothelium and internal elastic lamina), media (mainly smooth muscle) and adventitia (mainly collagen).

questions.stem: Arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: The aorta is an elastic artery whose recoil maintains flow in diastole

options.label: B
options.text: Smaller arteries and arterioles have a thicker smooth muscle layer

options.label: C
options.text: The labial anastomosis between the two facial arteries is an actual anastomosis

options.label: D
options.text: Coronary artery anastomoses are actual, freely compensating channels

options.label: E
options.text: In some tissues arterioles empty into venules through arteriovenous shunts

notes.A: Elastic tissue in the aortic media stretches during systole and recoils in diastole, sustaining forward flow between heartbeats.
notes.B: Smooth muscle is prominent relative to lumen size in small arteries and arterioles, so changes in its tone strongly affect resistance.
notes.C: Superior or inferior labial branches of the facial arteries meet their counterparts across the midline of the corresponding lip.
notes.D: Small arterial connections can enlarge over time, but may deliver too little blood when a major coronary artery closes suddenly.
notes.E: Arteriovenous channels in sites such as the skin divert blood directly to venules, allowing it to bypass the capillary exchange bed.

questions.why: The aorta stores energy during ventricular ejection, and muscular vessels regulate where the blood goes. Links between arterial territories differ in their ability to restore distal flow after an occlusion.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a single capillary bed is regulated mainly by:

options.label: B
options.text: the tunica adventitia of the venule

options.label: C
options.text: the valves of the small veins

options.label: D
options.text: the elastic lamina of the arteriole

questions.why: A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the entrance to a true capillary. Relaxation opens the capillary to local flow, while constriction diverts blood towards other routes.

notes.B: Venular adventitia supports the outgoing vessel and has no sphincter at the entrance to the capillaries.
notes.C: Venous valves prevent reverse flow on the return side of the circulation, downstream from the capillary bed.
notes.D: The elastic lamina supports the arterial wall, while smooth muscle contraction controls entry into capillaries.
notes.E: Channels between endothelial cells permit fluid and solute exchange across the wall after blood has entered the bed.

questions.stem: Capillaries:

options.label: A
options.text: are the narrowest vessels, about 7–10 µm across

options.label: B
options.text: are the functional exchange unit of the circulation

options.label: C
options.text: have smooth muscle and connective tissue layers in their wall

options.label: D
options.text: of the CNS lack intercellular channels, contributing to the blood–brain barrier

options.label: E
options.text: are wide enough for the red cell, which is about 6–8 µm

notes.A: Typical narrow capillaries have lumens on the order of a few micrometres, roughly matching the diameter of circulating red cells.
notes.B: Their very thin wall makes them the site of exchange between blood and tissues.
notes.C: Capillaries have endothelium and a basal lamina that can be shared with pericytes, with no separate muscle or adventitial coat.
notes.D: Endothelial tight junctions close the paracellular route in brain capillaries, contributing to the barrier between plasma and neural tissue.
notes.E: Erythrocytes deform as they squeeze through narrow capillaries, often moving one at a time.

questions.why: The capillary lumen is only slightly wider than an erythrocyte, and a single endothelial layer provides a short exchange path. Tight junctions greatly restrict this exchange in the brain.

questions.stem: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are found in all of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The kidney has fenestrated capillaries.

notes.A: Sinusoids.
notes.C: Sinusoids.
notes.D: Sinusoids.
notes.E: Sinusoids.

questions.stem: Veins:

options.label: A
options.text: have thinner walls and wider lumens than the companion arteries

options.label: B
options.text: have three coats but no elastic lamina

options.label: C
options.text: in the limbs are doubled as superficial veins and venae comitantes

options.label: D
options.text: of the limbs and neck commonly have valves that prevent reflux

options.label: E
options.text: have a thicker tunica media than arteries of the same size

notes.A: Low pressure means thinner walls and wider lumens than the companion arteries.
notes.B: They have the three coats but no distinct elastic lamina.
notes.C: Limb veins are doubled: superficial veins plus deep venae comitantes.
notes.D: Valves in limb and neck veins prevent backflow.
notes.E: Veins have much less smooth muscle in the media than arteries of the same size.

questions.why: Veins are low-pressure vessels: thin walls, wide lumens, a thin media and valves that stop reflux.

questions.stem: In pulmonary artery catheterisation, the catheter passes in order through the:

options.label: A
options.text: femoral artery, aorta, left ventricle, then the pulmonary trunk

options.label: B
options.text: subclavian vein, left atrium, mitral valve, pulmonary trunk

options.label: C
options.text: internal jugular, right atrium, tricuspid valve, pulmonary trunk

options.label: D
options.text: internal jugular vein, right ventricle, mitral valve, aorta

options.label: E
options.text: external jugular vein, coronary sinus, right ventricle, aorta

questions.why: From the internal jugular vein a flow-directed catheter reaches the right atrium via the superior vena cava, then crosses the tricuspid valve, right ventricle and pulmonary valve to enter the pulmonary trunk.

notes.A: A femoral arterial catheter can reach the aorta and can enter the left ventricle, whose outflow leads back to the aorta.
notes.B: The subclavian vein drains via the brachiocephalic vein and superior vena cava into the right atrium, upstream of the tricuspid valve.
notes.D: The mitral valve connects the left atrium and ventricle, while the right ventricle ejects through the pulmonary valve.
notes.E: The external jugular drains through the subclavian vein, while the coronary sinus independently drains the myocardium into the right atrium.

questions.stem: Which is an unpaired (visceral) branch of the thoracic aorta?
questions.why: Oesophageal branches arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta to supply the thoracic oesophagus. They leave as individual visceral branches, in contrast to the paired arteries of the body wall.

notes.A: The posterior intercostal arteries arise in right and left pairs to supply the intercostal spaces.
notes.B: A right and a left subcostal artery run below the twelfth ribs to supply the adjacent body wall.
notes.C: The superior phrenic arteries are paired branches to the upper surface of the diaphragm.
notes.E: The inferior phrenic arteries are paired vessels that usually arise below the diaphragm and supply its inferior surface.

questions.stem: The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta at the:
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery leaves the aorta at the lower border of L1, just below the coeliac trunk (T12); the inferior mesenteric arises lower, at L3.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk arises near T12 and distributes blood to foregut organs above the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
notes.B: L3 is the usual origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, which supplies hindgut structures below the midgut territory.
notes.C: The abdominal aorta branches at about L4 to form the common iliac arteries, well below its major gut branches.
notes.D: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm near T10, above the level where the aorta enters the abdomen at T12.

questions.stem: The splenic artery is a branch of the:
questions.why: The splenic artery arises from the coeliac trunk and follows a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas to the spleen. It shares its origin with two other foregut arteries.

notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut and branches independently from the abdominal aorta below the coeliac trunk.
notes.C: The common hepatic artery is another direct coeliac branch, carrying blood towards the liver and proximal duodenum.
notes.D: The left gastric artery branches separately from the coeliac trunk to supply the cardia and lesser curvature of the stomach.
notes.E: The inferior mesenteric artery arises low on the abdominal aorta and supplies the hindgut, far from the splenic hilum.

questions.stem: The vessel that crosses in front of the aorta, just below the origin of the SMA, is the:
questions.why: The left renal vein runs from the left renal hilum to the inferior vena cava on the right. It crosses the front of the aorta in the angle between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery.

notes.A: The right renal artery passes behind the inferior vena cava as it travels from the aorta to the right kidney.
notes.C: The left gonadal vein ascends on the left to join the left renal vein before that vein crosses the aorta.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava ascends on the right of the abdominal aorta and receives the vessel after its midline crossing.
notes.E: The splenic vein passes behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.

questions.stem: The elastic recoil that keeps blood flowing in diastole is a property mainly of the:
questions.why: The aorta and other large elastic arteries distend as the ventricle ejects and store energy in the elastic lamellae of their media. Recoiling in diastole sustains pressure and forward flow.

notes.A: Arterioles and small arteries chiefly regulate resistance by varying smooth muscle tone, with less capacity to store elastic energy.
notes.B: Capillaries specialise in exchange and venules collect their outflow after the arterial pressure pulse has largely been damped.
notes.D: Medium veins collect blood at low pressure and return it with the help of valves and surrounding muscle movement.
notes.E: Muscular arteries distribute blood and adjust their calibre through smooth muscle, whereas elastic arteries supply most arterial recoil.

questions.stem: An example of an actual (true) arterial anastomosis is between the:

options.label: B
options.text: segmental branches of the renal artery

options.label: C
options.text: segmental branches of the splenic artery

options.label: D
options.text: labial branches of the facial arteries

questions.why: The right and left labial branches of the facial arteries unite across the midline of the lips. Their patent connections allow blood to pass between the two arterial territories.

notes.A: Small coronary collaterals exist but may carry too little blood to rescue myocardium after a sudden blockage.
notes.B: Segmental renal branches have little effective collateral supply, so obstruction may infarct the supplied wedge of kidney.
notes.C: Splenic arterial segments have limited cross-connections, which permits segmental resection and leaves little immediate collateral flow.
notes.E: The central retinal artery has limited effective collateral flow, so its occlusion interrupts perfusion of the inner retina.

questions.stem: Sudden blockage of a coronary artery often causes infarction because its anastomoses are:
questions.why: Coronary branches have small collateral connections that can enlarge when narrowing develops gradually. An abrupt blockage may leave those channels too small to deliver enough blood, causing ischaemia and ultimately infarction.

notes.A: Coronary collateral channels are demonstrable and vary in size and functional capacity between individuals.
notes.B: These collateral routes connect arterial branches and can redistribute oxygenated blood between adjacent myocardial territories.
notes.C: The problem is insufficient collateral calibre after abrupt occlusion, which limits how much flow can reach the threatened myocardium.
notes.D: Collateral channels may occur at several depths, but their calibre determines whether they can deliver enough blood.

questions.stem: The aortic sinuses (of Valsalva) give origin to the:
questions.why: The right and left coronary ostia open in the corresponding aortic sinuses just above the valve cusps, giving the myocardium its arterial supply. The third sinus ordinarily has no coronary ostium.

notes.B: The brachiocephalic trunk arises as the first major branch of the aortic arch, distal to the ascending aorta.
notes.C: Bronchial arteries usually originate from the descending thoracic aorta or one of its branches and supply the airways.
notes.D: The pericardiacophrenic arteries are branches of the internal thoracic arteries and travel with the phrenic nerves.
notes.E: Each internal thoracic artery arises from the subclavian artery and descends along the inside of the anterior chest wall.

questions.stem: The ascending aorta begins at the level of the:
questions.why: The ascending aorta begins at the aortic valve and left ventricular outflow, projected behind the lower border of the left third costal cartilage. It then ascends to the right towards the arch.

notes.A: The left second cartilage is higher than the aortic root and is commonly used to mark the pulmonary auscultation area.
notes.C: The sternal-angle plane approximates the transition to the arch, above the level of the left ventricular outflow.
notes.D: The aortic root projects to the left of the sternum, although the ascending aorta curves towards the right as it rises.
notes.E: The arch meets the descending aorta around the lower border of T4, posterior to the anterior chest wall landmark of the root.

questions.stem: The arch of the aorta ends at the:

options.label: A
options.text: right side of the body of T2

options.label: C
options.text: left side of the body of T4

questions.why: The arch curves backwards over the left lung root and continues as the descending thoracic aorta on the left of the T4 body, near its lower border at the sternal-angle plane.

notes.A: The arch passes to the left of the trachea and meets the descending aorta on the left at about T4.
notes.B: At T6 the thoracic aorta is already descending in the posterior mediastinum, below the end of the arch.
notes.D: Near T12 the descending thoracic aorta traverses the aortic hiatus and becomes abdominal, far below the arch.
notes.E: The right second costal cartilage marks the anterior transition from ascending aorta to arch rather than its posterior end.

questions.stem: The baroreceptors of the aortic arch lie in its:
questions.why: Sensory endings in the outer aortic wall detect arterial distension and send afferent signals towards the brainstem through the vagus. Their firing increases as the vessel wall stretches.

notes.A: The intima is the innermost coat next to the blood, while the sensory endings are concentrated in the outer wall.
notes.B: The media uses elastic lamellae and smooth muscle to bear pressure and transmit distension to endings in the adventitia.
notes.C: Endothelium forms the blood-contacting lining of the intima and senses shear, but is not the location of these nerve endings.
notes.E: Vasa vasorum deliver blood to the outer layers of the aorta, while baroreceptors are mechanosensitive nerve endings in that region.

questions.stem: The ligamentum arteriosum connects the arch of the aorta to the:
questions.why: The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, spanning the inferior aortic arch and proximal left pulmonary artery. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the arch nearby.

notes.A: The right pulmonary artery crosses the mediastinum behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava to reach the right lung.
notes.B: The left main bronchus passes under the arch to the left lung, close to the ligament but without forming its attachment.
notes.C: The left subclavian artery is a branch of the superior aspect of the arch near the aortic attachment of the ligament.
notes.D: The superior vena cava is a right-sided vein that returns blood to the right atrium and is separate from the fetal arterial shunt.

questions.stem: Which pulmonary artery is longer and wider?

options.label: A
options.text: Right, passing under the aortic arch

options.label: B
options.text: Left, passing under the aortic arch

options.label: C
options.text: Right, passing in front of the SVC

questions.why: It passes behind the ascending aorta and SVC to the right lung.

notes.B: The left is shorter.
notes.C: It passes BEHIND the SVC.
notes.D: Not its course.
notes.E: They differ.

questions.stem: The posterior intercostal arteries from the thoracic aorta supply which spaces?
questions.why: The descending thoracic aorta supplies the third through eleventh posterior intercostal spaces. The first two normally receive branches from the supreme intercostal artery, and the subcostal arteries run below rib 12.

notes.A: The first two posterior spaces are usually supplied by the supreme intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk.
notes.C: The first and second spaces form the usual territory of the supreme intercostal artery instead of the descending aorta.
notes.D: The second posterior space is usually outside the direct aortic series, and the vessel below rib 12 is called subcostal.
notes.E: The direct aortic series extends from the third intercostal space to the eleventh, above the subcostal vessel.

questions.stem: The aorta enters the abdomen at the level of:
questions.why: The thoracic aorta reaches the abdomen through the aortic hiatus at T12. It passes between the crura, posterior to the median arcuate ligament, rather than piercing the muscular dome.

notes.A: The oesophageal hiatus is at about T10 and also transmits the vagal trunks as they pass towards the stomach.
notes.B: The caval opening through the central tendon is at about T8 and transmits the inferior vena cava.
notes.D: The aorta is already abdominal at L1, near the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
notes.E: The common iliac arteries begin near L4 where the abdominal aorta bifurcates, several levels below the diaphragm.

questions.stem: The abdominal aorta divides into the common iliac arteries at the level of:

options.label: C
options.text: S1, at the sacral promontory level

options.label: D
options.text: L4, slightly left of the midline

questions.why: The abdominal aorta usually bifurcates near the fourth lumbar vertebral body, slightly left of the midline. The two common iliac arteries descend towards the pelvic brim, where they divide again.

notes.A: The upper lumbar level near L1 is where the superior mesenteric artery arises, above the termination of the aorta.
notes.B: The inferior mesenteric artery leaves the aorta near L3, and the umbilicus is a variable surface landmark.
notes.C: The sacral promontory lies below the usual aortic bifurcation and near the level at which the common iliac arteries divide.
notes.E: The aortic bifurcation can vary in height, but is usually near L4 and slightly to the left of midline.

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the pelvic viscera?
questions.why: The internal iliac artery enters the pelvis and gives visceral branches to organs such as the bladder and reproductive tract. It also supplies parts of the pelvic wall, perineum and gluteal region.

notes.A: The external iliac artery runs towards the inguinal ligament and continues as the femoral artery to supply the lower limb.
notes.B: The common iliac artery is the parent trunk that divides into internal and external iliac arteries near the pelvic brim.
notes.C: The median sacral artery descends on the midline over the sacrum and supplies a small posterior pelvic territory.
notes.D: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut, including the upper rectum, but the main arterial source for pelvic viscera is internal iliac.

questions.stem: The middle colic artery is a branch of the:
questions.why: The middle colic artery arises from the superior mesenteric artery and travels in the transverse mesocolon, chiefly supplying the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, which is derived from midgut.

notes.B: The inferior mesenteric artery gives the left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal branches to the hindgut territory.
notes.C: The coeliac trunk supplies foregut organs such as the stomach, proximal duodenum and liver through its three principal branches.
notes.D: The common hepatic artery provides blood to the liver and via the gastroduodenal artery to the proximal duodenum.
notes.E: The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature and lower oesophagus, outside the superior mesenteric territory.

questions.stem: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the:
questions.why: After giving off left colic and sigmoid branches, the inferior mesenteric artery continues into the pelvis as the superior rectal artery. This vessel supplies the upper rectum.

notes.A: The internal iliac artery may give rise to the middle rectal artery, which supplies part of the rectum from the side.
notes.C: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut and terminates in ileal and ileocolic territories, proximal to the rectum.
notes.D: The median sacral artery follows the front of the sacrum and supplies neighbouring tissues rather than forming the main superior rectal artery.
notes.E: The external iliac artery runs to the lower limb and becomes the femoral artery beneath the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: The arterial supply of the gut changes from the SMA to the IMA at the:

options.label: A
options.text: ileocaecal junction of the right colon

options.label: B
options.text: hepatic flexure of the ascending colon

options.label: C
options.text: distal third of the transverse colon

options.label: D
options.text: junction of descending and sigmoid colon

options.label: E
options.text: duodenojejunal flexure of the small gut

questions.why: The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon belongs to the midgut territory supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The distal third belongs to the hindgut territory supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.

notes.A: The terminal ileum and caecum are both in the superior mesenteric territory and receive branches of the ileocolic artery.
notes.B: The hepatic flexure lies in the proximal part of the colonic circuit, where both adjacent regions receive superior mesenteric branches.
notes.D: The descending and sigmoid colon both receive inferior mesenteric branches, so their junction is already within hindgut territory.
notes.E: The duodenojejunal flexure lies in the small intestine, well proximal to the transition between the two large bowel arterial territories.

questions.stem: The marginal artery is formed by anastomoses along the:
questions.why: The marginal artery runs along the mesenteric border of the colon. It links successive colic branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, providing a collateral route between their territories.

notes.A: The greater curvature is supplied by the right and left gastro-omental vessels, which join along the stomach wall.
notes.B: The right and left gastric arteries join along the lesser gastric curvature as part of the coeliac circulation.
notes.C: Jejunal arterial arcades are loops in the small bowel mesentery that deliver blood to the jejunum via vasa recta.
notes.E: The oesophagus has an arterial network supplied by cervical, thoracic and abdominal sources, separate from the colonic arcade.

questions.stem: The left renal vein usually passes:

options.label: A
options.text: behind the aorta, above the coeliac trunk

options.label: B
options.text: in front of the SMA at the L1 level

options.label: C
options.text: behind the IVC near the renal hilum

options.label: D
options.text: in front of the IVC, below the renal artery

options.label: E
options.text: in front of the aorta, below the SMA

questions.why: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta and posterior to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery on its way to the cava. Compression in that angle can impair renal venous drainage.

notes.A: A retroaortic left renal vein is a variant and ordinarily crosses near the level of the renal hilum, below the coeliac origin.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery is anterior to the vein and can compress it against the aorta from the front.
notes.C: The vein enters the cava on its left side after crossing the aorta, whereas the right renal artery normally passes behind the cava.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava receives the vein at its lateral wall, after the vein has already crossed the anterior aorta.

questions.stem: A catheter for pulmonary artery monitoring reaches the right atrium most commonly through the:

options.label: C
options.text: great saphenous or common femoral vein

questions.why: The right internal jugular vein gives a comparatively direct route to the superior vena cava and right atrium. Subclavian access also travels through the brachiocephalic vein to the superior vena cava.

notes.B: The femoral and radial arteries lead towards the aorta and cannot provide the usual venous route into the right atrium.
notes.C: The common femoral vein is an alternative through the inferior vena cava, while great saphenous access is uncommon for this catheter.
notes.D: Arm veins can be used for some right-heart catheterisations, but the internal jugular and subclavian veins offer standard central routes.
notes.E: The facial vein usually drains indirectly into the internal jugular, and the external jugular is less direct than usual central access.

questions.stem: Portocaval anastomoses are clinically important because in portal hypertension they:

options.label: C
options.text: divert blood into the pulmonary veins

options.label: D
options.text: raise pressure in the coronary sinus

questions.why: High portal pressure diverts blood through pre-existing links to systemic veins. These channels may enlarge into fragile varices, especially around the lower oesophagus, where rupture can cause major haemorrhage.

notes.A: The collateral veins dilate to carry blood around the portal obstruction, creating a route for drainage rather than blocking gut arteries.
notes.C: Lower oesophageal collaterals drain into the azygos system, part of the systemic venous circulation, rather than the pulmonary veins.
notes.D: The coronary sinus drains cardiac muscle into the right atrium and is not part of the usual portal collateral pathways.
notes.E: The characteristic lesions are enlarged veins under elevated portal pressure, while an aneurysm involves a separate dilation of a vessel wall.

questions.stem: Continuous capillaries are typical of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: Glomerular endothelial cells contain fenestrations that allow rapid passage of water and small solutes across the filtration barrier. The basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms provide additional selectivity.

notes.A: Most skeletal muscle capillaries have an uninterrupted endothelium and support exchange without endothelial fenestrations.
notes.B: Alveolar capillary endothelium is continuous and lies close to the alveolar epithelium, giving a short diffusion path for gases.
notes.D: Adipose capillaries generally have continuous endothelium and transport substrates across a bounded endothelial barrier.
notes.E: Most central nervous system capillaries have continuous endothelium sealed by tight junctions, which helps limit paracellular exchange.

questions.stem: Fenestrated capillaries are characteristic of the:
questions.why: Fenestrae in villous capillaries allow absorbed water-soluble nutrients to enter the bloodstream efficiently. Most long-chain dietary lipids use the villous lacteals after packaging into chylomicrons.

notes.A: Skeletal muscle usually has continuous capillaries for controlled exchange across an uninterrupted endothelial wall.
notes.B: Brain capillaries generally use tight junctions and lack fenestrations to maintain the blood–brain barrier.
notes.C: Hepatic sinusoids are discontinuous capillaries with fenestrae and an incomplete basal lamina, allowing exchange with hepatocytes.
notes.E: Bone marrow contains discontinuous venous sinusoids that allow mature blood cells to enter the circulation.

questions.stem: The blood–brain barrier depends on brain capillaries that:
questions.why: Tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells remove the open paracellular route typical of many peripheral capillaries. Most polar substances therefore need selective transport across the endothelial cells to reach brain tissue.

notes.A: Large fenestrae would increase permeability, whereas most brain capillaries have a continuous, non-fenestrated endothelial lining.
notes.B: Discontinuous endothelium is typical of certain sinusoids and would provide an unsuitable barrier to circulating solutes.
notes.C: The endothelium itself forms the principal physical blood–brain barrier, supported by pericytes and astrocytic end-feet.
notes.D: Valves are features of certain veins, while brain capillary permeability depends on the endothelial cells and their junctions.

questions.stem: Red cells pass through capillaries in single file because the capillary diameter is about:
questions.why: A typical capillary lumen is roughly 7–10 µm, close to the diameter of a red cell. The cells often deform to pass singly through narrower regions, which brings them close to the exchange surface.

notes.B: A 20–30 µm lumen could accommodate several red cells side by side and is nearer the calibre of a larger microvessel.
notes.C: A calibre of 0.1–1 mm is far wider than a red cell and occurs in small arteries or veins.
notes.D: A diameter of 1–2 µm is far below the usual width of a functional capillary and would make erythrocyte transit difficult.
notes.E: A 50–100 µm lumen is typical of a larger arteriole or venule and has ample room for more than one red cell across.

questions.stem: The deep veins that accompany limb arteries in pairs are called:
questions.why: Venae comitantes are deep accompanying veins, often paired around a medium-sized artery in a limb. They share its connective tissue bed, and nearby arterial pulsation can help propel venous blood.

notes.A: Perforating veins pass through the deep fascia to connect the superficial venous system with deep veins.
notes.C: Emissary veins connect extracranial veins to intracranial dural venous sinuses through openings in the skull.
notes.D: Vasa vasorum are small vessels that nourish the walls of larger arteries and veins, rather than paired veins accompanying an artery.
notes.E: Communicating veins link veins to other veins, often within the same system, without implying a paired relationship to an artery.

questions.stem: The pulse felt just in front of the tragus of the ear is from the:
questions.why: The superficial temporal artery crosses the zygomatic arch just anterior to the ear. Its pulse is palpable there because the artery runs close to the skin over bone.

notes.A: The facial artery pulse can be felt where it crosses the lower border of the mandible just anterior to the masseter.
notes.B: The occipital artery supplies the posterior scalp and is palpated behind the head, away from the anterior aspect of the tragus.
notes.D: The posterior auricular artery runs behind the auricle between the ear and mastoid region, on the opposite side of that landmark.
notes.E: The maxillary artery runs deep to the mandibular ramus into the infratemporal region and is not accessible at this surface point.

questions.stem: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt:

options.label: A
options.text: behind the medial malleolus at the ankle

options.label: B
options.text: deep in the roof of the popliteal fossa

options.label: C
options.text: at the midinguinal point below the ligament

options.label: D
options.text: on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to EHL

options.label: E
options.text: below and behind the lateral malleolus

questions.why: The dorsalis pedis artery continues the anterior tibial artery onto the dorsum of the foot. Its pulse is usually sought just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

notes.A: Behind the medial malleolus lies the posterior tibial artery, which reaches the plantar foot through the tarsal tunnel.
notes.B: The popliteal pulse is sought deep in the popliteal fossa at the back of the knee, far proximal to the dorsum of the foot.
notes.C: The femoral pulse is felt just below the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, where the artery enters the thigh.
notes.E: The region behind the lateral malleolus contains fibular tendons and sural nerve structures, without the dorsal arterial pulse.

questions.stem: A "bovine arch" of the aorta is one in which:

options.label: A
options.text: the arch passes to the right of the trachea

options.label: B
options.text: the left vertebral artery arises from the arch

options.label: C
options.text: the right subclavian arises last from the arch

options.label: D
options.text: the left subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic

options.label: E
options.text: brachiocephalic and left carotid share an origin

questions.why: In this common aortic arch variant, the brachiocephalic trunk and left common carotid artery share a proximal origin. There are therefore fewer separate ostia than in the standard three-branch arrangement.

notes.A: A right-sided arch describes the course of the arch relative to the trachea, rather than a common origin of arch branches.
notes.B: The left vertebral artery can originate directly from the arch, which adds a distinct branch rather than combining two origins.
notes.C: An aberrant right subclavian artery often arises as the last branch of the arch and passes behind the oesophagus.
notes.D: The left subclavian normally arises independently and remains separate from the shared brachiocephalic and left carotid origin in this pattern.

questions.stem: In the fetus, blood bypasses the lungs from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta through the:
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus carries blood from the pulmonary arterial outflow to the aorta while fetal pulmonary resistance is high. After birth it normally closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

notes.B: The ductus venosus conveys much of the oxygenated umbilical venous blood past the fetal liver towards the inferior vena cava.
notes.C: The foramen ovale allows right-to-left flow between the fetal atria, upstream of the pulmonary trunk.
notes.D: The umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta to the fetus and then drains into the hepatic venous pathways.
notes.E: The crista dividens is associated with the atrial septum and helps direct fetal blood towards the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: The fetal ductus venosus allows blood to bypass the:
questions.why: The ductus venosus links the intrahepatic umbilical venous route to the inferior vena cava near the hepatic veins. It lets a substantial fraction of placental blood reach the heart without passing through hepatic sinusoids.

notes.A: The ductus arteriosus diverts pulmonary arterial blood to the aorta, bypassing the fetal pulmonary capillary bed.
notes.C: The foramen ovale lets blood cross from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the right ventricle on that route.
notes.D: Fetal kidneys receive blood from renal arterial branches of the aorta, separate from the hepatic venous shunt.
notes.E: The left atrium receives blood shunted through the foramen ovale, downstream of venous blood returning to the right atrium.

questions.stem: The left pulmonary artery lies in front of the:

options.label: B
options.text: arch of the aorta and the thymus

questions.why: It is joined to the arch by the ligamentum arteriosum.

notes.A: Below and behind.
notes.B: It lies below the arch; thymus is in front.
notes.D: Above.
notes.E: The right PA passes behind these.

questions.stem: The right renal artery passes:
questions.why: The right renal artery must cross farther than the left because the aorta lies left of the inferior vena cava. It runs posterior to the cava on its way to the right renal hilum.

notes.A: The inferior vena cava lies anterior to the right renal artery where the artery crosses rightward towards the kidney.
notes.B: The right renal artery originates from the lateral aorta, while the left renal vein is the vessel that crosses anterior to it.
notes.C: The renal pelvis lies posterior to the major renal vessels at the hilum and leads inferiorly into the ureter.
notes.E: The renal arteries originate below the coeliac trunk and generally just inferior to the superior mesenteric origin.

questions.stem: The SMA crosses anterior to which part of the duodenum?
questions.why: The third part of the duodenum crosses the posterior abdominal wall horizontally. The superior mesenteric vessels pass in front of it, and the aorta lies behind it, making this segment vulnerable to vascular compression.

notes.A: The first part begins at the pylorus and takes a superior rightward course above the horizontal segment crossed by the mesenteric root.
notes.B: The second part descends on the right of the pancreatic head and contains the opening of the bile and pancreatic ducts.
notes.C: The fourth part ascends on the left of the aorta towards the duodenojejunal flexure, beyond the horizontal crossing.
notes.D: The duodenal cap is the widened proximal part immediately after the pylorus, upstream of the mesenteric vessels' crossing.

questions.stem: The inferior phrenic arteries supply the diaphragm and the:
questions.why: The inferior phrenic arteries supply the undersurface of the diaphragm. Small oesophageal branches, particularly from the left inferior phrenic artery, can also supply the short abdominal segment of the oesophagus.

notes.B: The spleen receives its main supply from the splenic artery, which reaches its hilum along the upper border of the pancreas.
notes.C: The gallbladder usually receives blood from the cystic artery, most commonly a branch of the right hepatic artery.
notes.D: The proximal rectum is supplied by the superior rectal artery, the downward continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery.
notes.E: The proximal duodenum receives branches from the gastroduodenal and neighbouring arteries, including superior pancreaticoduodenal branches.

questions.stem: The gallbladder and duodenum are supplied through branches of the:
questions.why: The common hepatic artery gives the gastroduodenal artery, which supplies the proximal duodenum, and continues as the proper hepatic artery. The right hepatic branch of the proper hepatic artery usually gives the cystic artery to the gallbladder.

notes.A: The splenic artery supplies the spleen and gives pancreatic and gastric branches rather than the usual cystic artery.
notes.C: The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature and abdominal oesophagus through branches of the coeliac circulation.
notes.D: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures, which lie distal to the gallbladder and duodenum.
notes.E: The middle colic artery is a superior mesenteric branch to the transverse colon, with a separate arterial territory.

questions.stem: Which is a paired (lateral) branch of the abdominal aorta?
questions.why: Each middle suprarenal artery usually arises separately from the lateral abdominal aorta and travels to its ipsilateral adrenal gland. It supplements superior branches from the inferior phrenic artery and inferior branches from the renal artery.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk is a single anterior branch that divides to supply the main foregut organs.
notes.B: The inferior mesenteric artery arises as a single anterior vessel and sends branches to the hindgut.
notes.D: The median sacral artery typically arises posteriorly near the aortic bifurcation and descends as a single midline vessel.
notes.E: The superior mesenteric artery arises from the front of the aorta as a single trunk to the midgut.

questions.stem: The inferior mesenteric artery arises at the level of:
questions.why: The inferior mesenteric artery typically branches from the abdominal aorta near L3, below the renal arteries and above the common iliac bifurcation. It provides the major arterial supply to the hindgut.

notes.A: The superior mesenteric artery originates around L1, above the main arterial supply to the hindgut.
notes.B: The aorta passes through the diaphragm around T12 and gives off the coeliac trunk just below that level.
notes.C: The common iliac arteries are formed by the aortic bifurcation around L4, below the inferior mesenteric origin.
notes.E: Renal arteries arise near L1–L2 depending on the individual, above the usual origin of the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: The appendicular artery usually arises from the:
questions.why: The appendicular artery usually arises from the ileocolic arterial tree and reaches the appendix through the mesoappendix. Its supply is important because the appendix has limited alternative flow once this artery is compromised.

notes.A: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon from the superior mesenteric circulation, while appendicular supply typically comes from ileocolic branches.
notes.B: The middle colic artery runs in the transverse mesocolon to supply the proximal transverse colon rather than the caecal region.
notes.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies distal colon and upper rectum, outside the midgut territory of the appendix.
notes.D: The left colic artery comes from the inferior mesenteric artery to supply the descending and adjacent transverse colon.

questions.stem: The short gastric arteries arise from the:
questions.why: Several small branches of the splenic artery cross the gastrosplenic ligament to reach the upper greater curvature and fundus. Their short course across that ligament gives them their name.

notes.B: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature and supplies the cardia and distal oesophagus.
notes.C: The common hepatic artery mainly supplies hepatic and gastroduodenal branches rather than the short vessels crossing the gastrosplenic ligament.
notes.D: The gastroduodenal artery gives the right gastro-omental branch for the greater curvature and pancreaticoduodenal branches for the proximal duodenum.
notes.E: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, whereas the stomach receives its main supply from the coeliac circulation.

questions.stem: Caput medusae in portal hypertension results from the portocaval anastomosis at the:
questions.why: Elevated portal pressure can send blood from the left portal vein through paraumbilical veins towards systemic veins of the abdominal wall. Their enlargement produces the radiating periumbilical pattern called caput medusae.

notes.A: Oesophageal tributaries link the left gastric vein and azygos system, so dilation produces distal oesophageal varices.
notes.C: The upper rectal portal drainage communicates with systemic rectal veins, creating a route for anorectal varices.
notes.D: Retroperitoneal veins can divert portal blood from colonic branches to systemic lumbar veins without producing superficial periumbilical dilation.
notes.E: The splenic hilum contains tributaries of the splenic vein and is remote from the subcutaneous abdominal veins that form the sign.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the four sites of portocaval anastomosis?
questions.why: The portocaval anastomoses are at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region and retroperitoneum; the pulmonary hilum has no portal-systemic connection.

notes.A: Lower oesophageal veins connect the left gastric vein of the portal system with tributaries of the azygos system.
notes.B: Paraumbilical veins link the portal system to abdominal wall veins, a pathway that can enlarge around the umbilicus.
notes.D: Rectal venous plexuses connect portal superior rectal drainage to systemic middle and inferior rectal veins.
notes.E: Colonic tributaries form connections with systemic retroperitoneal veins where the colon contacts the posterior abdominal wall.

questions.stem: If the IVC is blocked below the renal veins, blood can return to the heart mainly through the:

options.label: A
options.text: pulmonary veins to the left atrium

questions.why: Ascending lumbar veins can receive blood from below an inferior caval obstruction. They connect with the azygos and hemiazygos systems, which carry that blood towards the superior vena cava and right atrium.

notes.A: Pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium after it has passed through the right heart and lung capillaries.
notes.B: The coronary sinus collects blood from cardiac veins, rather than receiving collateral flow from the abdomen.
notes.C: Some abdominal collaterals can involve portal tributaries, but the direct posterior connection to the superior vena cava uses ascending lumbar and azygos veins.
notes.E: Jugular veins drain the head and neck and have no direct collateral connection to the lower inferior caval territory.

questions.stem: The left gonadal vein usually drains into the:
questions.why: The left gonadal vein ascends to the left renal vein, which carries its blood across the aorta to the inferior vena cava. The right gonadal vein usually enters the cava directly.

notes.A: Direct drainage into the inferior vena cava is usual for the right gonadal vein, while the left generally uses the renal vein.
notes.B: The left common iliac vein drains the lower limb and pelvis, while normal left gonadal drainage enters a vein higher in the abdomen.
notes.C: The left suprarenal vein also drains into the left renal vein, as a separate tributary from the adrenal gland.
notes.D: The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein and belongs to the hepatic portal circulation.

questions.stem: The brachiocephalic vein is formed by the union of the:
questions.why: On each side the internal jugular vein meets the subclavian vein behind the sternoclavicular joint. This junction forms the brachiocephalic vein, and the right and left brachiocephalic veins subsequently unite as the superior vena cava.

notes.B: The external jugular usually empties into the subclavian vein, and the axillary vein has already become subclavian at the first rib.
notes.C: The right and left internal jugular veins each join a subclavian vein on their own side and do not join one another.
notes.D: The axillary vein changes name to subclavian at the lateral border of the first rib and is continuous with it.
notes.E: The hemiazygos vein usually drains across to the azygos vein, which arches into the superior vena cava.

questions.stem: Which artery is a branch of the internal carotid?
questions.why: The ophthalmic artery usually branches from the intracranial internal carotid artery and travels with the optic nerve through the optic canal. It provides much of the blood supply to the orbit.

notes.A: The facial artery springs from the external carotid and supplies much of the superficial face after crossing the mandible.
notes.C: The lingual artery arises from the external carotid and passes deep to hyoglossus to supply the tongue.
notes.D: The superior thyroid artery typically arises low on the external carotid and supplies the superior part of the thyroid gland and neighbouring structures.
notes.E: The maxillary artery is a terminal external carotid branch that supplies deep facial, nasal and meningeal structures.

questions.stem: The vertebral artery arises from the:
questions.why: The vertebral artery typically arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It ascends through cervical transverse foramina, enters the skull through the foramen magnum, and joins its fellow to form the basilar artery.

notes.A: The common carotid usually terminates by dividing into the internal and external carotid arteries, separate from the vertebral system.
notes.B: The external carotid supplies most extracranial head and neck structures through branches such as facial and lingual arteries.
notes.D: The brachiocephalic trunk normally gives the right common carotid and right subclavian, with the right vertebral arising downstream from subclavian.
notes.E: Direct origin from the aortic arch is a recognised left vertebral variant, while the usual origin on either side is subclavian.

questions.stem: The ascending aorta lies with the SVC on its right and the:
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk lies to the left of the ascending aorta, and both lie within the fibrous pericardium.

notes.A: The oesophagus runs posterior to the trachea and heart, away from the anterior surface of the ascending aorta.
notes.B: The left atrium lies chiefly posterior in the heart and receives pulmonary veins, rather than occupying the space beside the superior vena cava.
notes.C: Thymic tissue or its remnants lie behind the sternum, anterior to the pericardium and adjacent great vessels.
notes.E: The trachea lies behind the anterior great vessels, with its bifurcation roughly at the sternal-angle plane.

questions.stem: The three circulatory systems are the pulmonary, the systemic (caval) and the:
questions.why: The three circulations are the pulmonary, the systemic (caval) and the portal; the portal system passes through a second (hepatic) capillary bed before returning blood to the heart.

notes.A: Not one of the three as taught.
notes.B: Part of the systemic.
notes.C: Part of the systemic.
notes.D: Not one of the three.

questions.stem: The tunica media of arteries and veins is composed mainly of:
questions.why: Smooth muscle is a defining component of the tunica media and changes vessel calibre as it contracts or relaxes. Elastic lamellae are prominent in elastic arteries, and veins generally have a thinner media.

notes.B: Collagen provides tensile strength and is particularly abundant in the adventitia, while medial smooth muscle actively changes vessel diameter.
notes.C: Simple squamous endothelial cells face the blood and constitute the luminal lining of the tunica intima.
notes.D: Loose connective tissue commonly supports vessels externally, whereas smooth muscle is organised into layers in the media.
notes.E: Elastic arteries contain extracellular elastic lamellae in their media, which are distinct from the cartilage found in structures such as the auricle.

questions.stem: The tunica intima consists of the endothelium and:

options.label: A
options.text: a thick layer of circular smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.text: an elastic lamina in collagenous tissue

options.label: C
options.text: a layer of loose fatty tissue

questions.why: The endothelium is simple squamous epithelium lining all vessels.

notes.A: Media.
notes.C: Adventitia.
notes.D: Not in vessels.
notes.E: Outer coats.

questions.stem: In the vascular lecture, an arteriovenous shunt is also called a:
questions.why: Blood passes from arteriole to venule directly.

notes.A: A capillary type.
notes.B: Deep companion vein.
notes.D: Alternative arterial route.
notes.E: Vessels of vessel walls.

questions.stem: In continuous capillaries, adjacent endothelial cells are:

options.label: A
options.text: widely separated, with large open gaps

options.label: B
options.text: loosely joined, with many large pores

questions.why: In most continuous capillaries the endothelial lining is uninterrupted, although narrow intercellular clefts allow limited exchange. In brain capillaries, tight junctions largely close this pathway and increase control over solute movement.

notes.A: Large gaps are characteristic of some discontinuous sinusoids, whose permeability exceeds that of continuous capillaries.
notes.B: Endothelial fenestrations allow rapid movement across cells in specialised beds such as intestinal villi and renal glomeruli.
notes.C: Capillary walls have a single endothelial layer, keeping the diffusion distance between blood and interstitial tissue short.
notes.E: Pericytes may lie outside the endothelial layer, but endothelial junctions link neighbouring cells rather than smooth muscle.

questions.stem: According to the vascular lecture, sinusoids are found in the liver, bone marrow, spleen and:
questions.why: The adrenal medulla contains wide sinusoidal vessels around chromaffin cell clusters. Their fenestrated endothelium facilitates uptake of secreted catecholamines into blood, although sinusoidal permeability and basement membrane structure depend on the organ.

notes.A: Renal glomeruli have fenestrated endothelial cells organised around a specialised basement membrane and podocyte filtration layer.
notes.B: The thyroid uses fenestrated capillaries around follicles to take up thyroid hormones, rather than the medullary sinusoidal arrangement of adrenal tissue.
notes.C: Villous capillaries have fenestrations that support nutrient absorption, while a separate lacteal carries chylomicrons.
notes.D: Most cerebral cortical capillaries have continuous endothelium with tight junctions, restricting transfer into the surrounding neural tissue.

questions.stem: Venous valves, which prevent reflux, are common in veins of the:
questions.why: Valves are numerous in the veins of the limbs (and are also found in the neck), opposing gravity to aid venous return; they are sparse or absent in the great central veins and viscera.

notes.B: Dural venous sinuses and many cerebral veins lack valves, allowing drainage between communicating intracranial channels.
notes.C: The hepatic portal circulation is generally valveless, so pressure can be transmitted to vessels draining the gut.
notes.D: Pulmonary veins generally have no valves, and the major cardiac valves regulate flow through the heart chambers.
notes.E: Renal and splenic venous channels are generally valveless and carry blood down pressure gradients rather than through a series of valves.

questions.stem: Which is NOT on the list of palpable arteries used clinically?
questions.why: Listed: temporal, carotid, facial, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis.

notes.A: Listed.
notes.C: Listed.
notes.D: Listed.
notes.E: Listed.

questions.stem: Anastomoses between arteries are valuable because, if one artery is blocked, they:

options.label: D
options.text: reduce the oxygen needs of tissue

options.label: E
options.text: convert the artery into a vein

questions.why: An effective arterial anastomosis provides a second inflow route to the tissue beyond a blockage. If the collateral vessels can supply enough oxygenated blood, they can prevent ischaemic necrosis.

notes.A: Local collateral flow redistributes blood between neighbouring arterial territories without requiring an increase in systemic pressure.
notes.B: The alternate route supplies capillaries, and their venous drainage is needed to carry away blood from the tissue.
notes.D: Anastomoses preserve oxygen delivery by carrying blood around the blockage, while the tissue's metabolic demand remains.
notes.E: These channels connect arteries to other arteries and preserve their arterial role without changing the original vessel type.

questions.stem: The ascending aorta ends, and the arch begins, at the level of the:
questions.why: The ascending aorta rises from the aortic valve to the level of the manubriosternal joint, near the right second costal cartilage. Here it curves posteriorly as the aortic arch.

notes.A: The third left costal cartilage approximates the start of the ascending aorta at the aortic valve.
notes.B: The xiphisternal joint is at the lower end of the sternal body, well below the transition into the arch.
notes.C: The descending aorta approaches the diaphragmatic hiatus around T12, several vertebral levels below the origin of the arch.
notes.E: The suprasternal notch is at the upper border of the manubrium, above the sternal-angle plane used for this landmark.

questions.stem: The branches of the aortic arch, in order from right to left, are the:

options.label: A
options.text: right subclavian, right common carotid, left subclavian

options.label: D
options.text: right carotid, left carotid, left subclavian

options.label: E
options.text: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian

questions.why: In the normal branching pattern, the first arch branch divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian then arise independently in that order.

notes.A: The first normal branch is the common parent of the two right-sided arteries, so they do not have separate arch origins.
notes.B: The left common carotid lies between the brachiocephalic trunk and the left subclavian along the usual arch.
notes.C: The brachiocephalic trunk arises closer to the ascending aorta than the left common carotid, making it the first branch.
notes.D: The right common carotid usually branches from the brachiocephalic trunk instead of joining the left-sided arteries as a separate arch branch.

questions.stem: The right subclavian artery normally arises from the:
questions.why: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first branch of the aortic arch and normally divides behind the right sternoclavicular region. Its terminal branches are the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

notes.B: A direct arch origin of the right subclavian is an anomaly, whereas the left subclavian normally arises directly from the arch.
notes.C: The right common carotid and right subclavian are branches of the brachiocephalic trunk and then pass into different territories.
notes.D: The ascending aorta normally gives off the coronary arteries near its root before continuing into the arch.
notes.E: The thyrocervical trunk usually arises from the first part of the subclavian artery, so it is a downstream branch.

questions.stem: The pulmonary trunk arises from the:

options.label: A
options.text: aortic vestibule of the left ventricle

questions.why: The infundibulum, also called the conus arteriosus, is the smooth-walled superior outflow tract of the right ventricle. Blood leaves it through the pulmonary valve and enters the pulmonary trunk.

notes.A: The aortic vestibule directs left ventricular blood through the aortic valve into the ascending aorta.
notes.C: The smooth right atrial sinus receives systemic venous return, which exits the atrium through the tricuspid valve.
notes.D: The left auricle is an atrial appendage with pectinate muscle and has no arterial outflow connection.
notes.E: The right ventricular apex is trabeculated, whereas the passage into the pulmonary trunk lies superiorly in the smooth outflow tract.

questions.stem: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth is called:
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus carries fetal blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta. If it remains open after birth it is a patent ductus arteriosus, usually permitting aortic blood to flow back towards the lungs.

notes.A: Coarctation is narrowing of the aorta, often close to where the ductus attaches, and is a different defect.
notes.B: A patent foramen ovale is an incomplete seal between the atria, anatomically separate from the persistent arterial connection.
notes.D: Persistent truncus arteriosus results when one arterial trunk supplies systemic and pulmonary circulations because the outflow fails to separate.
notes.E: Tetralogy of Fallot combines right ventricular outflow obstruction, a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: In the fetal heart, the crista dividens directs blood from the IVC through the:
questions.why: The crista dividens helps split the stream entering the right atrium from the inferior vena cava. Oxygen-rich blood from the placenta is preferentially directed through the foramen ovale into the left atrium.

notes.A: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood after it has entered the right ventricular outflow, farther downstream than the atrial stream divider.
notes.B: The ductus venosus connects the umbilical venous route to the inferior vena cava before the inflow reaches the right atrium.
notes.C: The tricuspid valve directs right atrial blood into the right ventricle, while the preferentially shunted stream crosses the atrial septum.
notes.E: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium to return blood from the myocardium and is separate from the foetal shunt.

questions.stem: The thoracic aorta becomes the abdominal aorta by passing behind the:
questions.why: The right and left crura flank the aortic hiatus near T12. The median arcuate ligament bridges between them anterior to the aorta, which continues below this level as the abdominal aorta.

notes.A: Each medial arcuate ligament arches over psoas major to the side of the aortic opening.
notes.B: Each lateral arcuate ligament arches over quadratus lumborum and extends towards the twelfth rib, well lateral to the aorta.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon near T8, while the aortic hiatus lies posterior and inferior.
notes.D: The right crus forms a side of the aortic hiatus, and the ligament connecting both crura bounds it anteriorly.

questions.stem: The subcostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta at the level of:
questions.why: The subcostal arteries are the last paired parietal branches of the descending thoracic aorta. They run below the twelfth ribs, continuing the posterior intercostal series near the T12 level.

notes.B: T10 corresponds to a higher part of the posterior intercostal series and approximates the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.C: T8 is a higher thoracic level near the caval opening, above the low origin of the subcostal arteries.
notes.D: Around T4 the aortic arch becomes the descending thoracic aorta, several levels above the subcostal vessels.
notes.E: By L1 the aorta has entered the abdomen and gives branches such as the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Which is a paired branch of the thoracic aorta?
questions.why: The right and left superior phrenic arteries arise from the lower thoracic aorta and supply the superior surface of the diaphragm. Their paired pattern reflects the body-wall territory they supply.

notes.A: Small pericardial branches supply the posterior pericardium and do not form a named right and left pair.
notes.C: Oesophageal branches leave the thoracic aorta individually along its course to supply the thoracic oesophagus.
notes.D: Mediastinal branches supply posterior mediastinal connective tissue and lymph nodes without a fixed paired arrangement.
notes.E: The median sacral artery arises as a single vessel from the abdominal aorta near its bifurcation.

questions.stem: The ventral branches of the abdominal aorta are the coeliac trunk, SMA, IMA and:
questions.why: The others listed are lateral (paired) branches.

notes.A: Paired.
notes.B: Paired.
notes.D: Paired.
notes.E: Paired.

questions.stem: Which artery is noted as having no branches before it divides?
questions.why: The common iliac artery runs from the aortic bifurcation to the pelvic brim and normally has no major named branches before dividing. It ends as the internal and external iliac arteries.

notes.A: The internal iliac gives named visceral and parietal branches to the pelvis, perineum and gluteal regions.
notes.B: The external iliac gives inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches before it passes under the inguinal ligament.
notes.C: The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut through its principal left gastric, splenic and common hepatic branches.
notes.E: The superior mesenteric artery gives multiple named jejunal, ileal and colic branches before finishing in the ileocaecal territory.

questions.stem: The left gastric artery supplies the stomach and the:
questions.why: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach and gives oesophageal branches to the lower oesophagus.

notes.A: The splenic artery supplies the spleen and gives branches to the pancreas, while the left gastric runs towards the cardia.
notes.B: Hepatic arteries supply the liver, and the cystic artery usually comes from the right hepatic to supply the gallbladder.
notes.C: The proximal duodenum receives gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal branches rather than the oesophageal branches of the left gastric.
notes.D: The transverse colon receives middle and left colic branches from the mesenteric arteries, separate from the gastric circulation.

questions.stem: The splenic artery supplies the spleen, stomach and:
questions.why: The splenic artery supplies the spleen, the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach (short gastric and left gastro-omental branches) and the body and tail of the pancreas.

notes.B: The liver receives arterial blood chiefly through the proper hepatic artery and its right and left branches.
notes.C: The gallbladder normally receives the cystic artery, most often from the right hepatic artery.
notes.D: Duodenal arterial supply is mainly from gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric branches through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades.
notes.E: A renal artery branching directly from the abdominal aorta provides the principal blood supply of the left kidney.

questions.stem: The midgut supplied by the SMA begins at the:
questions.why: The major duodenal papilla marks the usual foregut–midgut transition in the second part of the duodenum. Beyond the entry of the bile duct, superior mesenteric branches supply the midgut, with overlap across the pancreaticoduodenal arcades.

notes.A: The pylorus is at the start of the duodenum, whose proximal part still belongs to the foregut.
notes.C: The duodenojejunal flexure marks the end of the duodenum, after the arterial transition has already occurred.
notes.D: The ileocaecal valve is supplied by the ileocolic artery but lies much farther along the midgut.
notes.E: The lower oesophagus is a foregut derivative supplied by oesophageal branches, including contributions from the left gastric artery.

questions.stem: The SMA lies anterior to the left renal vein, the third part of the duodenum and the:
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery emerges from behind the pancreatic neck, then descends anterior to the uncinate process and horizontal duodenum. The left renal vein crosses behind the artery near its origin.

notes.A: The pancreatic neck lies anterior to the proximal superior mesenteric vessels, so it is in front of the artery.
notes.B: The pancreatic tail extends towards the splenic hilum on the far left, away from this central descent.
notes.D: The body of the stomach lies anterior to the pancreas across the lesser sac, rather than behind the mesenteric artery.
notes.E: The splenic vein passes behind the pancreas to join the superior mesenteric vein at the portal confluence, rather than lying under the descending artery.

questions.stem: The lowest point of the gut supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery is the:
questions.why: The inferior mesenteric artery continues as the superior rectal artery, whose terminal branches supply the upper anal canal down to the pectinate line. Below the line, inferior rectal branches provide the main supply.

notes.A: The rectosigmoid junction lies above the rectum, which still receives the descending superior rectal branch of the inferior mesenteric artery.
notes.B: The anal verge is below the pectinate line and is supplied chiefly by inferior rectal branches of the internal pudendal artery.
notes.C: The splenic flexure is near the proximal edge of hindgut blood supply and is far above the distal reach of the superior rectal artery.
notes.E: The sigmoid colon receives sigmoid arteries, but the same parent artery continues to supply more distal bowel through the superior rectal artery.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery?
questions.why: The right colic artery normally belongs to the superior mesenteric circulation and supplies the ascending colon. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal colon and upper rectum instead.

notes.A: The left colic artery normally arises from the inferior mesenteric artery and supplies the descending colon and adjacent transverse colon.
notes.B: Sigmoid arteries branch from the inferior mesenteric artery to supply the sigmoid colon through mesenteric arcades.
notes.C: The superior rectal artery is the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and supplies the proximal rectum.
notes.D: Rectosigmoid branches supply the transition from sigmoid colon to rectum within the distal inferior mesenteric territory.

questions.stem: Which is a branch of the external carotid artery?
questions.why: The lingual artery arises from the anterior aspect of the external carotid artery, usually near the greater horn of the hyoid. It passes deep to hyoglossus to reach the tongue.

notes.B: The ophthalmic artery usually arises from the internal carotid artery and enters the orbit through the optic canal.
notes.C: The anterior choroidal artery usually arises from the internal carotid and supplies deep structures including part of the internal capsule.
notes.D: The vertebral artery normally arises from the subclavian artery and enters the posterior cranial circulation.
notes.E: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the vertebral arteries and runs on the ventral surface of the pons.

questions.stem: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two:
questions.why: The paired vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity and join near the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. It ascends along the ventral pons and supplies pontine and cerebellar branches.

notes.A: The internal carotid arteries supply the anterior circulation and remain separate trunks on either side of the cerebral arterial circle.
notes.C: Posterior cerebral arteries normally arise where the basilar artery ends, so they are its terminal branches.
notes.D: Anterior cerebral arteries arise from the internal carotids and communicate through the anterior communicating artery.
notes.E: Posterior communicating arteries link internal carotid flow with posterior cerebral arteries rather than uniting to form one midline trunk.

questions.stem: The right suprarenal vein drains into the:
questions.why: The short right suprarenal vein passes directly into the adjacent inferior vena cava, an important relation during adrenal surgery. The longer left suprarenal vein generally drains into the left renal vein.

notes.A: The right renal vein drains the right kidney separately into the inferior vena cava, below the right adrenal drainage.
notes.B: The right gonadal vein normally drains independently into the inferior vena cava from a much lower origin.
notes.D: The azygos vein drains the thoracic wall towards the superior vena cava and is not the normal exit for adrenal venous blood.
notes.E: The portal vein carries blood from abdominal digestive organs and the spleen to the liver, separate from adrenal drainage.

questions.stem: The azygos vein ends by joining the:
questions.why: The azygos vein ascends beside the thoracic vertebral bodies before arching over the root of the right lung. It empties into the superior vena cava and offers a collateral route between the caval systems.

notes.A: Inferior caval territory can communicate with the azygos system through ascending lumbar veins, but the azygos terminates in the superior cava.
notes.B: The right brachiocephalic vein helps form the superior vena cava above the point where the azygos arch enters it.
notes.C: The azygos system reaches the right atrium through the superior vena cava rather than opening into the chamber independently.
notes.E: The hemiazygos usually crosses from the left to drain into the azygos vein, which then continues to the superior vena cava.

questions.stem: The carotid sinus lies at the:

options.label: B
options.text: end of the external carotid artery

options.label: E
options.text: start of the internal carotid artery

questions.why: The carotid sinus is the dilated start of the internal carotid artery; its wall has baroreceptors supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

notes.A: The brachiocephalic trunk originates from the aortic arch, well proximal to the common carotid bifurcation where the sinus is located.
notes.B: The external carotid terminates as the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries near the parotid gland, above the sinus.
notes.C: The vertebral artery usually originates from the subclavian and carries blood to the posterior cerebral circulation, separate from the carotid bifurcation.
notes.D: The aortic arch contains another group of arterial baroreceptors, whose afferents run in the vagus rather than the glossopharyngeal nerve.

questions.stem: About compact organs:

options.label: B
options.text: Their stroma encloses and supports the parenchyma

options.label: C
options.text: Trabeculae or septa from the capsule divide them into compartments

options.label: D
options.text: Their blood vessels usually enter at a hilum

notes.A: A solid organ has no single central lumen, even though its parenchyma can contain many small ducts or tubules.
notes.B: Stromal connective tissue provides structural and vascular support for the specialised cells that make up the parenchyma.
notes.C: Connective tissue extensions from the capsule can separate the parenchyma into lobes, lobules or other smaller regions.
notes.D: In many compact organs, major vessels and ducts converge at a defined hilum before distributing through the stroma.
notes.E: Some septa are incomplete, so adjacent regions can remain continuous despite division into visible lobes or lobules.

questions.why: The parenchyma of a solid organ carries out its specialised functions within a supporting stromal framework. The framework often brings vessels inward from a hilum and may partly or completely subdivide the organ.

questions.stem: The parenchyma of compact organs is arranged in all of the following patterns EXCEPT:
questions.why: Concentric coats are layers built around the central lumen of a tubular organ. In a compact organ, parenchymal cells instead form functional groups such as cords, follicles or tubules within supporting stroma.

notes.B: In some endocrine organs, secretory cells are arranged in clusters, as in the islets of the pancreas.
notes.C: The adrenal cortex provides an example of parenchymal cells arranged in long cords alongside capillaries.
notes.D: Thyroid follicles contain epithelial cells surrounding pockets of colloid within an otherwise solid gland.
notes.E: Renal tubules are functional epithelial structures within the solid kidney and do not form concentric coats around the organ itself.

questions.stem: Tubular (hollow) organs:

options.label: A
options.text: include segments of the digestive, respiratory and genitourinary tracts

options.label: B
options.text: include blood and lymphatic vascular channels

options.label: C
options.text: have epithelium immediately surrounding the central cavity

options.label: D
options.text: are usually made of three coats: mucosa, muscularis and adventitia or serosa

options.label: E
options.text: have the same number of coats and layers whatever their function

notes.A: Segments of the digestive, respiratory and genitourinary tracts are hollow organs.
notes.B: Blood and lymphatic vessels are also tubular organs.
notes.C: The mucosal epithelium lines the lumen directly.
notes.D: The usual pattern is mucosa, muscularis and an outer adventitia or serosa.
notes.E: The number of coats and layers varies with the organ's function.

questions.why: Hollow organs share a basic plan of mucosa, muscularis and adventitia or serosa around a lumen, but function decides how many coats and layers each has.

questions.stem: A tubular organ lying in a retroperitoneal area is covered externally by:
questions.why: The bare retroperitoneal surface of a hollow organ usually has an adventitia that blends with surrounding connective tissue and helps anchor it. Any surface that is peritonealised instead has a serosal covering.

notes.A: Serosa is a mesothelial covering with thin underlying connective tissue on surfaces covered by visceral peritoneum.
notes.C: A capsule encloses many solid organs and can send septa inward, whereas adventitia blends into adjacent tissues.
notes.D: Lamina propria is the connective tissue just beneath an epithelium in a mucosa, close to the lumen.
notes.E: Mesothelium lines serosal surfaces and is absent where an organ's external connective tissue blends into the retroperitoneum.

questions.stem: The system whose tubular organs typically have FOUR coats is the:
questions.why: The gastrointestinal wall is usually organised into mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and an outer serosa or adventitia. The separate submucosa provides support and carries vessels and nerves between mucosa and muscle.

notes.A: A ureter is usually described as mucosa, muscularis and adventitia, without the typical discrete gastrointestinal submucosal layer.
notes.B: Larger blood vessels have intima, media and adventitia, a wall plan organised around circulating blood.
notes.D: Reproductive ducts such as the ductus deferens have mucosa, a thick muscular coat and adventitia.
notes.E: Respiratory passages have specialised wall components such as plates or rings of cartilage, so their layers follow a different plan.

questions.stem: The mediastinum:

options.label: A
options.text: is the interpleural space in and near the midline of the chest

options.label: B
options.text: extends from the sternum to the vertebral column

options.label: C
options.text: contains almost all the thoracic viscera except the lungs

options.label: D
options.text: is divided by a plane from the sternal angle to the lower part of T4

options.label: E
options.text: has the inferior part divided into superior, middle and posterior parts

notes.A: The mediastinum occupies the space between the right and left pleural sacs near the midline of the thorax.
notes.B: Its anterior boundary is the sternum and its posterior boundary is the thoracic vertebral column.
notes.C: It houses the heart and other central thoracic structures, while the lungs occupy the pleural spaces to each side.
notes.D: The transverse plane from the sternal angle to the lower T4 region, often described at the T4–T5 disc, marks the division.
notes.E: The anterior subdivision is in front of the pericardium, the middle contains it, and the posterior lies behind it.

questions.why: The sternal-angle plane divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior portions. The inferior portion is further divided around the pericardium into anterior, middle and posterior regions.

questions.stem: The superior mediastinum contains:
