options.label: A
options.text: the arch of the aorta and its three branches

options.label: B
options.text: the brachiocephalic veins and upper half of the SVC

options.label: D
options.text: the trachea, oesophagus and thoracic duct

notes.A: The brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise from the arch within this compartment.
notes.B: The brachiocephalic veins unite here to form the superior vena cava, whose upper portion remains in the compartment.
notes.C: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches off the vagus and loops under the arch near the ligamentum arteriosum.
notes.D: The trachea, oesophagus and thoracic duct pass through this compartment on their routes between the neck and deeper thorax.
notes.E: The pericardium enclosing the heart occupies the middle mediastinum below the transverse thoracic plane.

questions.why: The superior mediastinum lies above the sternal-angle plane and conveys vital structures between the neck and lower thorax. It includes the aortic arch and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve looping beneath it.

questions.stem: Which structure lies in the middle mediastinum?
questions.why: The middle mediastinum contains the pericardium, heart and intrapericardial roots of the great vessels. The ascending aorta runs within this compartment before turning into the arch in the superior mediastinum.

notes.A: The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and then passes through the superior mediastinum towards the neck.
notes.B: The thoracic sympathetic trunks lie alongside the vertebral column, behind the central compartment that encloses the heart.
notes.C: Most of the azygos trunk ascends in the posterior mediastinum before its arch runs over the right lung root.
notes.E: The oesophagus passes from the superior into the posterior mediastinum, behind the pericardium.

questions.stem: A finger passed behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk lies in the:
questions.why: A finger behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the atria, lies in the transverse pericardial sinus, which separates the arterial from the venous end of the heart.

notes.A: The oblique sinus is a blind recess posterior to the left atrium between the pulmonary venous and caval reflections.
notes.B: The costodiaphragmatic recess lies within the pleural space where costal and diaphragmatic pleura meet below the lung.
notes.C: The coronary sulcus is an external cardiac groove separating atria from ventricles and carrying coronary vessels.
notes.D: The fossa ovalis is a depression in the interatrial septum visible within the right atrium, outside the pericardial space.

questions.stem: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial cavity that compresses the heart is called:
questions.why: Fluid accumulating under pressure in the pericardial sac limits the ability of the heart chambers to expand in diastole. This reduces ventricular filling and cardiac output, producing cardiac tamponade.

notes.B: Constrictive pericarditis impairs filling through a thickened or fibrotic pericardium, usually without an acute pressurised effusion.
notes.C: Cor pulmonale is right ventricular remodelling or failure caused by pulmonary hypertension from lung or pulmonary vascular disease.
notes.D: Myocardial hypertrophy is enlargement of the heart muscle itself, commonly in response to pressure or volume loading.
notes.E: Cardiomyopathy primarily affects the myocardium, while tamponade produces external compression from fluid in the pericardial space.

questions.stem: The normal apex beat lies in the:

options.label: A
options.text: 4th left intercostal space at the sternal border

options.label: B
options.text: 5th left intercostal space, 8–9 cm from the midline

options.label: C
options.text: 6th left intercostal space at the anterior axillary line

options.label: D
options.text: 5th right intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: E
options.text: 2nd left intercostal space near the sternum

questions.why: In a typical adult, the left ventricular apex contacts the chest around the fifth left intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line. It is usually about 8–9 cm from the midline.

notes.A: The parasternal fourth intercostal space is medial and superior to the usual site of the left ventricular impulse.
notes.C: The sixth space at the anterior axillary line is lower and more lateral than the usual adult site.
notes.D: A right parasternal impulse lies on the opposite side from the usual location of the left ventricular apex.
notes.E: The left second parasternal interspace is used to listen to the pulmonary valve and is well above the apical impulse.

questions.stem: Trabeculae carneae whose apices give rise to the chordae tendineae are the:
questions.why: The papillary muscles are the conical projections of ventricular trabeculae carneae whose apices anchor the chordae tendineae to the atrioventricular valve cusps.

notes.A: The moderator band carries part of the right bundle branch from the interventricular septum towards the anterior papillary muscle.
notes.B: Pectinate muscles form ridges in the atrial walls and auricles, away from the ventricular attachments of the chordae.
notes.D: The crista terminalis is a right atrial ridge that separates the smooth sinus venarum from the pectinate region.
notes.E: The septomarginal trabecula is another name for the moderator band, a muscular bridge in the right ventricle.

questions.stem: The mitral area of auscultation lies at the:

options.label: A
options.text: right 2nd intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: B
options.text: left 2nd intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: C
options.text: right 5th intercostal space at the sternum

options.label: D
options.text: left 5th intercostal space at the MCL

options.label: E
options.text: left 4th costal cartilage at the sternum

questions.why: The anatomical mitral valve lies opposite the left 4th costal cartilage, but it is heard best at the apex.

notes.A: The second right parasternal interspace is the usual auscultation site for the aortic valve.
notes.B: The second left parasternal interspace is the usual site for listening to the pulmonary valve.
notes.C: The tricuspid area is near the lower left sternal border, rather than a right-sided site at the fifth space.
notes.E: The mitral valve projects near the fourth left costal cartilage, but its sounds are transmitted towards the apex.

questions.stem: Which is a branch of the left coronary artery?
questions.why: The anterior interventricular artery is a major terminal branch of the left coronary artery, also called the left anterior descending artery. It travels towards the apex in the anterior interventricular groove.

notes.A: The conus artery usually branches from the proximal right coronary artery or has its own ostium in the right aortic sinus.
notes.B: The right marginal artery typically branches from the right coronary artery and supplies the free wall of the right ventricle.
notes.C: In the usual right-dominant circulation, the AV nodal branch is given off by the right coronary near the crux.
notes.D: The posterior interventricular artery is usually a right coronary branch, although it comes from the circumflex in left dominance.

questions.stem: The connective tissue framework that supports the parenchyma of a compact organ is the:
questions.why: The stroma is the connective tissue framework of a solid organ. It can include a capsule and internal septa that support specialised cells and guide blood vessels towards them.

notes.B: The mucosa lines a lumen and includes an epithelium and its associated connective tissue, as in the intestine.
notes.C: The muscularis is a muscle layer of a hollow organ that helps move its contents through the lumen.
notes.D: Serosa is a mesothelial covering with underlying connective tissue on an organ surface exposed to a serous cavity.
notes.E: Lamina propria is connective tissue located directly under a mucosal epithelium, rather than the entire framework of a solid organ.

questions.stem: The innermost coat of a tubular organ consists of:
questions.why: The mucosa.

notes.A: Muscularis.
notes.C: Serosa.
notes.D: Compact organ.
notes.E: Outer coats.

questions.stem: The plane dividing the superior from the inferior mediastinum passes from the sternal angle to the:
questions.why: The transverse thoracic plane passes from the manubriosternal joint to the T4–T5 disc, at the lower border of T4. It divides the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum.

notes.A: T2 lies above the division, within the vertebral levels bordering the superior mediastinum.
notes.B: T6 lies below the sternal-angle plane, along the vertebral boundary of the inferior mediastinum.
notes.D: T8 is near the level of the caval opening in the diaphragm, well below the sternal-angle plane.
notes.E: T1 is close to the superior thoracic aperture, which marks the upper boundary of the superior mediastinum.

questions.stem: The thymus remnant in an adult lies in the:
questions.why: After puberty the thymus gradually involutes and is largely replaced by fat. Residual tissue typically lies anterior to the great vessels in the superior mediastinum and can extend into the anterior inferior mediastinum.

notes.A: The middle mediastinum contains the heart and pericardium, while the thymic bed is anterior to the great vessels.
notes.B: The posterior mediastinum contains structures such as the descending thoracic aorta and oesophagus behind the heart.
notes.C: The pericardial cavity is a potential space between serous pericardial layers and does not contain thymic tissue.
notes.E: The costodiaphragmatic recess is a dependent region of the pleural cavity, remote from the anterior thymic bed.

questions.stem: The lower half of the superior vena cava lies in the:
questions.why: The superior vena cava begins above the transverse thoracic plane and descends into the middle mediastinum. Its distal part is enclosed by the pericardium before opening into the right atrium.

notes.A: The upper part of the superior vena cava is in the superior mediastinum, before the vein enters the pericardium.
notes.B: The anterior mediastinum is the space between sternum and pericardium, in front of the intrapericardial venous segment.
notes.C: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and contains structures such as the descending aorta and azygos trunk.
notes.D: The right mediastinal pleura lies lateral to the superior vena cava, whose wall stays outside the pleural cavity.

questions.stem: The thoracic duct lies in the posterior mediastinum between the:
questions.why: In the lower posterior mediastinum the thoracic duct ascends behind the oesophagus, between the descending aorta on the left and the azygos vein on the right. It crosses leftwards higher in the thorax.

notes.B: The oesophagus lies behind the trachea higher up, while the thoracic duct ascends behind the oesophagus in the posterior mediastinum.
notes.C: The space between sternum and pericardium is the anterior mediastinum, on the opposite side of the heart from the thoracic duct.
notes.D: The phrenic nerves run laterally on the pericardium, while the duct ascends deep in the posterior mediastinum.
notes.E: The inferior vena cava connects directly to the right atrium, separate from the posterior course of the thoracic duct.

questions.stem: The fibrous pericardium is firmly attached inferiorly to the:

options.label: D
options.text: left and right crura of the diaphragm

questions.why: The fibrous pericardium blends inferiorly with the central tendon of the diaphragm, anchoring the heart and allowing the sac to move with respiration. It also blends superiorly with the outer coats of the great vessels.

notes.A: Sternopericardial ligaments connect the sac anteriorly to the sternum, distinct from its broad inferior diaphragmatic attachment.
notes.C: The xiphoid lies anterior to the diaphragm and can serve as a surface landmark over the inferior pericardial region.
notes.D: The crura form the lateral margins of the aortic hiatus and anchor the diaphragm posterior to the pericardial attachment.
notes.E: The costal margin is an attachment site for peripheral diaphragm muscle, while the fibrous pericardium is fused to the central tendon.

questions.stem: The phrenic nerves descend on the pericardium:

options.label: A
options.text: on its posterior surface, behind both lung roots

options.label: C
options.text: on its lateral surfaces, in front of the lung roots

options.label: E
options.text: on the posterior surface of the oesophagus

questions.why: Each phrenic nerve passes anterior to its lung root and descends between mediastinal pleura and fibrous pericardium. It accompanies the pericardiacophrenic vessels towards the diaphragm.

notes.A: The vagus nerves run posterior to the lung roots, whereas the phrenic nerves remain anterior to them.
notes.B: The pericardial cavity lies between serous layers, deep to the fibrous pericardium on which the phrenic nerve runs.
notes.D: The anterior interventricular groove carries the anterior interventricular artery and great cardiac vein on the heart itself.
notes.E: The vagal trunks are formed by the oesophageal plexus, while the phrenic nerves descend lateral to the fibrous pericardium.

questions.stem: The oblique sinus of the pericardium lies behind the:
questions.why: The oblique pericardial sinus is a blind pocket behind the left atrium. Reflections of serous pericardium around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava form its boundaries.

notes.A: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior heart surface, away from the posterior pericardial blind pocket.
notes.B: The ascending aorta is anterior to the transverse sinus, which is different from the blind recess behind the left atrium.
notes.C: The pulmonary trunk forms part of the anterior boundary of the transverse sinus at the arterial reflection.
notes.E: The right atrium receives the caval veins, but the oblique sinus lies behind the left atrium between the pulmonary venous reflections.

questions.stem: Pain from the pericardium is carried mainly by the:
questions.why: The phrenic nerves carry pain from the fibrous pericardium and the parietal layer of serous pericardium. Their cervical roots explain why irritation can be referred to the shoulder.

notes.A: The vagus provides parasympathetic supply to the heart, while the pain-sensitive pericardial layers have phrenic afferents.
notes.B: Intercostal nerves supply the thoracic wall, but the parietal pericardium takes its main sensory supply from the phrenic nerves.
notes.C: Sympathetic afferents carry much of the pain from myocardial ischaemia, which is distinct from pain in the parietal sac.
notes.D: The greater splanchnic nerves carry fibres to and from upper abdominal viscera rather than the fibrous pericardium.

questions.stem: Pericardiocentesis is performed to relieve:
questions.why: In cardiac tamponade, fluid under pressure in the pericardial cavity limits diastolic filling. Pericardiocentesis removes the fluid, reducing external pressure and allowing the cardiac chambers to fill.

notes.B: Constrictive pericarditis is usually caused by a stiffened pericardial layer that cannot be relieved simply by draining fluid.
notes.C: A myocardial infarction results from loss of coronary perfusion, and pericardial drainage does not restore that perfusion.
notes.D: Angina is a manifestation of transient myocardial ischaemia and is unrelated to a pressurised pericardial fluid collection.
notes.E: Cor pulmonale involves increased right ventricular load from pulmonary vascular or lung disease rather than external compression.

questions.stem: The base (posterior surface) of the heart is formed mainly by the:
questions.why: The left atrium forms most of the posterior surface of the heart and receives the pulmonary veins there. This places it immediately anterior to the oesophagus across the pericardium.

notes.A: The right atrium contributes a smaller part of the posterior base and chiefly forms the right border.
notes.C: The left ventricle forms the apex and much of the diaphragmatic surface, rather than the atrial surface at the base.
notes.D: The right ventricle forms most of the sternocostal surface, facing anteriorly rather than towards the oesophagus.
notes.E: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricular outflow and lies anterior to much of the posterior atrial surface.

questions.stem: The right border of the heart is formed by the:
questions.why: The right atrium forms the visible right cardiac border between the entry points of the superior and inferior venae cavae. The right ventricle lies mainly anterior and forms much of the inferior border.

notes.A: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface and contributes to the lower rather than right cardiac border.
notes.B: The superior vena cava is part of the vascular silhouette above the heart, beyond the right atrial border.
notes.D: The right auricle projects near the arterial roots, while the right ventricular free wall forms much of the anterior surface.
notes.E: The left atrium is largely posterior and occupies much of the base rather than the right cardiac contour.

questions.stem: The left auricle appears on the heart's:
questions.why: The left auricle is a muscular appendage of the left atrium that projects anteriorly alongside the pulmonary trunk. Its projection contributes to the upper left cardiac contour.

notes.A: The inferior border is formed mainly by the right ventricle, with a smaller left ventricular contribution near the apex.
notes.B: The upper part of the right cardiac contour is related to the right atrium and superior vena cava.
notes.C: Ventricles form most of the diaphragmatic surface, while the auricle projects near the great arteries above it.
notes.E: The left ventricular tip forms the cardiac apex, inferior to the left atrial appendage.

questions.stem: The conus arteriosus (infundibulum) differs from the rest of the right ventricle in having:
questions.why: The conus arteriosus is the smooth right ventricular outflow that channels blood towards the pulmonary valve. Its lining contrasts with the muscular trabeculae of the ventricular inflow and apical regions.

notes.A: Papillary muscles and chordae support the tricuspid valve in the inflow region rather than occupying the smooth pulmonary outflow.
notes.B: The interventricular septum separates the ventricles, while the absence of internal trabeculae is what distinguishes the outflow tract.
notes.C: Pectinate muscles are atrial ridges, while irregular muscular ridges within ventricles are trabeculae carneae.
notes.D: The fossa ovalis is a depression on the interatrial septum in the right atrium.

questions.stem: The crista terminalis separates the right atrium into:

options.label: B
options.text: inflow and outflow tracts of the ventricle

questions.why: The crista terminalis is an internal ridge in the right atrium corresponding to the external sulcus terminalis. It marks the boundary between the smooth posterior sinus venarum and the anterior pectinate region.

notes.B: In the right ventricle the supraventricular crest helps separate the tricuspid inflow from the pulmonary outflow.
notes.C: The interatrial septum separates the right and left atrial cavities, whereas the crista is on the right atrial free wall.
notes.D: The limbus surrounds the fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum rather than dividing the right atrial free wall.
notes.E: Both venous openings lie in the smooth region of the right atrium, without the crista separating them.

questions.stem: The fossa ovalis is a remnant of the:
questions.why: The fetal foramen ovale conducts blood from the right to the left atrium. Its closure leaves a depression on the right side of the interatrial septum called the fossa ovalis.

notes.A: The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary arterial outflow to the aorta and closes to become the ligamentum arteriosum.
notes.C: The ductus venosus allows fetal blood to bypass hepatic sinusoids and forms the ligamentum venosum after closure.
notes.D: The intra-abdominal umbilical vein forms the round ligament of the liver, separate from the interatrial septum.
notes.E: The right horn of the sinus venosus is incorporated into the smooth posterior right atrial wall.

questions.stem: The AV nodal artery usually arises from the:
questions.why: In the usual right-dominant pattern the right coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node through a small branch at the crux. In left dominance the circumflex can supply that branch instead.

notes.A: The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior interventricular septum and anterior ventricular wall rather than usually reaching the crux.
notes.B: The circumflex can supply the atrioventricular nodal artery in left dominance, whereas right dominance is more common.
notes.D: The left marginal artery is a circumflex branch to the lateral wall of the left ventricle.
notes.E: Diagonal arteries arise from the left anterior descending artery and supply the anterolateral left ventricular wall.

questions.stem: The great cardiac vein runs with the:
questions.why: The great cardiac vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove beside the anterior interventricular artery. It then turns left into the coronary sulcus and ultimately drains through the coronary sinus.

notes.A: The posterior interventricular artery runs alongside the middle cardiac vein on the diaphragmatic surface.
notes.B: The right marginal artery runs along the acute cardiac margin, where it can accompany the small cardiac vein.
notes.C: The conus artery supplies the right ventricular outflow near the origin of the pulmonary trunk.
notes.E: The sinoatrial nodal artery supplies the upper right atrial region, outside the anterior interventricular groove.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is produced by closure of the:
questions.why: The second heart sound occurs when falling ventricular pressure allows the aortic and pulmonary valves to close at the end of ejection. Their closure marks the beginning of ventricular diastole.

notes.A: Mitral and tricuspid closure at the start of ventricular systole produces the two components of the first heart sound.
notes.B: Mitral closure contributes the left-sided component of the first heart sound as left ventricular pressure rises.
notes.C: Tricuspid closure contributes the right-sided component of the first sound at the beginning of ventricular contraction.
notes.D: The pulmonary valve contributes to the second sound, while mitral closure produces a component of the first sound.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland is the example used for parenchyma arranged as:
questions.why: Thyroid epithelial cells form spherical follicles and secrete thyroglobulin into their central colloid. The gland can use this extracellular store when producing and releasing thyroid hormones.

notes.B: Tubules are elongated epithelial structures that carry or process fluid, as the nephron tubules do in the kidney.
notes.C: Cords are elongated arrangements of cells, such as the radial rows of secretory cells in the adrenal cortex.
notes.D: Clusters of secretory cells occur in endocrine tissues such as pancreatic islets and do not have a central colloid lumen.
notes.E: Strands describe elongated groups of cells, whereas thyroid secretory epithelium encloses discrete rounded pockets of colloid.

questions.stem: The kidney is the example used for compact-organ parenchyma arranged as:
questions.why: Much of the renal parenchyma consists of epithelial tubules that transport and modify the glomerular filtrate. Their segments occupy both cortex and medulla and are continuous with a collecting system.

notes.A: Thyroid follicles have an enclosed colloid store, while renal tubules have continuous lumens for the passage of filtrate.
notes.C: Endocrine cells such as those in the adrenal cortex may be arranged in cords alongside capillaries.
notes.D: Endocrine pancreatic islets are discrete clusters, while most functional renal tissue is organised as luminal tubules.
notes.E: Hepatocytes are organised in plates associated with sinusoids, a different plan from the epithelium surrounding renal tubular lumens.

questions.stem: In a tubular organ, the vessels and nerves mainly run in the:

options.label: E
options.text: smooth muscle cells of the muscularis

questions.why: The wall alternates muscle and connective tissue layers.

notes.A: Avascular.
notes.B: Outer lining cells.
notes.D: Not a carrier layer.
notes.E: Vessels run between, not within, the muscle cells.

questions.stem: Which function of the cardiovascular system is classed as "protection"?

options.label: A
options.text: Carrying hormones to their target organs

options.label: B
options.text: Carrying oxygen and carbon dioxide gases

options.label: D
options.text: Carrying white cells and clotting factors

questions.why: Circulating white cells contribute to defence against infection, and platelets with plasma clotting factors limit blood loss after injury. These are protective functions supported by the cardiovascular system.

notes.A: Hormones in the bloodstream carry regulatory signals between organs, rather than directly providing defence or haemostasis.
notes.B: Oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported between tissues and lungs to support metabolism and gas exchange.
notes.C: Waste removal involves carrying metabolic products to organs such as the kidneys, which then excrete them.
notes.E: Delivery of absorbed nutrients is a transport function that provides cells with energy and raw materials.

questions.stem: The circulatory system is made up of the:

options.label: A
options.text: heart and the arterial tree only

options.label: C
options.text: heart, lungs and the circulating blood

options.label: D
options.text: lymph nodes, spleen and the thymus

questions.why: In the broad anatomical sense the circulatory system includes cardiovascular and lymphatic pathways. The heart drives blood through closed vessels, while lymphatics recover excess interstitial fluid and return it to venous blood.

notes.A: The heart and arterial tree form the pump and outflow pathway, leaving out venous return and lymphatic drainage.
notes.B: Arteries, capillaries and veins form the blood vascular network but do not account for its pump or lymphatic drainage.
notes.C: The heart and lungs participate in pulmonary circulation, which supplies neither the complete systemic vascular nor lymphatic pathway.
notes.D: Lymph nodes, spleen and thymus are lymphoid organs and represent only part of the structures involved in circulation.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes are placed along lymphatic pathways mainly to:

options.label: A
options.text: filter lymph before it reaches the veins

options.label: B
options.text: pump lymph back towards the heart

options.label: C
options.text: produce red cells for the circulation

options.label: D
options.text: store excess tissue fluid until needed

options.label: E
options.text: absorb fat directly from the small gut

questions.why: Lymph nodes sit along the lymphatic pathways to filter lymph of debris and antigens before it drains into the venous system.

notes.B: Lymphatic collecting vessels use smooth muscle contraction and valves to propel lymph, while nodes filter it along the way.
notes.C: Bone marrow produces circulating red cells, whereas lymph nodes contain immune cells that survey lymph.
notes.D: Excess interstitial fluid enters lymphatic capillaries and normally proceeds through nodes towards the venous system rather than being stored.
notes.E: Intestinal lacteals absorb chylomicrons in the villi before the resulting lymph reaches filtering nodes.

questions.stem: Which structure lies in the superior mediastinum but NOT in the middle mediastinum?
questions.why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the vagus and loops beneath the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum. It then ascends towards the larynx without accompanying the pericardium.

notes.A: The phrenic nerves run through the superior mediastinum and then along the lateral pericardium in the middle mediastinum.
notes.C: The ascending aorta is enclosed by the pericardium and belongs to the middle mediastinum until it becomes the arch.
notes.D: The pulmonary trunk is divided within the middle mediastinum beneath the aortic arch, in front of the tracheal bifurcation.
notes.E: The lower superior vena cava enters the pericardial sac and runs through the middle mediastinum to the right atrium.

questions.stem: The lowest parts of which muscles arise in the superior mediastinum?
questions.why: The lowest attachments of these muscles reach the upper chest: sternohyoid and sternothyroid attach behind the sternum, while longus colli attaches to upper thoracic vertebral bodies. Their lower ends relate to the superior mediastinum.

notes.A: The scalenes attach to the first and second ribs from the lateral neck, while sternocleidomastoid has anterior superficial attachments.
notes.B: The pectoral muscles are superficial to the rib cage on the anterior chest wall, outside the mediastinum.
notes.D: These scapular muscles have attachments on the back of the neck and thorax rather than within the interpleural space.
notes.E: Transversus thoracis and subcostal muscles lie against the internal chest wall instead of forming the lower continuations of cervical muscles.

questions.stem: The left superior intercostal (highest intercostal) vein is found in the:
questions.why: It crosses the arch to join the left brachiocephalic vein.

notes.A: Not as listed.
notes.B: Not here.
notes.C: Not here.
notes.E: Outside the mediastinum.

questions.stem: The anterior mediastinum contains:

options.label: A
options.text: the heart and roots of the great vessels

options.label: B
options.text: the thoracic duct and azygos vein

options.label: C
options.text: the phrenic and the vagus nerves

options.label: E
options.text: lymphatics from the liver and a few nodes

questions.why: The anterior mediastinum is the narrow space behind the sternum and in front of the pericardium. Loose tissue in this space contains lymphatic channels including drainage from the liver and a few nodes.

notes.A: The heart and intrapericardial roots of the great vessels lie in the middle mediastinum within the fibrous pericardium.
notes.B: The thoracic duct and main azygos trunk run behind the pericardium in the posterior mediastinum.
notes.C: The phrenic nerves run on the lateral pericardial surfaces, and the vagus nerves pass behind the lung roots.
notes.D: The trachea and oesophagus pass through the superior mediastinum, with the oesophagus continuing posterior to the heart below it.

questions.stem: The anterior mediastinum is best developed on the left because:

options.label: A
options.text: the left pleura diverges from the midline

options.label: B
options.text: the heart lies mainly to the right

options.label: C
options.text: the left lung is the larger lung

options.label: D
options.text: the sternum deviates towards the left side

options.label: E
options.text: the thymus lies wholly on the left

questions.why: The left pleural reflection diverges from the midline near the heart, leaving a wider space between the left pleura and the pericardium behind the sternum. This makes the anterior mediastinum wider on the left.

notes.B: The heart projects mostly left of the midline, contributing to the asymmetry in the anterior pleural reflections.
notes.C: The left lung is usually smaller and has a cardiac notch that accommodates the heart on that side.
notes.D: The sternum lies near the midline, while the divergence of the pleural reflections creates the relevant asymmetry behind it.
notes.E: Thymic tissue lies in the anterior superior chest but does not explain the characteristic divergence of the left pleural reflection.

questions.stem: The splanchnic nerves and sympathetic trunks lie in the:
questions.why: The thoracic sympathetic trunks lie beside the vertebral column. Their splanchnic branches pass through the posterior mediastinal region towards the diaphragm on their way to autonomic plexuses in the abdomen.

notes.A: The middle mediastinum contains the pericardium, while the thoracic sympathetic chains are located farther back beside the spine.
notes.C: The anterior mediastinum lies immediately behind the sternum and contains loose tissue and lymphatics instead of the paravertebral trunks.
notes.D: Both trunks extend inferiorly throughout the thorax and give splanchnic branches that descend towards the abdominal viscera.
notes.E: The pericardial cavity is a potential space between serous layers and has no paravertebral sympathetic trunk within it.

questions.stem: The bronchial lymph nodes listed among mediastinal contents lie in the:
questions.why: Bronchopulmonary nodes cluster around the main bronchi and pulmonary vessels at the lung roots. These hilar nodes are associated with the middle mediastinal contents and receive lymph from the lungs.

notes.A: The retrosternal anterior mediastinum contains a small set of lymph nodes, distinct from hilar nodes alongside the bronchi.
notes.B: Superior mediastinal nodes can receive drainage from below, but the bronchopulmonary nodes are located at the lung roots.
notes.D: Posterior mediastinal nodes lie by structures such as the oesophagus and descending aorta rather than at the pulmonary hila.
notes.E: The pericardial cavity contains a film of serous fluid and does not enclose the nodes at the lung roots.

questions.stem: Behind, the pericardium rests on the:

options.label: A
options.text: sternum and remains of the thymus

options.label: C
options.text: trachea and the left main bronchus

options.label: E
options.text: arch of the aorta and its branches

questions.why: The oesophagus and descending thoracic aorta lie in the posterior mediastinum, behind the fibrous pericardium. In particular, the oesophagus passes immediately posterior to the left atrial region.

notes.A: The sternum and remnants of the thymus lie anterior to the pericardium, particularly at the upper part of the sac.
notes.B: The phrenic nerves run along the lateral pericardial surfaces between fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
notes.C: The tracheal bifurcation and main bronchi lie near the superior aspect of the sac rather than along most of its posterior wall.
notes.E: The aortic arch and its branches lie superiorly above the intrapericardial ascending aorta.

questions.stem: Venous blood from the pericardium drains mainly into the:
questions.why: Arteries: pericardiacophrenic, musculophrenic, bronchial, thoracic aorta.

notes.A: Heart wall.
notes.B: Gut.
notes.C: Lungs.
notes.D: Head and neck.

questions.stem: Constrictive pericarditis impairs the heart mainly by:
questions.why: A stiff, fibrotic pericardium resists expansion of the ventricles once they reach a limited volume. This abruptly restricts diastolic filling and raises upstream venous pressures.

notes.B: Coronary obstruction causes myocardial ischaemia, while constriction primarily limits expansion from outside the myocardium.
notes.C: The sinoatrial node initiates the heartbeat, and loss of its function would cause a rhythm disorder rather than the usual filling limitation.
notes.D: Valve cusp damage produces stenosis or regurgitation, distinct from a rigid sac restricting all cardiac chambers.
notes.E: High pulmonary vascular resistance increases right ventricular afterload, while pericardial constriction directly limits filling during diastole.

questions.stem: The average adult heart measures about:
questions.why: A typical adult heart is about the size of a clenched fist, roughly 12 cm long, 8–9 cm wide and about 300 g. Size varies with body size and other factors.

notes.A: A mass of 150 g and a length of 8 cm are below usual adult reference values.
notes.C: A mass of 500 g is above the usual adult range and may reflect a large body size or cardiac enlargement.
notes.D: A mass near 400 g exceeds the cited average, and the typical heart is longer than it is wide.
notes.E: A length of 20 cm with a mass near 600 g is substantially above normal average adult measurements.

questions.stem: Which opens into the right atrium?
questions.why: The coronary sinus collects most cardiac venous blood and opens into the right atrium near the inferior vena caval opening and tricuspid orifice. Several smaller veins also reach the atrium independently.

notes.A: The right pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the right lung into the posterior left atrium.
notes.B: The great cardiac vein usually joins the coronary sinus, so its blood enters the right atrium indirectly.
notes.D: The ascending aorta receives blood from the left ventricle through the aortic valve and has no right atrial opening.
notes.E: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and carries blood to the lungs.

questions.stem: The cavity of the right ventricle appears semilunar in cross section because:

options.label: A
options.text: its wall is three times thicker

questions.why: The left ventricle has a roughly round cross-sectional cavity, and the interventricular septum curves towards the right ventricle. The right ventricular free wall wraps around this curve, leaving a crescent-shaped cavity.

notes.A: The left ventricular free wall is substantially thicker than the right and handles the pressure of systemic circulation.
notes.B: Trabeculae carneae are present in the right ventricle and change its surface texture rather than causing the crescent shape.
notes.C: The conus arteriosus is the smooth superior outflow tract and does not determine the shape of the main cavity.
notes.E: The tricuspid orifice receives blood from the right atrium, while septal curvature determines the crescent in a short-axis section.

questions.stem: The pulmonary veins entering the left atrium:

options.label: E
options.text: are four and have no valves

questions.why: Typically two pulmonary veins from each lung enter the posterior left atrium. Their ostia generally lack valves, although a shared opening or extra pulmonary vein can change the usual arrangement.

notes.A: A common ostium can reduce the number of openings, but the usual pulmonary venous arrangement includes two veins from each lung.
notes.B: Four veins is the usual count, but their openings lack the valves found in many peripheral veins.
notes.C: The absence of valves fits normal anatomy, but two veins is the usual count for one lung rather than both.
notes.D: The pulmonary veins open into the smooth posterior left atrial wall, whereas the auricle is an anterior appendage.

questions.stem: Musculi pectinati in the left atrium are:

options.label: D
options.text: more numerous than on the right

questions.why: The left atrial appendage retains a ridged wall of pectinate muscles. Most of the rest of the left atrium, including the region receiving the pulmonary veins, has a smooth inner surface.

notes.B: Most of the left atrial chamber is smooth, with prominent pectinate musculature limited to the appendage.
notes.C: The left auricle has pectinate muscle even though the main left atrial chamber appears smooth.
notes.D: Pectinate muscles are more extensive in the right atrium, where they extend from the crista terminalis into the anterior chamber.
notes.E: The interatrial septum is separate from the muscular ridges in the left atrial appendage.

questions.stem: The mitral orifice lies in relation to the aortic orifice:

options.label: E
options.text: to the right at the same level

questions.why: The mitral orifice lies below and to the left of the centrally placed aortic orifice within the fibrous skeleton of the heart.

notes.A: The aortic orifice is at the superior end of left ventricular outflow, above the mitral inlet.
notes.C: The aortic orifice is anterosuperior to the mitral orifice, so the mitral inlet lies more posteriorly.
notes.D: The mitral inlet does lie posterior to the aortic outlet, but its position is also inferior and leftward.
notes.E: The two left-sided orifices are joined by fibrous continuity, and the mitral one lies further to the left.

questions.stem: The trigonum fibrosum of the cardiac skeleton lies between the:
questions.why: The right and left fibrous trigones reinforce the cardiac skeleton where the aortic and atrioventricular rings approach one another. The right trigone is related to both atrioventricular rings and forms part of the central fibrous body.

notes.A: The pulmonary valve is supported by the right ventricular outflow and is relatively separate from the central fibrous trigones.
notes.B: The tricuspid ring is related to the right fibrous trigone near the aortic ring, rather than near the separated pulmonary ring.
notes.D: The atrial auricles are muscular appendages projecting outside the regions of fibrous continuity between valve orifices.
notes.E: The coronary sinus and inferior vena cava open into the right atrium as venous channels and do not form fibrous valve rings.

questions.stem: The tricuspid valve is surface-marked:

options.label: D
options.text: behind the lower half of the sternum

questions.why: The tricuspid orifice projects behind the lower body of the sternum around the fourth and fifth interspaces. Its projection is distinct from the usual listening area along the lower left sternal edge.

notes.A: The left fourth costal cartilage is closer to the conventional surface projection of the mitral orifice.
notes.B: The third left parasternal space is higher than the tricuspid projection and closer to the outflow valve region.
notes.C: The second right parasternal interspace is an auscultation site for the aortic valve, not the anatomical tricuspid projection.
notes.E: The left fifth interspace may be used near the sternum to listen to tricuspid sounds, while the valve itself projects behind the sternum.

questions.stem: The pulmonary valve lies at the left sternal border at the level of the:
questions.why: The pulmonary valve projects near the medial end of the left third costal cartilage at the start of the pulmonary trunk. Its sounds are usually heard higher, in the left second intercostal space.

notes.A: The left second intercostal space is the usual pulmonary listening area, higher than the anatomical position of the valve.
notes.B: The mitral valve projects near the fourth left cartilage and is inferior to the pulmonary valve.
notes.C: At the left fifth interspace near the midclavicular line lies the cardiac apex used for mitral auscultation.
notes.D: The sternal angle is at the level of the second costal cartilage, above the valve projection at the third cartilage.

questions.stem: The aortic area of auscultation is at the:

options.label: A
options.text: right 2nd intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: B
options.text: left 2nd intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: C
options.text: left 3rd intercostal space at the sternum

options.label: E
options.text: left 5th intercostal space at the MCL

questions.why: Aortic valve sounds are best heard at the right second parasternal interspace because they travel into the ascending aorta. This listening area lies above and to the right of the valve's anatomical projection.

notes.B: The left second parasternal interspace is the standard location for pulmonary rather than aortic auscultation.
notes.C: The left third parasternal interspace is often used for additional assessment of cardiac sounds but is not the standard aortic area.
notes.D: The right fifth interspace is inferior to the usual area where aortic outflow sounds are transmitted to the chest wall.
notes.E: The left fifth interspace at the midclavicular line corresponds to the apex and is the standard mitral area.

questions.stem: The AV node lies in the:

options.label: A
options.text: posterior wall of the right atrium

options.label: B
options.text: lower part of the interatrial septum

questions.why: The atrioventricular node lies in the lower part of the interatrial septum, near the opening of the coronary sinus (within the triangle of Koch).

notes.A: The atrioventricular node is near the low septal aspect of the right atrium, rather than broadly within its posterior free wall.
notes.C: The atrioventricular bundle passes near the membranous interventricular septum after leaving the node.
notes.D: The muscular ventricular septum carries bundle branches below the atrioventricular node, which lies above it on the atrial side.
notes.E: The node is approached from the right atrium within the triangle bounded partly by the coronary sinus opening.

questions.stem: The bundle of His divides into right and left branches in the:
questions.why: The atrioventricular bundle passes through the central fibrous body and near the inferior margin of the membranous septum. It separates into right and left bundle branches near the crest of the muscular interventricular septum.

notes.A: The undivided bundle runs along the inferior margin of the membranous portion before dividing near its junction with the muscular crest.
notes.B: The lower atrial septal region contains the atrioventricular node, upstream of the site of bundle division.
notes.D: The crista terminalis is in the right atrium near the sinoatrial node and is remote from the ventricular septum.
notes.E: Posterior atrial tissue lies above the cardiac skeleton and is not where the atrioventricular bundle splits into ventricular branches.

questions.stem: The normal resting rate set by the SA node is about:
questions.why: At a typical resting rate of about 70–80 beats per minute, spontaneous depolarisation in the sinoatrial node sets the pace for other cardiac cells. Autonomic tone can raise or lower this rate.

notes.A: Rates around 40–60 beats per minute are typical of a junctional escape rhythm, though sinus rates can be low in trained people.
notes.B: Rates around 20–40 beats per minute are typical of slower ventricular escape pacemakers below the atrioventricular junction.
notes.C: Rates of 100–120 can occur with exercise, illness or other sympathetic stimulation and are above the typical resting range.
notes.E: A rate of 150–180 is well above normal resting sinus rate and may occur during strenuous exercise or tachycardia.

questions.stem: In about 40% of people, the SA nodal artery arises from the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial nodal artery arises from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery in roughly two-fifths of people. In most of the rest it arises from the proximal right coronary artery.

notes.A: The right coronary artery gives the sinoatrial nodal branch most often, in roughly three-fifths rather than two-fifths of people.
notes.B: The posterior interventricular artery supplies the inferior septal region, whereas nodal supply normally comes from a more proximal vessel.
notes.C: The right marginal artery supplies the right ventricular free wall along the acute border, away from the sinoatrial node.
notes.D: The conus artery supplies the right ventricular outflow tract, not the nodal area near the superior vena cava.

questions.stem: In about 10% of hearts, the posterior interventricular artery comes from the:
questions.why: The posterior interventricular artery arises from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery in a left-dominant heart. The circumflex then reaches the crux and sends a branch down the posterior interventricular groove.

notes.B: The anterior interventricular artery runs in the anterior groove and supplies the anterior septum rather than defining left dominance.
notes.C: The right marginal branch supplies the acute margin of the right ventricle and normally ends near the apex.
notes.D: The conus artery supplies the right ventricular outflow region superiorly, away from the posterior interventricular groove.
notes.E: Diagonal arteries arise from the anterior interventricular artery and run over the anterolateral surface of the left ventricle.

questions.stem: The middle cardiac vein runs in the:
questions.why: The middle cardiac vein ascends from near the apex in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery. It drains into the coronary sinus near its right atrial opening.

notes.A: The anterior interventricular groove contains the great cardiac vein alongside the anterior interventricular artery.
notes.C: The left atrioventricular groove contains the circumflex artery and, in its posterior part, the coronary sinus.
notes.D: The right atrioventricular groove contains the right coronary artery and can carry the small cardiac vein.
notes.E: The obtuse margin is the rounded left ventricular edge, where marginal vessels travel outside the posterior septal groove.

questions.stem: The smallest cardiac veins (venae cordis minimae) drain:
questions.why: The venae cordis minimae are tiny veins with individual openings into the cardiac chambers. They can deliver venous blood directly to the cavity instead of collecting in a larger coronary vein.

notes.A: The coronary sinus collects larger cardiac veins and has a single major opening into the right atrium.
notes.B: The great cardiac vein collects blood along the anterior interventricular groove and carries it towards the coronary sinus.
notes.D: The azygos vein drains the thoracic wall and mediastinal structures into the superior vena cava.
notes.E: Anterior cardiac veins carry part of the right ventricular drainage through independent openings into the right atrium.

questions.stem: Cor pulmonale is enlargement of the:

options.label: B
options.text: left atrium due to mitral stenosis

options.label: C
options.text: right atrium due to tricuspid disease

options.label: D
options.text: right ventricle due to lung disease

questions.why: Pulmonary hypertension due to lung or pulmonary vascular disease increases the resistance against which the right ventricle ejects. The resulting right ventricular hypertrophy, dilatation or failure is called cor pulmonale.

notes.A: Systemic hypertension increases left ventricular workload and can cause left ventricular hypertrophy, a different pressure-loading pattern.
notes.B: Mitral stenosis increases left atrial pressure and can enlarge that chamber, but it is primary left-sided heart disease.
notes.C: Tricuspid disease can enlarge the right atrium but does not define right ventricular remodelling caused by pulmonary disease.
notes.E: Severe anaemia can increase cardiac output and enlarge the heart more generally rather than specifically loading the right ventricle.

questions.stem: Chest pain due to reversible myocardial ischaemia without cell death is:
questions.why: Angina pectoris is chest discomfort caused by a temporary mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. When the ischaemia resolves without myocardial cell death, it fits angina rather than infarction.

notes.A: Myocardial infarction involves acute myocardial injury with cell death because the oxygen shortage is sufficiently severe or prolonged.
notes.B: Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac, often causing sharp pain associated with respiration or posture.
notes.C: Tamponade impairs cardiac filling by raising pericardial pressure rather than causing the defining reversible myocardial oxygen mismatch.
notes.D: Cardiomyopathy is disease of heart muscle that alters its structure or function, rather than the name for transient ischaemic pain.

questions.stem: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) of the right ventricle carries the:
questions.why: Part of the right bundle branch runs through the moderator band from the interventricular septum to the anterior papillary muscle. This pathway helps activate the right ventricular free wall and papillary muscle promptly.

notes.B: The left bundle branch runs along the left side of the ventricular septum towards the left ventricular myocardium.
notes.C: The atrioventricular nodal artery supplies the node near the cardiac crux, rather than travelling across the ventricular cavity.
notes.D: The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular groove on the epicardial surface, not inside the moderator band.
notes.E: The undivided bundle of His passes through the cardiac skeleton and proximal septum before the right bundle branch reaches the band.

questions.stem: The outermost connective tissue covering of a compact organ is the:
questions.why: A connective tissue capsule forms the outer supporting framework of many compact organs. Septa or trabeculae can extend from it into the parenchyma and carry vessels to the internal compartments.

notes.A: A serosa is an additional mesothelial covering on a body-cavity surface and can overlie the structural capsule.
notes.C: An adventitia blends with surrounding tissues and commonly forms the outer coat of a nonperitoneal hollow organ.
notes.D: A mucosa is a lining of an interior surface exposed to a lumen, rather than the outer solid-organ framework.
notes.E: A trabecula is a supporting projection extending inward from the capsule, not the enclosing layer itself.

questions.stem: Blood vessels enter a compact organ through its:
questions.why: A hilum is a localised gateway where major blood vessels enter or leave many solid organs. Nerves and ducts may use the same gateway before branching into the organ.

notes.A: A capsule forms a covering around the organ, but major vessels usually converge at a specific entry region in a hilar organ.
notes.B: The cortex is an outer functional region that receives branches after the main vessels enter a hilar organ.
notes.D: The medulla is a deeper region whose blood supply is distributed through branches of the organ's arterial tree.
notes.E: A serosa covers exposed organ surfaces and is not the equivalent of the gateway for its principal vessels.

questions.stem: A compact organ suspended within a body cavity may also be covered externally by:
questions.why: A solid organ exposed to a serous cavity may have a visceral serosa on its free surface. This thin mesothelial layer and its connective tissue support provide a smooth, lubricated interface.

notes.A: A mucosa consists of epithelium and supporting tissue around an internal lumen, rather than covering a free outer surface.
notes.B: An adventitia blends with surrounding connective tissue where an organ has no free mesothelial covering.
notes.C: A muscularis is a contractile coat of a hollow organ and provides movement rather than a slippery surface.
notes.E: A submucosa supports the mucosa inside a tubular organ, well away from the serous covering.

questions.stem: In a section of young thymus, the connective tissue septa separate lobules that each show:

options.label: A
options.text: an outer medulla and inner cortex

options.label: E
options.text: an outer cortex and inner medulla

questions.why: Each apparent thymic lobule has a darker peripheral cortex packed with developing T cells and a paler medulla containing Hassall corpuscles. The medullary tissue can remain continuous between adjacent lobules.

notes.A: The darker cortex is peripheral, while the lighter medulla occupies the central part of the lobule.
notes.B: Thymic lobules are solid lymphoid tissue and have no central cavity lined by epithelium.
notes.C: Colloid-filled follicles characterise the thyroid, whose secretory epithelium forms closed spaces around stored thyroglobulin.
notes.D: Renal corpuscles and tubules are the filtering and processing structures of the kidney, absent from thymic lobules.

questions.stem: The tissue that immediately surrounds the central cavity of a tubular organ is:
questions.why: A tubular organ typically presents an epithelial lining to its lumen. The epithelial cells protect or exchange material with the contents, while supporting connective and muscle layers lie farther out.

notes.B: Smooth muscle surrounds the lining farther out in many hollow organs and helps move their contents.
notes.C: Loose connective tissue supports the luminal epithelium, but the epithelium is the layer in direct contact with the lumen.
notes.D: Mesothelium covers serous surfaces exposed to a body cavity rather than lining the internal lumen of a typical tubular organ.
notes.E: Hyaline cartilage supports certain airways from outside their mucosa, leaving respiratory epithelium in contact with the lumen.

questions.stem: The muscularis of a tubular organ is usually made of:
questions.why: Most hollow visceral organs use smooth muscle embedded in connective tissue to propel contents or change the lumen's diameter. Muscle layers are arranged to suit the mechanical work of the organ.

notes.A: Skeletal muscle does occur in selected regions, such as the upper oesophagus, but does not form most visceral muscularis.
notes.C: Cardiac muscle and Purkinje fibres are specialisations of the heart that generate and distribute ventricular contraction.
notes.D: Elastic cartilage provides flexible support in structures such as the external ear and epiglottis rather than a contractile coat.
notes.E: Collagen contributes passive support between fibres, but the defining cells of the muscularis generate active contraction.

questions.stem: Which system is given as having tubular organs with VARIED coats?
questions.why: Three coats: urinary, cardiovascular, male and female reproductive. Four: GI tract.

notes.A: Three coats.
notes.B: Three coats.
notes.D: Three coats.
notes.E: Four coats.

questions.stem: In a tubular organ, the arrangement of the muscle mainly reflects the organ's:
questions.why: A tubular organ's smooth muscle is organised to perform its mechanical task. Circular fibres can narrow the lumen, while longitudinal fibres shorten a segment, allowing coordinated movement when propulsion is needed.

notes.A: Blood supply sustains the wall but does not account for whether its muscle narrows, shortens or holds the lumen open.
notes.B: Development influences tissue origin, while the adult arrangement of muscle layers is adapted to the work the organ performs.
notes.C: Nerves coordinate contractions, but the arrangement of the contractile fibres reflects how contents need to move.
notes.E: Body position affects anatomical relations, while muscles are arranged chiefly to suit the organ's mechanical action.

questions.stem: The lymphatic system returns tissue fluid to the:
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid. After it passes through collecting vessels and nodes, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct return it to the venous circulation near the jugular–subclavian junctions.

notes.A: The arterial tree distributes blood away from the heart and has no normal terminal connection for the main lymphatic ducts.
notes.B: The pericardial cavity contains a small amount of lubricating fluid rather than receiving the body's collected lymph.
notes.C: Alveolar spaces are sites of gas exchange, and pulmonary lymph drains away from their tissue towards nodes.
notes.D: The portal vein carries venous blood to the liver and is separate from the main terminal lymphatic connections in the neck.

questions.stem: The mediastinum extends vertically from the:

options.label: A
options.text: thoracic inlet to the thoracic outlet

options.label: C
options.text: hyoid bone to the xiphoid process

options.label: D
options.text: thoracic inlet to the sternal angle

options.label: E
options.text: T4 vertebra to the T12 vertebra

questions.why: The mediastinum is continuous with the root of the neck at the superior thoracic aperture and extends down to the diaphragm, which closes most of the inferior thoracic aperture.

notes.B: The sternal angle is the landmark for the transverse dividing plane, so this range covers only the inferior mediastinum.
notes.C: The hyoid is a cervical structure above the thorax, while the xiphoid is an anterior landmark near the lower sternum.
notes.D: The thoracic inlet to the sternal-angle plane is the extent of the superior portion alone.
notes.E: T4 to T12 approximates the span of the inferior mediastinum along the vertebral column and omits the superior portion.

questions.stem: The mediastinum contains almost all the thoracic viscera EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The mediastinum occupies the central compartment between the two pleural sacs. The lungs are contained in the pleural compartments on either side, while their roots connect to mediastinal structures.

notes.A: The heart lies inside the pericardium, which occupies the middle mediastinum between the pleural sacs.
notes.C: The oesophagus passes through the superior and posterior mediastinum before traversing the diaphragm.
notes.D: The thoracic trachea runs through the superior mediastinum and divides near the sternal-angle plane.
notes.E: The thymus lies in the anterior superior mediastinal region and can extend inferiorly in front of the pericardium.

questions.stem: The inferior mediastinum is subdivided into:
questions.why: Below the sternal-angle plane the pericardium divides the inferior mediastinum into three regions. The anterior and posterior regions lie respectively in front of and behind the middle region holding the pericardium.

notes.A: Superior and inferior describe the principal division of the whole mediastinum, while the subdivisions below that plane are front to back.
notes.B: The pleural compartments lie to the right and left of the mediastinum, which is subdivided around the pericardium in the sagittal direction.
notes.D: The compartment names describe relations to the pericardial sac rather than upper, lower and lateral divisions.
notes.E: The pericardium itself occupies the middle subdivision and must be included along with the spaces in front and behind it.

questions.stem: The broadest part of the interpleural space is the:
questions.why: The middle mediastinum is the widest of the mediastinal subdivisions because it accommodates the heart within its pericardium. The roots of the great vessels also occupy this compartment.

notes.A: The anterior mediastinum is a comparatively narrow space between the sternum and the pericardium.
notes.B: The posterior mediastinum is a smaller space behind the heart that provides passage to the oesophagus and descending aorta.
notes.C: The superior mediastinum is the region above the sternal-angle plane, where structures pass between thorax and neck.
notes.E: The costomediastinal recess belongs to the pleural cavity and is outside the interpleural mediastinum.

questions.stem: The anterior mediastinum is bounded in front by the sternum and the left:
questions.why: The left pleural reflection diverges at the lower sternum, exposing the region of the left fifth to seventh costal cartilages alongside the sternum. This contributes to the anterior boundary of the anterior mediastinum.

notes.A: The first to third cartilages are higher, near the anterior chest wall over the superior mediastinum.
notes.B: The second cartilage locates the sternal-angle plane, while the anterior subdivision extends below that level.
notes.C: The eighth to tenth cartilages contribute to the lower costal margin and lie below the boundary in question.
notes.D: The third and fourth cartilages lie above most of the lower left parasternal area where the pleural reflection diverges.

questions.stem: The small arteries in the anterior mediastinum are mediastinal branches of the:
questions.why: The small arteries of the anterior mediastinum are mediastinal and pericardial branches of the internal thoracic artery.

notes.B: The descending thoracic aorta gives small branches to structures in the posterior mediastinum rather than the retrosternal space.
notes.C: Bronchial arteries mainly supply the lower airways and supporting lung tissues, with origins commonly in the posterior mediastinum.
notes.D: The superior phrenic arteries arise near the lower thoracic aorta to supply the superior surface of the diaphragm.
notes.E: The musculophrenic artery follows the costal margin and supplies the diaphragm and lower anterior intercostal spaces.

questions.stem: The posterior mediastinum is bounded behind by the vertebral column from:

options.label: A
options.text: T1 to the lower border of T4

options.label: B
options.text: the lower border of T4 to T12

options.label: C
options.text: C7 to the upper border of T4

options.label: D
options.text: the lower border of T6 to L1

options.label: E
options.text: T2 to the upper border of T10

questions.why: The posterior mediastinum starts just below the sternal-angle plane at the lower border of T4. Its posterior boundary follows the thoracic vertebral column down to T12 at the diaphragm.

notes.A: The vertebral levels from T1 to the lower part of T4 form the posterior boundary of the superior mediastinum.
notes.C: C7 lies above the thoracic inlet, and the upper border of T4 is above the start of the posterior compartment.
notes.D: The compartment starts above T6, and at L1 the descending aorta has already left the thorax.
notes.E: T2 lies in the superior mediastinal region, and the posterior compartment extends below T10 towards the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve runs through the posterior mediastinum on the oesophagus?
questions.why: The vagus nerves pass behind the lung roots and form a plexus on the oesophagus in the posterior mediastinum. Fibres regroup into vagal trunks that follow the oesophagus through the diaphragm.

notes.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies pharyngeal structures and carries afferents from the carotid sinus, without descending into the thoracic plexus.
notes.B: The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius in the neck and has no oesophageal thoracic course.
notes.D: The hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles and remains above the thorax.
notes.E: The phrenic nerve descends in front of the lung root along the lateral pericardium rather than running on the oesophagus.

questions.stem: The pericardium has two components, the:
questions.why: The pericardium combines a tough outer fibrous sac and an inner serous membrane. The serous membrane has a parietal layer lining the sac and a visceral layer covering the heart.

notes.A: Parietal describes part of the serous pericardium, while mediastinal is a designation used for pleura.
notes.B: Visceral describes the inner serous layer covering the heart, while costal identifies pleura lining the ribs.
notes.C: The fibrous sac is a genuine component, but myocardium is cardiac muscle and lies beneath the pericardial covering.
notes.E: Epicardium is the visceral serous pericardium, while endocardium is the separate lining of the heart chambers.

questions.stem: Superiorly, the fibrous pericardium fuses with the:
questions.why: At the superior end of the fibrous pericardium, the sac blends with the adventitia of the great vessels entering or leaving the heart. This anchors the sac around the vascular roots.

notes.A: The suprapleural membrane provides support to the cervical pleural cupola, above and lateral to the pericardial attachment.
notes.B: Pretracheal fascia can blend with the fibrous pericardium, whose immediate attachment at the vessel roots is adventitial.
notes.C: The sternum connects to the front of the pericardium through sternopericardial ligaments rather than through the great vessel sleeves.
notes.D: The azygos arch drains into the superior vena cava, but sits outside the sac and is not its superior anchor.

questions.stem: Because the fibrous pericardium resists acute expansion, a rapid pericardial effusion causes:
questions.why: Fluid that collects quickly cannot stretch the fibrous pericardium, so pressure rises and compresses the heart (cardiac tamponade), limiting filling.

notes.B: The pericardium attaches to the diaphragm, which does not normally rupture when pressure rapidly rises inside the sac.
notes.C: The pleural cavities are separate from the pericardial cavity, so a typical effusion primarily compresses the heart.
notes.D: Rising pericardial pressure limits ventricular expansion, reducing chamber filling instead of causing primary ventricular dilatation.
notes.E: The phrenic nerves run along the sac and may carry pain, but the main effect is pressure on the cardiac chambers.

questions.stem: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between the:
questions.why: The parietal serous pericardium lines the fibrous sac and the visceral layer covers the heart. A thin film of fluid between these layers lubricates movement as the heart beats.

notes.A: The mediastinal pleura lies outside the fibrous pericardium, separated from it locally by the phrenic nerve and associated vessels.
notes.C: The fibrous pericardium attaches to the central tendon below, where it does not border the serous cavity from outside.
notes.D: The epicardium, or visceral serous layer, adheres to the cardiac surface over the myocardium with no intervening pericardial cavity.
notes.E: The parietal serous layer closely lines the fibrous sac, so the cavity lies on its opposite side.

questions.stem: The oblique sinus is formed by the reflection of serous pericardium around the:
questions.why: The transverse sinus is formed around the arterial trunks.

notes.A: Transverse sinus.
notes.B: Not so.
notes.D: Not so.
notes.E: Not so.

questions.stem: The pericardiacophrenic artery is a branch of the:
questions.why: The pericardiacophrenic artery leaves the internal thoracic artery and follows the phrenic nerve between pericardium and mediastinal pleura. It supplies these structures and contributes to the blood supply of the diaphragm.

notes.A: The thoracic aorta gives separate pericardial and superior phrenic branches that approach from posterior or inferior relations.
notes.B: The subclavian artery supplies the pericardiacophrenic artery indirectly through its internal thoracic branch.
notes.C: Superior phrenic arteries usually come from the descending thoracic aorta and supply the upper surface of the diaphragm.
notes.E: Bronchial arteries chiefly supply airway tissues and reach the lungs through the hila rather than following the phrenic nerves.

questions.stem: Which layer of the pericardium is insensitive to pain?
questions.why: The visceral serous layer adheres to the heart as the epicardium and lacks the phrenic somatic pain supply of the outer layers. The fibrous and parietal layers can produce referred shoulder pain when irritated.

notes.A: The parietal serous layer is sensitive to pain because it receives sensory fibres from the phrenic nerves.
notes.B: The fibrous sac receives somatic sensory fibres from the phrenic nerves and can be painful when irritated.
notes.C: The outer two layers have phrenic pain fibres, whereas the visceral layer has different innervation.
notes.D: The visceral layer has no somatic pain supply from the phrenic nerves, although both outer layers do.

questions.stem: About what fraction of the heart lies to the right of the midline?
questions.why: The normal heart lies obliquely across the mediastinum with its apex projecting leftwards. Roughly one-third of the cardiac mass lies right of the midline and two-thirds to the left.

notes.B: The leftward apex makes the distribution asymmetric, with more of the heart lying left of the midline.
notes.C: Two-thirds is the approximate proportion on the left, where most of the left ventricle projects.
notes.D: The right atrium and part of the right ventricle are usually visible to the right of midline, occupying approximately one-third of the projection.
notes.E: The right atrial contour lies well to the right of the sternum, so the rightward portion exceeds one-tenth.

questions.stem: The heart pumps about how much blood per day?
questions.why: A resting stroke volume near 70 mL and a heart rate near 75 beats per minute give about 5.25 litres per minute. Multiplied by 1,440 minutes, this is about 7,600 litres per day.

notes.A: 760 litres per day averages roughly half a litre per minute, too little for typical resting cardiac output.
notes.C: 76 litres per day is roughly 50 mL per minute, less than the volume of a typical single beat.
notes.D: 76,000 litres per day would require a sustained output above 50 litres per minute, far above the resting estimate.
notes.E: 2,000 litres per day averages about 1.4 litres per minute, whereas a typical resting heart ejects about 5 litres per minute.

questions.stem: The inferior border of the heart is formed mostly by the:
questions.why: The sharp inferior border marks the transition between the anterior and diaphragmatic surfaces. It is formed mostly by the right ventricle, with a small left ventricular contribution close to the apex.

notes.A: The right atrium forms most of the right or vertical border between the openings of the two venae cavae.
notes.B: The left ventricle forms the apex and only the short adjacent part of the inferior border.
notes.D: The left atrium forms most of the posterior base of the heart rather than its sharp inferior edge.
notes.E: The left auricle is part of the upper left contour near the pulmonary trunk, far from the inferior margin.

questions.stem: The sternocostal surface of the heart is formed mainly by the:
questions.why: The right ventricle lies immediately behind much of the sternum and adjacent costal cartilages. It therefore forms most of the sternocostal surface, with smaller contributions from the right atrium and left ventricle.

notes.A: The left ventricle contributes a narrower strip on the left and forms most of the diaphragmatic surface.
notes.B: The right atrium is visible at the right edge of the anterior surface, but most of that surface is ventricular.
notes.C: The left atrium lies chiefly posteriorly and forms most of the cardiac base rather than the sternocostal surface.
notes.E: The left auricle lies near the pulmonary trunk superiorly and forms only a small part of the anterior surface.

questions.stem: The diaphragmatic surface of the heart is formed by the:

options.label: C
options.text: right atrium and the right ventricle equally

options.label: D
options.text: left atrium and the left ventricle equally

questions.why: The lower surface rests on the diaphragm and is formed roughly two-thirds by the left ventricle and one-third by the right. The posterior interventricular groove separates the two ventricular contributions.

notes.A: Both ventricles form this surface, with the left ventricle accounting for the larger area against the diaphragm.
notes.B: The atria contribute principally to the posterior base and do not account for the ventricular surface facing the diaphragm.
notes.C: The right atrium mainly forms the right border, while the right ventricle contributes a smaller area than the left.
notes.D: The left ventricle does make up most of this surface, but its main partner there is the right ventricle.

questions.stem: The right border of the heart is surface-marked from the right:
questions.why: The right atrial margin is projected as a slightly convex line just to the right of the sternum. It extends approximately from the right third to the right sixth costal cartilage.

notes.B: The first to third cartilages are above most of the right cardiac contour and mainly overlie the upper mediastinal region.
notes.C: The right second cartilage is near the ascending aorta and aortic listening area, above the usual right atrial border.
notes.D: Starting at the fifth would omit much of the upper right atrial contour, and the eighth lies below it.
notes.E: The fourth and ninth cartilages are too low as paired endpoints for the usual right cardiac projection.

questions.stem: The left border of the heart runs from the apex up to the left:

options.label: A
options.text: 4th costal cartilage, about 6 cm from the sternum

options.label: B
options.text: 2nd costal cartilage, about 2 cm from the sternum

options.label: C
options.text: 1st costal cartilage, at the sternal margin

options.label: D
options.text: 3rd intercostal space, in the midclavicular line

options.label: E
options.text: 5th costal cartilage, about 2 cm from the sternum

questions.why: The left border of the heart runs from the apex up to the left 2nd costal cartilage about 2 cm from the sternum (overlying the left auricle).

notes.A: The fourth cartilage is lower than the usual superior endpoint, and 6 cm from the sternum places it farther laterally.
notes.C: The first cartilage is too high and near the upper mediastinum, above the normal upper left cardiac contour.
notes.D: The midclavicular line is the usual lateral landmark for the apex rather than the superior end near the sternum.
notes.E: The fifth cartilage lies near the lower left cardiac region and does not locate the superior end of the border.

questions.stem: The endocardium is continuous with the:
questions.why: Endocardium provides the endothelial surface of the heart chambers and covers valve leaflets. Its lining is continuous with the vascular endothelium at the openings of the great vessels.

notes.A: Visceral serous pericardium covers the outside of the heart as epicardium, separated from the endocardium by myocardial tissue.
notes.B: The fibrous skeleton supports the valve orifices and can underlie endocardium, but it is not a continuous endothelial lining.
notes.D: Mediastinal pleura lies outside the fibrous pericardium and is mesothelium rather than cardiac or vascular endothelium.
notes.E: Myocardium lies deep to both chamber lining and external epicardium, while endocardial continuity refers to the luminal endothelial layer.

questions.stem: The ear-shaped extension of each atrium is the:
questions.why: Each atrium bears a small ear-shaped muscular pouch, the auricle, which increases its capacity.

notes.A: The infundibulum is the smooth ventricular outflow leading to the pulmonary valve, not an atrial appendage.
notes.B: The sinus venarum is the smooth venous receiving region of the right atrium, distinct from its pectinate appendage.
notes.C: The limbus is the raised rim around the fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum.
notes.E: The conus arteriosus is the right ventricular outflow tract and directs blood towards the pulmonary trunk.

questions.stem: The trabeculae carneae occur in how many varieties?
questions.why: Trabeculae carneae are ventricular muscle projections classically grouped into ridges attached throughout, bridges attached at both ends, and papillary muscles attached at one end. The free papillary tips give rise to chordae tendineae.

notes.A: Grouping them into two classes omits one of the three distinct attachment patterns in the classical description.
notes.B: The classical arrangement has three patterns based on muscle attachment, with no separate fourth class for bridges in a particular wall.
notes.C: Variation in shape and position occurs within the three attachment patterns rather than creating five recognised classes.
notes.D: The muscular projections share a ventricular location but differ in attachment, so they are not all of a single type.

questions.stem: The papillary muscles of the right ventricle are named:
questions.why: The right ventricle has anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscle groups supporting the tricuspid leaflets through chordae. The septal group can be small or variable.

notes.B: The anterior and posterior groups are present, but this pair alone omits the usual septal group on the ventricular septum.
notes.C: The named right ventricular groups are based on anterior, posterior and septal origins, rather than a right-and-left pair.
notes.D: The free wall has anterior and posterior papillary groups, while the septal group takes origin on the interventricular septum.
notes.E: A two-group description suits the mitral papillary system better than the tricuspid support in a typical right ventricle.
