questions.stem: Compared with the right atrium, the left atrium is:
questions.why: The left atrium usually has a smaller capacity and a thicker wall than the right atrium. Most of its chamber lies posteriorly, where it receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins.

notes.A: The right atrium usually has the larger capacity and thinner wall, receiving blood from the venae cavae.
notes.C: Smaller capacity fits the left atrium, but its wall is generally thicker than the right atrial wall.
notes.D: A thicker wall fits the left atrium, while the larger cavity is usually the right atrium.
notes.E: The atria have different wall thicknesses and capacities despite each having an appendage and a venous receiving region.

questions.stem: The wall of the left ventricle is about how many times as thick as that of the right?
questions.why: The left ventricular free wall is roughly three times as thick as the right because it must generate pressure for the higher-resistance systemic circulation. Both ventricles eject about the same volume per beat.

notes.A: Twice the thickness underestimates the conventional ratio of the adult left ventricular free wall to the right.
notes.B: Five times the thickness is higher than the usual teaching estimate, although measurements vary with site and cardiac phase.
notes.D: A tenfold difference is well beyond the normal anatomical comparison and does not describe a typical adult heart.
notes.E: Equal wall thickness would ignore the substantially greater pressure required of the left ventricle in systemic circulation.

questions.stem: The fibrous rings of the heart are stronger on the:
questions.why: Fibrous support is stronger on the left, where the mitral annulus and aortic–mitral continuity contain substantial fibrous tissue. The tricuspid support on the right is less completely fibrous.

notes.A: Right-sided valve support does include fibrous tissue near the central fibrous body, but it is less extensive around the tricuspid annulus.
notes.B: The annular structures support the valve openings at their junctions, rather than being stronger simply on their atrial surface.
notes.C: Anterior describes a direction in the heart but does not capture the difference between mitral and tricuspid fibrous support.
notes.E: The apex is predominantly ventricular muscle, distant from the valve rings that form much of the heart's fibrous framework.

questions.stem: The trigonum fibrosum of the human heart represents the animal:
questions.why: The right human fibrous trigone is a dense part of the central cardiac skeleton. In some mammals that region contains an os cordis, a bone within the fibrous supporting tissue.

notes.A: The moderator band is ventricular muscle carrying conduction fibres, while the trigone is dense connective tissue near valve rings.
notes.B: The ductus arteriosus is a fetal arterial connection that normally closes to become a ligament outside the cardiac skeleton.
notes.C: The sinus venosus is an embryonic receiving chamber that contributes to atrial and coronary venous structures.
notes.D: The conus arteriosus is the smooth right ventricular outflow tract, not a bony or fibrous mass between annuli.

questions.stem: The anatomical position of the mitral valve is opposite the left:
questions.why: The mitral valve projects around the left fourth costal cartilage near the sternum. Its sounds conduct towards the left ventricular apex, so the auscultation site is farther down and lateral.

notes.B: The second left costal cartilage is high near the root of the great arteries rather than the mitral valve.
notes.C: The third parasternal interspace is closer to the outflow region than the anatomical mitral position.
notes.D: The fifth interspace near the midclavicular line is where mitral sounds are usually best heard, not the valve projection.
notes.E: The sixth costal cartilage is below the typical projection of the mitral valve and closer to the inferior heart border.

questions.stem: The tricuspid area of auscultation is the:
questions.why: In this lecture's scheme the tricuspid valve is auscultated low over the sternum, at the right 5th intercostal space at the lower sternal border.

notes.A: Mitral area.
notes.C: Aortic area.
notes.D: Pulmonary area.
notes.E: Anatomical aortic valve.

questions.stem: Heart sounds are heard best:

options.label: A
options.text: exactly over the anatomical site of each heart valve

options.label: B
options.text: only at the apex of the heart

options.label: C
options.text: where the chamber or vessel lies near the chest wall

options.label: D
options.text: only along the right sternal border

options.label: E
options.text: over the back between the scapulae

questions.why: Valve sounds are transmitted along the direction of blood flow towards areas where a chamber or vessel approaches the chest wall. The best listening site may therefore differ from the valve's surface projection.

notes.A: The anatomical projection locates the valve itself, while transmitted vibrations can be louder at a different site.
notes.B: The apex is the usual mitral area, whereas the aortic and pulmonary sounds have separate parasternal sites.
notes.D: The right upper sternal border is useful for aortic sounds but does not contain all four listening areas.
notes.E: Interscapular listening can help assess certain transmitted murmurs, but normal valve areas are on the anterior chest.

questions.stem: The first and second heart sounds are described phonetically as:
questions.why: The first sound, lub, accompanies mitral and tricuspid closure at the onset of ventricular systole. The second sound, dub, accompanies aortic and pulmonary closure at the start of diastole.

notes.A: Dub refers to semilunar closure at the end of ejection, which occurs after the first sound.
notes.B: Clicks and snaps can occur with valvular abnormalities and are distinct from the normal pair of closure sounds.
notes.C: A whoosh describes a murmur from turbulent flow rather than the normal first closure sound.
notes.E: The normal pair reflects two different groups of closing valves and is conventionally described as lub-dub.

questions.stem: The gross-anatomy lecture places the SA node in the:

options.label: E
options.text: posterior wall of the right atrium

questions.why: The sinoatrial node lies near the superior cavoatrial junction at the upper end of the sulcus terminalis. Its position in the right atrial wall contrasts with the low septal position of the atrioventricular node.

notes.A: The lower interatrial septal region near the coronary sinus is the location of the atrioventricular node.
notes.B: The atrioventricular bundle passes near the membranous septum after leaving the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: The left atrial wall receives the pulmonary veins but lacks the normal sinoatrial pacemaker near the superior vena cava.
notes.D: The muscular interventricular septum carries ventricular bundle branches rather than the primary atrial pacemaker.

questions.stem: The Purkinje fibres lie within the:
questions.why: Purkinje fibres branch from the ventricular bundle branches and form a network just beneath the ventricular endocardium. They rapidly spread excitation to the contractile myocardium of both ventricles.

notes.B: Atrial myocardium receives and conducts the sinoatrial impulse before it reaches the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: The lower interatrial septal region contains the atrioventricular node, which relays impulses before ventricular activation.
notes.D: The fibrous skeleton insulates atria from ventricles, except where the atrioventricular bundle penetrates it.
notes.E: The coronary sulcus carries vessels in the external atrioventricular groove, away from the subendocardial conduction network.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a branch of the right coronary artery?
questions.why: The obtuse marginal artery arises from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery. It supplies the lateral left ventricular wall, in contrast to the right marginal branch along the acute edge.

notes.A: A conus branch often arises from proximal right coronary artery and supplies the right ventricular outflow tract.
notes.C: The right marginal artery usually branches from the right coronary artery and supplies the right ventricular free wall.
notes.D: In the usual right-dominant pattern the atrioventricular nodal artery is a right coronary branch near the crux.
notes.E: The posterior interventricular artery normally arises from the right coronary artery in a right-dominant heart.

questions.stem: The diagonal artery is a branch of the:
questions.why: Diagonal arteries arise from the anterior interventricular artery, which is a major branch of the left coronary artery. They cross the anterolateral left ventricle to supply its free wall.

notes.A: The right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove and gives branches such as the right marginal.
notes.B: The right marginal artery supplies the acute margin of the right ventricle, opposite the usual diagonal territory.
notes.D: The posterior interventricular artery runs in the diaphragmatic groove and supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum.
notes.E: The conus artery primarily supplies the right ventricular outflow rather than the anterolateral left ventricle.

questions.stem: The cusp of the aortic valve that has no coronary artery arising above it is the:
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries arise above the right and left cusps, so the posterior cusp has none and is called the non-coronary cusp.

notes.A: The right coronary ostium is normally in the aortic sinus immediately above the right coronary cusp.
notes.B: The left coronary ostium opens in the left aortic sinus above the corresponding valve cusp.
notes.C: Anterior is a traditional term for the right coronary cusp, whose adjacent sinus gives origin to the right coronary artery.
notes.E: Septal is a designation for a tricuspid leaflet rather than a recognised cusp of the aortic valve.

questions.stem: The coronary sinus has how many named tributaries?
questions.why: The usual anatomical list includes the great, middle and small cardiac veins, the posterior vein of the left ventricle and the oblique vein of the left atrium. Smaller branches and individual anatomy can vary.

notes.A: Counting the three named cardiac veins alone leaves out the posterior ventricular and oblique atrial tributaries.
notes.B: The great and middle cardiac veins are two important tributaries, but three additional veins belong to the classical list.
notes.C: Smaller venous channels can vary, but the standard list has five rather than seven principal named tributaries.
notes.D: A four-vein list is incomplete because it usually leaves out a small tributary such as the oblique vein.

questions.stem: Which vein drains directly into the right atrium, not into the coronary sinus?

options.label: E
options.text: Oblique vein of the left atrium

questions.why: Anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior right ventricular wall through separate openings in the right atrium. Their blood bypasses the coronary sinus, unlike blood carried by the main posterior venous channels.

notes.B: The great cardiac vein drains the anterior interventricular region and passes into the coronary sinus.
notes.C: The middle cardiac vein follows the posterior interventricular artery and usually enters the coronary sinus near its opening.
notes.D: The small cardiac vein runs with right-sided coronary branches and usually ends in the coronary sinus.
notes.E: The oblique vein of the left atrium descends along its posterior wall and joins the coronary sinus.

questions.stem: The coronary sinus lies in the:
questions.why: The coronary sinus runs along the posterior atrioventricular groove between the left atrium and left ventricle. It opens into the right atrium near the orifice of the inferior vena cava.

notes.A: The anterior interventricular groove contains the anterior interventricular artery and great cardiac vein on the sternocostal surface.
notes.C: The posterior interventricular groove contains the middle cardiac vein as it approaches the coronary sinus.
notes.D: The sulcus terminalis is an external right atrial landmark marking the boundary between smooth and pectinate regions.
notes.E: The transverse pericardial sinus is a passage behind the arterial roots, separate from the cardiac venous channel.

questions.stem: In the right atrium, the opening of the inferior vena cava is guarded by:
questions.why: The inferior vena cava may have a rudimentary crescentic fold at its right atrial opening, called the Eustachian valve. In the fetus this fold helps direct inferior caval blood towards the foramen ovale.

notes.A: The three-leaflet tricuspid valve is at the passage from the right atrium to the right ventricle.
notes.B: The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge separating the smooth and pectinate regions of the right atrium.
notes.D: The limbus forms the raised rim of the fossa ovalis on the right side of the interatrial septum.
notes.E: The Eustachian fold can be inconspicuous or absent in some adults, but it is a recognised anatomical feature.

questions.stem: Components of the respiratory system:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: The conducting division includes the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea

options.label: B
options.text: The respiratory division is the lungs and alveoli

options.label: C
options.text: The upper respiratory tract includes the trachea

options.label: D
options.text: The lower respiratory tract includes the larynx

options.label: E
options.text: Respiratory movements are produced by the diaphragm and thoracic wall muscles

notes.A: The conducting division moves air without gas exchange: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea.
notes.B: The respiratory division, where gas exchange happens, is the lungs and alveoli.
notes.C: In the lecture's scheme the upper tract runs from the nose down to the trachea.
notes.D: The larynx is upper tract; the lower tract is the bronchi, bronchioles and lungs.
notes.E: The diaphragm and thoracic wall muscles change chest volume to move air.

questions.why: The lecture splits the tract at the trachea: nose, pharynx, larynx and trachea form the upper tract; bronchi, bronchioles and lungs the lower.

questions.stem: The nose and nasal cavity:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: The anterior openings are the external nares

options.label: B
options.text: The posterior openings into the pharynx are the choanae

options.label: C
options.text: The vestibule lies just inside the external nares

options.label: D
options.text: The posterior half of the septum is formed by the vomer and perpendicular plate of the ethmoid

options.label: E
options.text: The anterior half of the septum is bony

notes.A: The external nares are the paired anterior nostrils giving access to the vestibules.
notes.B: The choanae are the paired posterior apertures that open into the nasopharynx.
notes.C: The vestibule is the widened area just inside each nostril and normally carries coarse hairs.
notes.D: The vomer forms much of the posteroinferior septum, while the ethmoid perpendicular plate contributes superiorly.
notes.E: Septal cartilage provides most of the anterior partition between the nasal cavities and supports the mobile nose.

questions.why: The nasal cavity extends from the external nares to the choanae. The anterior vestibule transitions into the main nasal passage, and a cartilaginous and bony septum separates the two sides.

questions.stem: The pharynx:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: is a fibromuscular tube about 12 cm long

options.label: B
options.text: extends from the base of the skull to the oesophagus

options.label: C
options.text: has superior, middle and inferior constrictors

options.label: D
options.text: is supplemented by stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus

options.label: E
options.text: communicates behind with the nose, mouth and larynx

notes.A: The pharynx is a fibromuscular channel roughly 12–14 cm long in adults.
notes.B: It attaches to the skull base above and continues with the oesophagus near the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.
notes.C: Three constrictors form an overlapping muscular wall that can narrow successively during swallowing.
notes.D: The stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles that help elevate and shorten the pharynx.
notes.E: The pharynx is posterior to the nose, mouth and larynx, and its openings to them face anteriorly.

questions.why: The pharynx is a muscular passage behind the nose, mouth and larynx. Its circular constrictors propel a swallowed bolus, while longitudinal muscles elevate the pharyngeal wall.

questions.stem: The pharyngeal recess and opening of the auditory tube are features of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube is on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall. Its cartilaginous prominence forms the torus tubarius, behind which lies the pharyngeal recess.

notes.B: The oropharynx is below the soft palate and contains the palatine tonsils rather than the tubal openings.
notes.C: The laryngopharynx leads down to the oesophagus and has a piriform recess on each side of the laryngeal inlet.
notes.D: The laryngeal vestibule extends from the laryngeal inlet to the vestibular folds within the larynx.
notes.E: The piriform recess is a depression beside the laryngeal inlet, well below the pharyngeal recess.

questions.stem: Parts of the pharynx:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: The oropharynx extends from the soft palate to the upper border of the epiglottis

options.label: B
options.text: The oropharynx has the palatine tonsil in its lateral wall

options.label: C
options.text: The vallecula and lingual tonsil relate to the anterior wall of the oropharynx

options.label: D
options.text: The laryngopharynx ends at the lower border of the thyroid cartilage

options.label: E
options.text: The piriform recess lies beside the laryngeal inlet

notes.A: The oropharynx occupies the segment below the soft palate and above the upper epiglottic region.
notes.B: Each palatine tonsil lies in the lateral oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
notes.C: The posterior tongue bears the lingual tonsil, and the valleculae lie between the tongue base and epiglottis.
notes.D: The lower border of the cricoid, below the thyroid cartilage, marks the usual start of the oesophagus.
notes.E: Each piriform recess lies lateral to the laryngeal inlet and directs swallowed material around it.

questions.why: The subdivisions of the pharynx are named for the cavities that open into them. The laryngopharynx passes behind the larynx and becomes the oesophagus below the cricoid at about C6.

questions.stem: From superior to inferior, Waldeyer's ring is made up of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil occupies the nasopharyngeal roof and the tubal tonsils flank the auditory tube openings. The palatine tonsils are lower in the oropharynx, and the lingual tonsil is at the tongue base.

notes.A: The adenoids hang from the nasopharyngeal roof, above the tubal tonsils, and the tongue base is below the palatine tonsils.
notes.C: The palatine tonsil lies in the oropharynx, below both of the tonsillar sites in the nasopharynx.
notes.D: The lingual tonsil lies at the tongue base, making this sequence run from lowest to highest.
notes.E: Tubal tonsils lie close to the auditory tube openings in the nasopharynx, above the palatine tonsils.

questions.stem: The laryngeal aditus is bounded laterally by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The aryepiglottic folds extend from the epiglottis towards the arytenoid region and form the sides of the laryngeal inlet. They separate the inlet from the piriform recesses.

notes.A: The free upper margin of the epiglottis forms the anterior boundary of the inlet rather than its lateral margins.
notes.B: The interarytenoid notch lies posteriorly between the arytenoid prominences at the back of the inlet.
notes.D: Corniculate cartilages form small posterior prominences within the folded mucosa rather than constituting the full lateral boundaries.
notes.E: The vocal folds lie deeper within the larynx and form the margins of the rima glottidis.

questions.stem: The smooth muscle and blood vessels of the trachea are supplied by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The mucous membrane gets the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

notes.A: Mucous membrane.
notes.B: Not tracheal.
notes.C: Not tracheal.
notes.E: Not tracheal.

questions.stem: The serratus posterior inferior:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: arises from C6–T2 and elevates ribs 2–5

options.label: B
options.text: arises from T1–T4 and elevates the upper ribs

options.label: C
options.text: arises from L1–L4 and elevates the lowest ribs

options.label: D
options.text: arises from T7–T10 and depresses ribs 7–10

options.label: E
options.text: arises from T11–L2, depresses lowest 4 ribs

questions.why: Serratus posterior inferior extends from lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinous processes to ribs 9–12. Its oblique fibres are traditionally described as depressing or stabilising the lower ribs, although its respiratory role is debated.

notes.A: Attachment to upper ribs and possible rib elevation are features of serratus posterior superior, which lies higher on the back.
notes.B: The upper-rib attachments belong to serratus posterior superior, while the inferior muscle has a thoracolumbar origin.
notes.C: Serratus posterior inferior spans the thoracolumbar junction and is traditionally classed as a depressor rather than an elevator.
notes.D: The muscle attaches to the four lowest ribs, below the seventh to tenth set in this sequence.

questions.stem: The thoracic duct passes through the diaphragm with the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: D
options.text: greater splanchnic nerve in the crus

questions.why: The thoracic duct ascends from the upper abdomen through the aortic hiatus at about T12. It enters the posterior mediastinum behind the diaphragm alongside the descending aorta.

notes.B: The oesophageal hiatus carries the oesophagus and vagal trunks at about T10, rather than the thoracic duct.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon around T8, well anterior to the thoracic duct.
notes.D: The greater splanchnic nerve can traverse a crus separately while the thoracic duct uses the aortic hiatus.
notes.E: The superior epigastric artery passes anteriorly near the sternocostal region, separate from the posterior duct.

questions.stem: Pain from irritation of the central diaphragm is referred to the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The central diaphragm has phrenic sensory supply from cervical segments C3–C5, especially C4. Overlap with the segmental origin of the supraclavicular nerves allows pain to be felt at the shoulder tip.

notes.A: The umbilical skin has a roughly T10 segmental supply, outside the cervical phrenic referral pattern.
notes.C: The groin has upper lumbar sensory supply, which does not share the central diaphragmatic phrenic segments.
notes.D: Interscapular pain can accompany some posterior thoracic conditions, but the central diaphragm typically refers through cervical afferents.
notes.E: The epigastrium can receive pain from upper abdominal viscera, while central diaphragmatic irritation characteristically refers towards the shoulder.

questions.stem: The costochondral joints are:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Costochondral joints are primary cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) between costal cartilage and bony rib, and are essentially immovable.

notes.A: Gliding between flat articular surfaces occurs in plane synovial joints, such as most sternocostal joints after the first.
notes.B: A symphysis contains fibrocartilage between bone surfaces, as in the joint between adjacent vertebral bodies.
notes.D: A saddle joint is a biaxial synovial joint with reciprocal curves, exemplified by the first carpometacarpal joint.
notes.E: Sutures join skull bones with fibrous tissue, whereas a costochondral junction is continuous through hyaline cartilage.

questions.stem: An inhaled foreign body most often lodges in the right main bronchus because the right bronchus is:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: An inhaled object usually enters the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter and more vertical (more in line with the trachea) than the left.

notes.A: The left main bronchus is longer and narrower, so these features describe the less direct route from the trachea.
notes.B: The longer, narrower and more horizontal bronchus is the left, which passes beneath the aortic arch.
notes.C: The right main bronchus passes posterior to the right pulmonary artery and is not defined by a course behind the oesophagus.
notes.E: The main bronchi retain cartilage to support the airway, whereas bronchioles farther downstream lack cartilage.

questions.stem: The number of segmental bronchi in the left upper lobe (as taught) is:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: In the five-segment teaching scheme the left upper lobe has apical, posterior, anterior, superior lingular and inferior lingular segmental bronchi. The apical and posterior branches often share an apicoposterior stem.

notes.A: The number two refers to the lobar divisions of the left lung, which has additional segmental subdivisions.
notes.B: Three is the usual segment count of the right upper lobe, whereas the left upper lobe includes the lingula.
notes.C: Four can result from counting a common apicoposterior branch as one, but the stated scheme counts apical and posterior territories separately.
notes.D: Ten is a teaching count for the segments of an entire lung, including the lower lobe.

questions.stem: Where the costal pleura becomes continuous with the diaphragmatic pleura is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Where the costal pleura turns to become diaphragmatic pleura is the costal line of pleural reflection, the lowest extent of the pleura.

notes.B: The sternal line is the anterior reflection where costal pleura turns onto the mediastinum behind the sternum.
notes.C: The vertebral reflection is the posterior turn between costal and mediastinal pleura near the vertebral column.
notes.D: Diaphragmatic describes one of the pleural surfaces that meet at the reflection termed the costal line.
notes.E: Cervical pleura is the cupola above the first rib, well above the inferior costal reflection.

questions.stem: Excess pleural fluid collects in the costodiaphragmatic recess because:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: the diaphragm is higher on the left side

options.label: B
options.text: the lungs stop short of the pleural reflection

options.label: C
options.text: the cervical pleura lies above the clavicle

options.label: D
options.text: the two pleural sacs meet behind the sternum

options.label: E
options.text: the pulmonary ligament holds fluid at the hilum

questions.why: The parietal pleura reaches farther inferiorly than the lung, creating a dependent recess between the costal and diaphragmatic surfaces. Gravity draws free pleural fluid into this space in an upright person.

notes.A: The right dome is usually higher because of the liver, but dependent recesses exist on both sides.
notes.C: Cervical pleura rises above the first rib and clavicle, an apical position away from dependent fluid.
notes.D: The pleural sacs are separate, even where their anterior reflections approach one another behind the sternum.
notes.E: The pulmonary ligament is a double pleural fold below the root and does not explain the inferior pleural gutter.

questions.stem: The posterior part of the nasal septum is formed by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid descends from the cranial base to form the upper bony septum. The vomer completes the posteroinferior septum, and septal cartilage forms its anterior part.

notes.A: The vomer is part of the posterior septum, but septal cartilage fits in front of the bony components.
notes.B: The nasal bones support the bridge of the nose rather than forming the two major plates of the posterior septum.
notes.D: The palatine crest and sphenoid help support the septum, but neither replaces its vomer and ethmoid components.
notes.E: The maxillary crest supports the lower margin of the septum, while septal cartilage accounts for much of the anterior partition.

questions.stem: The nasal cavity opens into the nasopharynx through the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The choanae are paired posterior nasal openings on either side of the vomer. They allow air to pass from the nasal cavities into the nasopharynx behind the nasal septum.

notes.A: The external nares are openings from the face into the anterior nasal vestibules.
notes.B: The vestibule is just inside each nostril and leads into the nasal cavity rather than opening into the pharynx.
notes.C: The pharyngeal recess is a blind pocket in the nasopharynx posterior to the tubal prominence.
notes.E: The auditory tube connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear and is a separate lateral opening.

questions.stem: The nasopharynx extends down to the level of:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The nasopharynx extends from the skull base to the level of the soft palate, approximately C1. The soft palate elevates during swallowing to separate it from the oropharynx.

notes.A: C3 is closer to the hyoid and upper epiglottic region, below the soft palate.
notes.B: C4 is near the thyroid cartilage and the laryngeal part of the pharynx, below the nasopharynx.
notes.C: C6 is the approximate level of the transition from laryngopharynx to oesophagus at the lower cricoid border.
notes.D: C2 lies below the conventional soft-palate level and behind a more caudal portion of the pharynx.

questions.stem: The pharynx becomes continuous with the oesophagus at the level of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The laryngopharynx narrows at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, usually at C6 in adults. Its lumen continues into the cervical oesophagus at the upper oesophageal sphincter.

notes.B: The upper border of the epiglottis helps mark the transition into laryngopharynx, several levels above the oesophagus.
notes.C: The hyoid lies near C3 and supports the tongue and larynx, above the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
notes.D: The thyroid prominence lies above the cricoid and therefore above the start of the cervical oesophagus.
notes.E: The first tracheal ring is an airway landmark, while the lower cricoid border marks the conventional transition of the pharynx.

questions.stem: The muscle arising from the auditory tube that joins the pharyngeal wall is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Salpingopharyngeus originates from the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube and descends in the salpingopharyngeal fold. It blends with palatopharyngeus and helps elevate the pharyngeal wall during swallowing.

notes.A: Stylopharyngeus originates from the styloid process and enters the pharyngeal wall between the superior and middle constrictors.
notes.C: Palatopharyngeus originates from the palate and blends with the muscle descending from the auditory tube.
notes.D: The superior constrictor is a circular muscle of the pharyngeal wall rather than a longitudinal muscle descending from the tube.
notes.E: Levator veli palatini attaches near the auditory tube but acts on the soft palate through the palatine aponeurosis.

questions.stem: Enlarged adenoids block the airway because they lie in the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The adenoids are the pharyngeal tonsil in the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Enlargement can narrow the passage behind the choanae and impede nasal airflow.

notes.A: The palatine tonsils lie in the lateral oropharynx between two palatal arches, below the site of adenoidal obstruction.
notes.B: The lingual tonsil lies at the tongue base and may affect the oropharyngeal rather than nasal airway.
notes.D: The piriform recesses are alongside the laryngeal inlet in the lower pharynx, remote from the choanae.
notes.E: The laryngeal vestibule lies inside the larynx above the vestibular folds, well below the nasopharyngeal roof.

questions.stem: The vallecula lies between the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: D
options.text: base of the tongue and epiglottis

questions.why: The epiglottic valleculae are paired depressions where the tongue base meets the anterior surface of the epiglottis. Glossoepiglottic folds form their margins and separate them at the midline.

notes.A: The palatine arches bound the fossa that contains the palatine tonsil in the lateral oropharyngeal wall.
notes.B: The area between the aryepiglottic fold and the thyroid cartilage forms the piriform recess at the side of the inlet.
notes.C: The soft palate contributes to the boundary between nasopharynx and oropharynx rather than enclosing the valleculae.
notes.E: The laryngeal ventricle lies between the vestibular and vocal folds, below the epiglottic valleculae.

questions.stem: A fish bone swallowed is most likely to lodge in the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The piriform recess is a gutter beside the laryngeal inlet that helps guide the swallowed bolus around it. A sharp bone can catch in its mucosa near the internal laryngeal nerve.

notes.A: The pharyngeal tonsil is high in the nasopharynx, outside the usual path of a swallowed bolus.
notes.B: The pharyngeal recess is behind the auditory tube opening in the nasopharynx, not alongside the food passage.
notes.C: The laryngeal ventricle is a recess inside the airway between the vestibular and vocal folds.
notes.D: A choana is a posterior nasal opening that normally carries air rather than swallowed food.

questions.stem: Which laryngeal cartilage forms a complete ring?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The cricoid is a complete ring of hyaline cartilage, with a broad posterior lamina and a narrow anterior arch. It supports the airway at the transition from larynx to trachea.

notes.B: The thyroid cartilage has two plates that meet anteriorly, leaving it open posteriorly.
notes.C: Each arytenoid is a small paired cartilage on the cricoid that positions a vocal fold.
notes.D: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped elastic cartilage at the inlet rather than a ring around the airway.
notes.E: Corniculate cartilages are small nodules on the arytenoid apices and do not surround the airway.

questions.stem: After puberty, the larynx in males differs most because:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: the larynx moves down to C7

options.label: E
options.text: the vocal folds lose their glands

questions.why: The thyroid cartilage also becomes prominent.

notes.A: It stays at C4–C6.
notes.C: Stays elastic.
notes.D: Stays a ring.
notes.E: True folds have no glands anyway.

questions.stem: The posterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet is formed by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The posterior margin of the laryngeal inlet is formed by the mucosa across the arytenoid region and the interarytenoid notch. The aryepiglottic folds run forward from there to form the lateral margins.

notes.A: The upper free edge of the epiglottis forms the anterior margin of the laryngeal inlet.
notes.B: The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral borders and approach the arytenoid region at their posterior ends.
notes.D: The thyroid laminae provide the anterior and lateral framework of the larynx rather than the posterior inlet margin.
notes.E: The vestibular folds are within the larynx below the inlet and bound the rima vestibuli.

questions.stem: The trachea divides at the carina at the level of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The trachea normally bifurcates near the sternal-angle plane at the T4–T5 disc, approximately the upper border of T5. The exact level can move with respiration and posture.

notes.A: The T3 body lies higher than the usual sternal-angle plane of tracheal bifurcation.
notes.B: T6 can be approached when the carina descends with inspiration, but the standard surface landmark is higher.
notes.C: The T7 body is too low for the usual resting projection near the sternal angle.
notes.E: The upper border of T3 is superior to the common T4–T5 landmark for the carina.

questions.stem: In a tracheostomy, the structure most likely to be cut in front of the upper trachea is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The thyroid isthmus bridges the front of the upper cervical trachea, typically over the second to fourth rings. It may have to be retracted or divided to expose the anterior tracheal wall.

notes.A: The left brachiocephalic vein normally runs across the upper mediastinum below the upper cervical trachea.
notes.B: The aortic arch lies in the superior mediastinum below the usual approach to the cervical tracheal rings.
notes.C: The common carotid arteries lie lateral in their sheaths, away from the midline structure crossing the trachea.
notes.D: The recurrent laryngeal nerves run in or near the tracheo-oesophageal grooves posterolaterally rather than across the front.

questions.stem: The anterior relations of the trachea in the thorax include the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: As the left brachiocephalic vein runs obliquely towards the superior vena cava, it crosses in front of the vessels and airway of the superior mediastinum. It is an anterior relation of the thoracic trachea.

notes.B: The oesophagus and thoracic duct lie posterior to the trachea within the superior mediastinum.
notes.C: The azygos arch and right vagus lie near the right side of the trachea and right lung root.
notes.D: The sympathetic trunks run beside the vertebral column, behind and lateral to the central air passage.
notes.E: The descending thoracic aorta lies well posterior and to the left of the central thoracic airway.

questions.stem: The neurovascular bundle of an intercostal space lies between the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The principal intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove under a rib. Their neurovascular plane is between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

notes.A: The external and internal intercostals form more superficial layers than the plane containing the main bundle.
notes.C: The pleura lies deeper than the innermost muscle and is separated from the bundle by that muscle where present.
notes.D: Serratus anterior lies outside the rib cage, superficial to the intercostal muscles and their main bundle.
notes.E: Transversus thoracis is a deep anterior chest-wall muscle, but the main bundle follows the costal groove laterally.

questions.stem: A chest drain is inserted just above a rib to avoid the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle runs along the lower edge of a rib in the costal groove. The anatomical reason to approach above the rib is to avoid this larger bundle.

notes.A: Internal thoracic vessels lie close to the sternum, rather than in the main costal groove of a lateral interspace.
notes.B: The long thoracic nerve runs superficially on serratus anterior and is separate from the bundle immediately inferior to a rib.
notes.D: The phrenic nerve runs on the lateral pericardium inside the mediastinum rather than along the ribs.
notes.E: The azygos vein ascends next to the thoracic vertebral bodies and is not in the chest-wall costal groove.

questions.stem: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: T12 vertebra, costal margins and xiphoid

options.label: C
options.text: T2 vertebra, 2nd ribs and sternal angle

questions.why: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by T1, laterally by the first ribs and their cartilages, and anteriorly by the upper border of the manubrium. This plane slopes downwards anteriorly.

notes.A: T12, the costal margins and the xiphisternal region form part of the much larger inferior thoracic aperture.
notes.B: The clavicles overlie the root of the neck, but the bony lateral boundaries of the inlet are the first ribs.
notes.C: The second ribs are landmarks of the sternal angle, below the superior thoracic aperture.
notes.E: T1 is the correct posterior limit, but the first ribs, rather than clavicles, form the lateral margins.

questions.stem: The right dome of the diaphragm is higher than the left mainly because of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The large right lobe of the liver occupies the space beneath the right hemidiaphragm and raises its dome. The left dome usually sits lower, although both move with respiration.

notes.A: The heart lies above the diaphragm and mainly left of midline, rather than elevating the right dome from below.
notes.B: The right crus is generally larger but forms a posterior muscular attachment rather than the primary support beneath the dome.
notes.C: Phrenic nerves activate both hemidiaphragms, and their relative thickness does not account for the usual height difference.
notes.D: The right lung is generally larger, but the right dome's position is chiefly related to the liver underneath it.

questions.stem: The IVC passes through the diaphragm at:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: T12, behind the median arcuate ligament

questions.why: The inferior vena cava traverses a right-sided opening in the central tendon at about T8. The tendinous margins help keep the venous route open as the diaphragm moves.

notes.B: The oesophageal hiatus is at T10 in muscular fibres mainly from the right crus.
notes.C: At T12 the aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament through the posterior aortic hiatus.
notes.D: T8 is appropriate for the caval opening, but it is in the central tendon rather than the left crus.
notes.E: The central tendon does contain the caval opening, but T10 usually marks the oesophageal opening.

questions.stem: The structures passing through the oesophageal hiatus are the oesophagus and:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks form from the oesophageal plexus in the lower thorax. They follow the oesophagus through its muscular hiatus, usually near the T10 level.

notes.A: The thoracic duct passes with the aorta, and the azygos vein may also use the aortic hiatus.
notes.C: Right phrenic branches can accompany the inferior vena cava near its opening in the central tendon.
notes.D: The diaphragmatic crura often provide separate passages for the greater splanchnic nerves outside the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.E: The sympathetic trunks lie behind the medial arcuate ligaments as they enter the upper lumbar region.

questions.stem: A congenital diaphragmatic hernia through the foramen of Bochdalek results from failure of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: A Bochdalek hernia occurs through a posterolateral defect where the pleural and peritoneal cavities should have separated. In the classical embryological account this reflects incomplete closure by the pleuroperitoneal fold or membrane.

notes.A: The septum transversum forms the central tendon in the classical account, away from the posterolateral defect.
notes.B: Cervical myotomes supply muscle precursor cells, while the classic posterolateral hernia involves closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal.
notes.D: The dorsal oesophageal mesentery provides tissue for the crura around the oesophagus, close to the midline.
notes.E: A defect at the meeting of the sternal and costal parts is anterior and is called a Morgagni hernia.

questions.stem: The central tendon of the diaphragm develops from the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: In the classical account, the septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm. The dorsal oesophageal mesentery gives rise to the crural region, while muscle precursors enter from cervical somites.

notes.A: Pleuroperitoneal membranes close the posterolateral canals, contributing tissue around the developing diaphragmatic partition.
notes.B: The dorsal oesophageal mesentery forms the tissue around the oesophagus that contributes to the diaphragmatic crura.
notes.C: The peripheral body wall contributes to the developing diaphragm, while the central tendon is assigned to the septum transversum in this scheme.
notes.E: Cervical myotomes provide the migrating muscle precursors, which accounts for the cervical roots of phrenic motor supply.

questions.stem: Which pairing of thoracic joint and type is correct?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The sternoclavicular joint has reciprocally curved articular surfaces and is classified as a synovial saddle joint. Its articular disc improves congruence and helps accommodate movement of the clavicle in several planes.

notes.A: At costochondral junctions the bony rib is continuous with hyaline cartilage in a primary cartilaginous joint.
notes.B: Many interchondral joints between adjacent costal cartilages are plane synovial joints rather than synchondroses.
notes.C: Between vertebral bodies the intervertebral disc forms a symphysis, while the separate facet joints are synovial.
notes.D: The manubriosternal joint is generally a symphysis and may ossify with age, rather than forming a gliding plane joint.

questions.stem: The eparterial bronchus supplies the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The right upper lobar bronchus branches above the right pulmonary artery at the lung root. This superior relation gives it the name eparterial, while the bronchus continuing below is hyparterial.

notes.B: The middle lobe is supplied by a branch of the right bronchus intermedius below the eparterial origin.
notes.C: The left upper lobar bronchus arises on the left, where the main pulmonary artery lies above the bronchus.
notes.D: The lingula is a part of the left upper lobe that receives lingular branches from its lobar bronchus.
notes.E: The right lower lobar bronchus is a distal branch from the bronchus intermedius below the right pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: The left main bronchus enters the lung opposite:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The left main bronchus takes a longer oblique course beneath the aortic arch to reach the left hilum near T6. There it divides into upper and lower lobar bronchi.

notes.A: The right lung root is commonly projected near T5, above the conventional left hilar level.
notes.C: T4 is close to the sternal-angle plane and carina, upstream of the descending left main bronchus.
notes.D: T8 lies below the usual left hilar entry and closer to more inferior posterior thoracic structures.
notes.E: T7 is one level below the standard surface projection of the left main bronchus entering the hilum.

questions.stem: Bronchial veins on the left drain into the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Superficial left bronchial veins can drain into the accessory hemiazygos or left superior intercostal vein. Deep bronchial veins can also communicate with pulmonary veins, so several drainage pathways exist.

notes.A: The azygos normally receives the right bronchial veins, whereas the left has tributaries to the left-sided azygos system.
notes.B: The brachiocephalic vein may receive blood indirectly through the left superior intercostal vein rather than through the usual direct route.
notes.D: Pulmonary veins can receive deep bronchial drainage, but superficial bronchial veins also have systemic venous routes.
notes.E: The coronary sinus receives venous blood from the myocardium rather than from the bronchial walls.

questions.stem: The cough reflex from the bronchial tree is carried by:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Sensory endings in the bronchial tree detect mechanical or chemical irritation and send signals to the brainstem through vagal afferents. Those signals trigger the coordinated motor response of coughing.

notes.A: Sympathetic fibres can regulate vascular tone, but airway irritation normally initiates the cough reflex via the vagus.
notes.B: Phrenic motor fibres activate the diaphragm during respiratory movements, downstream of the sensory trigger for cough.
notes.C: Intercostal nerves drive parts of the thoracic wall during coughing rather than carrying the principal bronchial sensory input.
notes.E: Glossopharyngeal afferents are important for pharyngeal sensation and the gag reflex, while bronchial cough input is vagal.

questions.stem: Bronchodilation is produced by:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Vagal efferents are bronchoconstrictor.

notes.A: Constrictor.
notes.B: Diaphragm.
notes.C: Sensory.
notes.D: Chest wall.

questions.stem: The pleura extends lowest posteriorly, to the level of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The inferior pleural reflection slopes down towards the back of the thorax. It crosses the twelfth rib and approaches the lower T12 level medially, below the inferior lung border.

notes.B: L2 is below the usual posterior pleural reflection and is already in the lumbar abdominal region.
notes.C: The eighth rib is a typical lateral landmark for the lower lung border, rather than the lowest posterior pleura.
notes.D: The pleura reaches about the tenth rib at the midaxillary line, then extends farther down posteriorly.
notes.E: T10 is above the lowest posterior pleural limit and nearer the level of the posterior lower lung margin.

questions.stem: The cervical pleura rises above the clavicle by about:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The cervical pleura forms a dome over the lung apex, commonly projecting about 2.5 cm above the medial clavicle. The suprapleural membrane supports it at the thoracic inlet.

notes.A: One centimetre underestimates the usual surface projection of the pleural dome above the medial clavicle.
notes.C: Five centimetres is higher than the normal projection of the pleural apex into the root of the neck.
notes.D: A height of 7.5 cm would place the pleural dome much farther up the neck than expected.
notes.E: Half a centimetre is below the conventional estimate of the supraclavicular projection of the dome.

questions.stem: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the preferred site for thoracocentesis because:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: B
options.text: the intercostal vessels are all absent there

options.label: C
options.text: the lung does not fill it in quiet breathing

options.label: D
options.text: it is free of the phrenic nerve

questions.why: In quiet breathing the lower lung margin leaves part of the costodiaphragmatic recess unoccupied. Fluid can collect there by gravity, although ultrasound is used to locate a suitable pocket before aspiration.

notes.A: Pleural thickness does not explain access to fluid, which depends on the position of lung and diaphragm.
notes.B: Intercostal vessels supply the adjacent thoracic wall even at the level of the recess and remain relevant to access.
notes.D: Separation from the mediastinal course of the phrenic nerve does not determine where most dependent fluid accumulates.
notes.E: The diaphragm moves during respiration, so the recess and adjacent organs have to be assessed in the intended position.

questions.stem: The hilum of the lung lies on its:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The lung hilum is the gateway on the concave mediastinal surface where the bronchus, pulmonary vessels and other root structures enter or leave. It is near the cardiac and mediastinal impressions.

notes.A: The costal surface is convex and lies against ribs and intercostal spaces, rather than admitting the lung root.
notes.B: The diaphragmatic surface forms the concave base of the lung and rests on the diaphragm.
notes.C: The anterior border is the thin junction between costal and mediastinal surfaces, with a notch on the left.
notes.E: The apex lies in the root of the neck beneath cervical pleura, above the mediastinal hilum.

questions.stem: The highest structure in the root of the left lung is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus at the hilum, making it the highest large root structure. On the right, the upper lobar bronchus instead lies above the artery.

notes.A: The left main bronchus sits below the pulmonary artery and enters the lung before giving lobar branches.
notes.B: The superior pulmonary vein is generally anterior in the root rather than being above the pulmonary artery.
notes.C: The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest large component and drains lower lobe blood towards the atrium.
notes.D: Bronchial arteries are small nutrient vessels associated with the bronchial wall, below the principal pulmonary artery at the left hilum.

questions.stem: The lingula is part of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The lingula is the tongue-like inferior projection of the left upper lobe beside the cardiac notch. Its two segments belong to the upper lobar bronchus and correspond broadly to the right middle lobe.

notes.B: The left lower lobe lies below the oblique fissure and has superior and basal segments, separate from the lingula.
notes.C: The right middle lobe is a separate lobe with its own bronchus, although it is the counterpart of the lingula.
notes.D: The right upper lobe lies above the horizontal fissure and has apical, posterior and anterior segments.
notes.E: The right lower lobe lies mainly behind and below the oblique fissure, on the opposite side from the lingula.

questions.stem: The bronchopulmonary segment is the surgical unit of the lung because it has its own:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Each segment has a segmental bronchus and accompanying branch of the pulmonary artery in its centre. Pulmonary veins often run between segments, allowing the surgeon to identify an intersegmental plane.

notes.A: Pleural fissures separate lobes, while the smaller segments are subdivisions of a lobe without individual pleural cavities.
notes.C: Lymphatic channels and pulmonary veins can cross or lie between segmental boundaries, unlike the central bronchus and artery.
notes.D: The pulmonary ligament and lung root are features of the entire lung rather than each smaller segment.
notes.E: A lobar bronchus supplies multiple segments and the main fissures delineate lobes rather than individual segments.

questions.stem: The lower respiratory tract is made up of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The upper tract is the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea.

notes.A: Larynx and trachea are upper.
notes.B: Upper.
notes.D: Trachea is upper.
notes.E: Upper.

questions.stem: The anterior part of the nasal cavity just inside the nostrils is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The vestibule is the short widened space just inside each nostril. It is lined by skin with coarse vibrissae that trap larger particles before air passes into the nasal cavity proper.

notes.A: A choana is one of the posterior nasal apertures opening into the nasopharynx.
notes.B: The middle meatal atrium relates to the middle concha farther inside the nasal cavity, not the entrance just inside the nostril.
notes.C: The sphenoethmoidal recess is high and posterior, above the superior concha where the sphenoidal sinus drains.
notes.E: The nasopharynx is the pharyngeal compartment behind both choanae, beyond the posterior end of the nasal cavity.

questions.stem: The lingual tonsil lies in the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third of the tongue. The tongue base forms much of the anterior boundary of the oropharynx, so that is the relevant wall.

notes.A: The lateral oropharyngeal wall contains the palatine tonsil between the palatal arches.
notes.B: The nasopharyngeal roof contains the pharyngeal tonsil, which enlarges to form the adenoids.
notes.C: The lateral nasopharynx contains the tubal tonsil beside the opening of the auditory tube.
notes.D: The posterior laryngopharyngeal wall lies against the cervical vertebral region, behind the larynx and below the tongue base.

questions.stem: The lower (hypopharyngeal) anterior wall of the laryngopharynx is formed by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: arytenoids and lamina of the cricoid

options.label: C
options.text: base of the tongue and the hyoid

questions.why: Below the laryngeal inlet, the anterior laryngopharyngeal wall lies against the back of the larynx. The mucosa over the arytenoids and posterior cricoid lamina forms the relevant lower surface.

notes.B: The epiglottis and valleculae lie near the tongue base and the upper entrance to the larynx.
notes.C: The tongue base and hyoid are near the oropharynx and epiglottis, above the lower laryngopharyngeal wall.
notes.D: The thyroid laminae support the larynx anterolaterally, and the vocal folds lie within its airway.
notes.E: The palatal arches define the lateral oropharyngeal tonsillar region and do not extend down behind the cricoid.

questions.stem: Which statement about the position of the larynx is correct?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: It lies opposite C1 to C3

options.label: B
options.text: It lies higher in females and children

options.label: C
options.text: It is lower in children than adults

options.label: E
options.text: It lies below the cricoid at C7

questions.why: The larynx lies proportionately higher in children and generally higher in adult women than in adult men. It descends with growth, especially during the greater pubertal enlargement in males.

notes.A: C1 to C3 is too high for the usual full extent of the adult larynx, whose lower limit is near C6.
notes.C: In children the larynx sits higher in the neck and moves down relative to the vertebrae during growth.
notes.D: The larynx lies anterior to the laryngopharynx, while the oesophagus continues inferiorly behind the trachea.
notes.E: The lower cricoid border is the transition from larynx to trachea near C6.

questions.stem: Which laryngeal cartilage is paired?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The corniculates are a pair of small cartilages on the tips of the right and left arytenoids. They produce prominences within the mucosal folds of the laryngeal inlet.

notes.A: The cricoid is a single complete cartilage ring at the base of the larynx.
notes.B: The thyroid cartilage is single, even though it has two laminae meeting at the anterior prominence.
notes.D: The epiglottis is a single leaf-shaped elastic cartilage attached near the inner angle of the thyroid cartilage.
notes.E: The hyoid is a single bone above the larynx that anchors muscles and the thyrohyoid membrane.

questions.stem: Which is an INTRINSIC laryngeal membrane or ligament?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Intrinsic: quadrangular membrane and cricothyroid ligament.

notes.A: Extrinsic.
notes.B: Extrinsic.
notes.C: Extrinsic.
notes.E: Listed as extrinsic.

questions.stem: The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery pierce the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The internal laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve enters with the superior laryngeal artery through the thyrohyoid membrane. The nerve carries sensation from the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds.

notes.A: The cricothyroid ligament lies between thyroid and cricoid cartilages, below the neurovascular entry through the thyrohyoid membrane.
notes.B: The cricotracheal ligament connects the lower cricoid border to the first tracheal ring, well below the entry point.
notes.C: The quadrangular membrane forms part of the internal supraglottic framework rather than the external passage for the nerve.
notes.D: The hyoepiglottic ligament helps attach the epiglottis to the hyoid in front of the named nerve's entry route.

questions.stem: The lower free edge of the quadrangular membrane forms the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The quadrangular membrane runs from the epiglottis to the arytenoid region. Its lower free margin thickens into the vestibular ligament, which lies within the vestibular fold above the true vocal fold.

notes.B: The vocal ligament forms the thickened upper edge of the conus elasticus and lies within the true vocal fold.
notes.C: The aryepiglottic fold contains the superior margin of the quadrangular membrane, at the opposite edge from the vestibular ligament.
notes.D: The hyoepiglottic ligament joins the epiglottis to the hyoid anteriorly, away from the vestibular fold.
notes.E: The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid anteriorly and is separate from the vestibular fold.

questions.stem: The thyroid lobes, inferior thyroid arteries and common carotids are relations of the trachea in the neck that lie:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The cervical trachea lies between the thyroid lobes, with the common carotids farther laterally in their sheaths. The inferior thyroid arteries approach the posterolateral thyroid and are also lateral relations.

notes.A: The thyroid isthmus crosses anterior to the trachea, while the lobes and associated vessels flank it.
notes.C: The oesophagus is directly behind the cervical trachea, distinct from the vascular structures beside it.
notes.D: The larynx and thoracic trachea bound the cervical segment vertically, while the paired structures named run to either side.
notes.E: The wall contains cartilage, trachealis and mucosa, while thyroid lobes and the named arteries are external relations.

questions.stem: Which is an extrinsic muscle of the thoracic wall?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Pectoralis minor arises from ribs and inserts on the coracoid process, linking the chest wall to the shoulder girdle. It moves or stabilises the scapula and is therefore an extrinsic thoracic muscle.

notes.A: Transversus thoracis lies inside the anterior chest wall and runs between sternum and costal cartilages.
notes.B: Innermost intercostal muscles form a deep layer within the rib spaces and have attachments on adjacent ribs.
notes.D: Subcostal muscles lie on the internal posterior thoracic wall and extend across more than one intercostal space.
notes.E: The internal intercostals form a layer within the rib spaces rather than attaching to the shoulder girdle.

questions.stem: The dorsal scapular nerve and vessels run between the rhomboids and the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The dorsal scapular nerve and its accompanying vessels descend near the medial scapular border on the deep surface of the rhomboids. Superiorly this plane can lie superficial to serratus posterior superior.

notes.A: Serratus posterior inferior lies lower on the back and attaches to the bottom ribs, below the relevant upper scapular plane.
notes.B: Serratus anterior lies mainly along the lateral chest wall and anterior scapula and is supplied by the long thoracic nerve.
notes.C: Levatores costarum are deep muscles extending from vertebral transverse processes to ribs, medial to the named pathway.
notes.E: Latissimus dorsi covers much of the lower back and inserts on the humerus rather than defining the upper rhomboid plane.

questions.stem: The thoracic cavity is much deeper behind than in front because the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: B
options.text: sternum is longer than the spine

questions.why: The inferior thoracic aperture slopes downwards from the xiphisternal region to the lower thoracic spine. The posterior thoracic wall therefore extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall of the rib cage.

notes.A: The inlet slopes down and forward, while the lower opening's posterior descent best accounts for the large inferior difference.
notes.B: The sternum is shorter than the thoracic vertebral column and ends above the lowest posterior ribs and vertebral attachments.
notes.C: Most ribs slope downwards as they pass forward, rather than rising anteriorly to explain the lower boundary.
notes.D: The diaphragm has curved domes and posterior crural attachments, rather than forming a flat posterior floor.

questions.stem: The costal part of the diaphragm interdigitates with the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The costal diaphragm arises from the inner aspects of the lower six ribs and their cartilages. Its muscular slips interdigitate there with slips of transversus abdominis at the junction of chest and abdominal walls.

notes.B: External oblique has rib attachments on the outer chest wall, whereas the costal diaphragm interdigitates along the inner surface.
notes.C: Quadratus lumborum lies behind the abdominal cavity, and the diaphragm arches over it at the lateral arcuate ligament.
notes.D: Psoas major lies deep against the lumbar spine beneath the medial arcuate ligament, away from the costal interdigitation.
notes.E: Rectus abdominis runs in the anterior abdominal wall from the pubis to the xiphoid and upper costal attachments.

questions.stem: The lateral arcuate ligament is a thickening of fascia over the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The lateral arcuate ligament is an arch of thickened fascia over quadratus lumborum. It extends from the L1 transverse process towards the twelfth rib and gives attachment to diaphragmatic fibres.

notes.A: Psoas major passes beneath the medial arcuate ligament, which is closer to the vertebral body.
notes.C: The median arcuate ligament connects the two crura in front of the aorta at the posterior hiatus.
notes.D: The oesophagus passes through a muscular sling of crural fibres rather than under the lateral fascial arch.
notes.E: Transversus abdominis interdigitates with costal diaphragmatic fibres, while the lateral arcuate ligament crosses quadratus lumborum.

questions.stem: The smallest leaflet of the central tendon of the diaphragm is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The diaphragm's central tendon is conventionally described as a three-leaf clover with right, left and anterior leaflets. In that description the left leaflet is the smallest and the right is the largest.

notes.A: The right leaflet is generally the largest and is adjacent to the caval opening in the central tendon.
notes.B: The middle leaflet is the anterior central part and is conventionally intermediate in size.
notes.D: Posterior is not one of the three usual leaflet names for the trefoil-shaped tendon.
notes.E: The anterior leaflet is another name for the middle one and is usually larger than the left leaflet.

questions.stem: The hemiazygos vein passes into the thorax through the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The hemiazygos vein usually receives blood from the left ascending lumbar and subcostal veins and enters the thorax through the left diaphragmatic crus. It then ascends on the left of the vertebral column.

notes.A: The aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct and can transmit the main azygos vein on the right.
notes.B: The oesophagus and vagal trunks use the oesophageal hiatus, separated from the hemiazygos entry through the left crus.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava uses the central tendon on the right, while hemiazygos drainage enters posteriorly on the left.
notes.E: The anterior sternocostal gap can transmit superior epigastric vessels, far in front of the hemiazygos vein.

questions.stem: The fibres of the right crus that encircle the oesophagus are supplied by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Each half is otherwise supplied by its own phrenic nerve.

notes.A: Not these fibres.
notes.B: Not motor to diaphragm.
notes.C: Proprioceptive, periphery.
notes.D: Visceral.

questions.stem: Proprioception from the central tendon of the diaphragm is carried by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Phrenic nerves carry sensory fibres from the central diaphragm and convey information about diaphragm movement and tension. They also provide motor innervation to the muscle, while intercostal nerves provide sensation more peripherally.

notes.B: Lower intercostal nerves supply the thoracoabdominal wall and peripheral diaphragmatic coverings rather than the central tendon region.
notes.C: The vagus carries visceral afferents and supplies thoracic and abdominal organs, but central diaphragmatic sensory fibres run in the phrenic nerves.
notes.D: The subcostal nerve continues below the twelfth rib into the abdominal wall, away from central tendon sensory supply.
notes.E: Sympathetic trunks provide autonomic pathways beside the vertebral column, distinct from central diaphragmatic mechanosensory fibres.

questions.stem: The superior phrenic arteries arise from the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The superior phrenic arteries are paired small branches of the lower descending thoracic aorta. They supply the upper surface of the diaphragm, particularly its posterior portion.

notes.A: The internal thoracic artery provides pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic branches, separate from the superior phrenic pair.
notes.C: The abdominal aorta commonly provides inferior phrenic arteries, which approach the diaphragm from below.
notes.D: The subclavian supplies the diaphragm indirectly through internal thoracic branches rather than giving the superior phrenic arteries.
notes.E: The coeliac trunk can give rise to inferior phrenic branches in variant anatomy, below the usual superior phrenic origin.

questions.stem: A retrosternal diaphragmatic hernia passes through the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: A Morgagni hernia passes through the sternocostal triangle between the sternal and costal slips of diaphragm. The defect lies immediately behind the lower sternum, rather than in the posterior diaphragm.

notes.A: A Bochdalek hernia is posterolateral, on the opposite side of the diaphragm from a retrosternal defect.
notes.B: The oesophageal hiatus is a posterior muscular opening through which the stomach can herniate in a hiatus hernia.
notes.D: The aortic hiatus lies behind the median arcuate ligament at the lower thoracic spine, not behind the sternum.
notes.E: The vena caval opening lies in the right central tendon and transmits the inferior vena cava.

questions.stem: A hiatus hernia in which the gastro-oesophageal junction moves up into the thorax is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: In a sliding hiatus hernia, the gastro-oesophageal junction and an adjacent portion of stomach move upwards through the oesophageal hiatus. The displacement of the junction distinguishes it from a pure rolling hernia.

notes.A: In a pure rolling hernia the fundus can enter the chest alongside the oesophagus while the junction stays below.
notes.B: Bochdalek herniation occurs through a posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic defect separate from the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.C: A Morgagni hernia occurs through the anterior sternocostal gap rather than travelling with the gastro-oesophageal junction.
notes.E: An incisional hernia occurs through a surgical scar, not through the native oesophageal opening described here.

questions.stem: The right pulmonary artery relates to the right main bronchus by lying:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: above it, then in front of it

options.label: B
options.text: behind it along its whole course

options.label: E
options.text: below it, then in front of it

questions.why: As the right pulmonary artery travels towards the right lung root it is first inferior and then anterior to the main bronchus. The azygos arch passes superiorly over the bronchus.

notes.A: The artery passes below the proximal bronchus, while the azygos arch rather than the artery lies above the root.
notes.B: At the hilum the right pulmonary artery lies anterior to the main bronchus, so a wholly posterior course is incorrect.
notes.C: A superior position relative to the main bronchus characterises the left pulmonary artery at its hilum.
notes.D: The initial inferior relation is right, but the artery comes to lie anterior rather than posterior towards the root.

questions.stem: The left main bronchus passes:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: below the aortic arch, in front of the oesophagus

options.label: B
options.text: above the aortic arch, behind the oesophagus

options.label: C
options.text: below the azygos arch, in front of the oesophagus

options.label: D
options.text: below the aortic arch, behind the oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: above the left pulmonary artery throughout

questions.why: The left main bronchus passes beneath the aortic arch and anterior to the oesophagus on its way to the left hilum. At the hilum the left pulmonary artery generally lies above the bronchus.

notes.B: The arch curves over the left bronchus, and the oesophagus lies behind it in the central thorax.
notes.C: The azygos arch passes over the right lung root, while the aortic arch is the left-sided superior relation.
notes.D: The bronchus does pass under the aortic arch but crosses in front of the oesophagus.
notes.E: The left pulmonary artery arches superior to the bronchus at the left root, reversing the relation stated here.

questions.stem: The usual number of bronchial arteries is:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The usual arrangement is two left bronchial arteries and one right, although variations are common. The left pair often arises directly from the descending thoracic aorta and the right may share an intercostal origin.

notes.A: The usual arrangement has more left than right bronchial arteries, rather than the reverse distribution.
notes.C: A single artery on each side can occur, but the standard pattern includes two on the left.
notes.D: Two on each side would add a right-sided vessel to the most common anatomical pattern.
notes.E: A right-sided count of three exceeds the common pattern, and the left side typically has two.

questions.stem: Lymph from the lower lobe of the lung drains to the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Lymph from a lower lobe usually reaches bronchopulmonary nodes at the hilum and then inferior tracheobronchial nodes beneath the carina. Some left lower-lobe drainage can continue towards right tracheobronchial nodes.

notes.A: Superior tracheobronchial nodes can receive lymph downstream, but the subcarinal group is a typical early mediastinal station for lower-lobe drainage.
notes.B: Axillary nodes principally receive lymph from the upper limb and chest wall rather than directly from lower lung lobes.
notes.D: Paratracheal nodes are farther along the drainage route and usually receive lymph through earlier hilar or tracheobronchial stations.
notes.E: Deep cervical nodes can receive downstream thoracic lymph, but do not directly drain the lower lobe.

questions.stem: The vagal efferent fibres to the bronchial tree are:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: B
options.text: sensory for the cough reflex only

questions.why: Vagal parasympathetic efferents increase airway smooth-muscle tone and promote gland secretion through cholinergic pathways. Vagal afferents have a separate sensory role in reflexes such as coughing.

notes.A: Vagally mediated cholinergic output causes bronchoconstriction, while adrenergic pathways can have different effects on smooth muscle and vessels.
notes.B: Cough sensation is carried by vagal afferents, whereas the efferents regulate smooth muscle and gland activity.
notes.C: The phrenic nerves supply motor fibres to the diaphragm, not the vagus branches to the bronchial tree.
notes.E: Parietal pleural pain travels in intercostal or phrenic nerves, rather than defining the bronchial vagal efferent pathway.

questions.stem: The costal pleura is separated from the inner surface of the thoracic wall by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The costal pleura is separated from the thoracic wall by the endothoracic fascia, a thin layer that lets the lung and pleura be stripped from the wall.

notes.A: The suprapleural membrane reinforces the apical pleura, while endothoracic fascia separates costal pleura from most of the wall.
notes.B: Visceral pleura covers the lung across the pleural cavity and does not lie between the costal pleura and ribs.
notes.C: Transversalis fascia lines the abdominal wall, while the corresponding inner thoracic layer is called endothoracic fascia.
