notes.D: Pretracheal fascia is mainly a deep cervical layer associated with the airway and other visceral structures.

questions.stem: Where the costal pleura meets the mediastinal pleura behind is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Along the vertebral line of reflection, the parietal pleura turns from the posterior rib cage onto the mediastinum. This reflection runs beside the thoracic vertebral column.

notes.B: The sternal line is the anterior reflection from costal to mediastinal pleura behind the sternum.
notes.C: The costal line is the inferior reflection between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, rather than the posterior mediastinal reflection.
notes.D: Diaphragmatic pleura lies on the superior surface of the diaphragm, below the vertebral pleural reflection.
notes.E: At the hilum mediastinal pleura becomes visceral pleura, rather than changing from one parietal surface to another.

questions.stem: At which costal cartilage does the left pleural reflection turn laterally after passing the cardiac notch?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The left anterior pleural reflection deviates laterally near the fourth costal cartilage to accommodate the heart. Around the sixth cartilage it turns into the inferior reflection between costal and diaphragmatic pleura.

notes.A: The fourth cartilage is near the start of the leftward divergence rather than the lower junction beyond the notch.
notes.C: The second cartilage is at the sternal angle, above the area where the left pleura diverges around the heart.
notes.D: At the eighth cartilage the reflection is already following its inferior course farther laterally on the chest wall.
notes.E: Near the fifth cartilage the pleura is still following the left-sided deviation beside the heart.

questions.stem: The pleura can be opened accidentally during a posterior incision for the kidney because it:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: E
options.text: ends at the lower border of the T10 body

questions.why: Near the spine the costodiaphragmatic reflection can descend below the medial part of the twelfth rib. A posterior renal incision near this overlap can therefore enter the pleural recess behind the diaphragm.

notes.A: The posterior pleura extends below the tenth rib, especially as it approaches the vertebral column.
notes.B: The eighth rib is an anterior landmark for the lower pleural reflection, not the posterior limit near the kidney.
notes.D: The costodiaphragmatic recess remains between the chest wall and diaphragm posteriorly and can extend near the upper kidney.
notes.E: The T10 body is higher than the approximate T12 level of the posterior pleural limit.

questions.stem: Injury to the cervical pleura is possible from a wound in the root of the neck because it:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: lies at the level of the hyoid

options.label: B
options.text: extends above the neck of the 1st rib

options.label: C
options.text: reaches the lower border of C3

options.label: D
options.text: rises about 2.5 cm above the clavicle

questions.why: The cervical pleura covers the lung apex and projects upward through the thoracic inlet. At the front its dome rises about 2.5 cm above the medial clavicle, putting it within the root of the neck.

notes.A: The hyoid is at a substantially higher neck level than the usual apex of cervical pleura.
notes.B: The first rib's neck is a posterior relation of the dome, while its anterior exposure is projected above the clavicle.
notes.C: C3 is several levels above the thoracic inlet and is well above the usual cervical pleural dome.
notes.E: The pleural dome is lateral to the cervical trachea and covers the lung apex rather than the front of the airway.

questions.stem: A fresh lung floats in water because it:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: An aerated lung has many air-filled alveoli within elastic tissue, lowering its average density below that of water. That accounts for its buoyancy and its soft, spongy feel.

notes.A: Visceral pleura invests the lung surface, but it is the volume of trapped alveolar air that makes the aerated lung buoyant.
notes.B: Lymphatic vessels drain interstitial fluid and do not provide most of the air volume responsible for flotation.
notes.C: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and helps prevent collapse, while the air itself accounts for the low average density.
notes.D: Pulmonary blood vessels support gas exchange, but their blood adds mass rather than providing the gas that permits flotation.

questions.stem: The pulmonary ligament is:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: a pleural fold hanging below the lung root

options.label: B
options.text: a fibrous band joining the lungs

options.label: C
options.text: a ligament joining the lung to the diaphragm

options.label: D
options.text: the attachment of the trachea to the carina

options.label: E
options.text: a remnant of the ductus arteriosus

questions.why: The pleural sleeve around the lung root continues inferiorly as a double layer called the pulmonary ligament. The fold joins the mediastinal surface of the lung and the mediastinum below the hilum.

notes.B: The right and left lungs occupy separate pleural sacs and are not joined by a common fibrous band.
notes.C: The fold descends towards the diaphragm, but it is a reflection of pleura rather than a direct fibrous attachment to diaphragm.
notes.D: The carina is the internal ridge at the tracheal bifurcation, separate from the pleural fold below the hilum.
notes.E: The ductus arteriosus forms the ligamentum arteriosum between the aortic arch and left pulmonary artery after closure.

questions.stem: The bronchopulmonary segments are supplied by:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: one lobar bronchus and vein each

options.label: B
options.text: a segmental bronchus and artery each

options.label: D
options.text: a single vein shared by a lobe

questions.why: Each bronchopulmonary segment receives a tertiary bronchus and a corresponding branch of the pulmonary artery. Their centre-to-periphery course differs from the mainly intersegmental course of major pulmonary veins.

notes.A: A lobar bronchus supplies an entire lobe, which contains several segments with separate tertiary branches.
notes.C: Bronchial arteries nourish supporting airway tissue, but ventilation of each segment requires its own segmental bronchus.
notes.D: Pulmonary veins often course between segments and are drainage channels rather than the paired inputs to each segment.
notes.E: The pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries before separate segmental branches are given off.

questions.stem: The costophrenic angle seen on a PA chest X-ray marks the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: On a frontal chest radiograph the sharp lateral costophrenic angle represents the costodiaphragmatic recess. Fluid in this dependent pleural space can make the angle look blunted.

notes.A: The cardiac notch is an indentation in the anterior edge of the left lung near the heart.
notes.B: The oblique fissure separates major lobes and does not correspond to the lateral inferior pleural angle.
notes.D: The hilum is a central region containing the lung root rather than a peripheral angle where chest wall meets diaphragm.
notes.E: The costomediastinal recess is beside the mediastinum anteriorly, not in the lateral inferior corner of the chest.

questions.stem: The anterior half of the nasal septum is formed by:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Quadrangular septal cartilage forms most of the anterior nasal septum and supports the mobile part of the nose. The vomer and perpendicular plate of the ethmoid make up most of the bony posterior septum.

notes.A: The vomer forms the posteroinferior bony septum rather than its flexible anterior portion.
notes.B: The perpendicular plate descends from the ethmoid to form the superior bony part of the septum.
notes.C: The nasal bones form the bridge externally and do not make up the anterior midline partition.
notes.E: The palatine bone forms a posterior part of the hard palate and gives support near the base of the septum.

questions.stem: The pharynx is a fibromuscular tube about:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The pharynx extends from the skull base to the inferior cricoid border near C6, where it continues into the oesophagus. In an adult this fibromuscular passage is about 12 cm long.

notes.A: Five centimetres is closer to a single short pharyngeal subdivision than to the full skull-base-to-cricoid distance.
notes.B: Twenty centimetres is longer than the typical pharynx and closer to the length of the adult oesophagus.
notes.C: Twenty-five centimetres is closer to the usual adult oesophageal length than to that of the pharynx.
notes.D: Eight centimetres is shorter than the typical adult pharynx extending through all three subdivisions.

questions.stem: The pillars of the fauces in the lateral wall of the oropharynx are the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The anterior pillar is the palatoglossal arch and the posterior pillar is the palatopharyngeal arch. They descend from the soft palate and enclose the tonsillar fossa between them.

notes.B: Aryepiglottic and vestibular folds are structures of the larynx, inferior to the faucial pillars.
notes.C: The salpingopharyngeal and salpingopalatine folds are associated with the auditory tube in the nasopharynx.
notes.D: The constrictors form the deeper muscular pharyngeal wall rather than the two mucosal arches around the palatine tonsil.
notes.E: Piriform recesses and valleculae are depressions near the laryngeal inlet and tongue base rather than arches at the fauces.

questions.stem: The oropharynx ends below at the upper border of the epiglottis, which is level with:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: At the upper border of the epiglottis, near C3 in the usual surface scheme, the pharynx transitions from oropharynx to laryngopharynx. The soft palate marks the oropharynx's upper limit.

notes.A: C1 is near the soft-palate level at the upper aspect of the oropharynx.
notes.C: C5 is near more inferior laryngeal structures, below the superior edge of the epiglottis.
notes.D: C6 is near the lower border of the cricoid, where the laryngopharynx becomes the oesophagus.
notes.E: T1 is at the superior thoracic aperture, below the epiglottis and the end of the pharynx.

questions.stem: Waldeyer's ring is most important as a barrier to infection:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Waldeyer's ring samples inhaled and ingested antigens at the entrances to the respiratory and digestive tracts. Its tonsils are especially active during early childhood and tend to involute after puberty.

notes.A: Tonsillar tissue can still be active at puberty, but it commonly starts to regress around that period.
notes.B: Tonsils can contribute to mucosal immunity in young adults, although their size and activity are often greater during childhood.
notes.D: In middle age, tonsillar tissue is generally less prominent than during its early development in children.
notes.E: Older adults retain mucosal immune defences, but the ring typically has less prominent lymphoid tissue than in early childhood.

questions.stem: The laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) is formed by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The right and left laminae of the thyroid cartilage meet in front to form the laryngeal prominence. Pubertal growth often makes that anterior angle more prominent in males.

notes.A: The cricoid is a complete ring below the thyroid cartilage and has a much narrower anterior arch.
notes.B: The hyoid is a bone above the thyroid cartilage connected to it by the thyrohyoid membrane.
notes.C: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped cartilage inside the inlet without forming the anterior prominence of the neck.
notes.E: The paired arytenoids lie posteriorly on the cricoid and control vocal fold position.

questions.stem: The larynx contains how many cartilages?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The larynx has three unpaired cartilages: thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis. Three pairs of smaller cartilages, the arytenoids, corniculates and cuneiforms, bring the total to nine individual cartilages.

notes.A: There are six types, but the three paired types contribute six separate cartilages rather than three.
notes.B: The total is nine, but it is made up of three unpaired and six paired individual cartilages.
notes.C: The arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform groups are all paired, so counting only two pairs leaves one out.
notes.D: The number three correctly describes the paired groups, but there are three unpaired cartilages rather than six.

questions.stem: Which is an EXTRINSIC ligament or membrane of the larynx?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The cricotracheal ligament joins the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring. Because it connects the laryngeal framework to the trachea below, it is an extrinsic ligament.

notes.B: The quadrangular membrane extends between laryngeal cartilages and forms part of the internal supraglottic framework.
notes.C: The cricothyroid ligament connects cartilages that both belong to the larynx, so it is intrinsic.
notes.D: The vocal ligament is the thickened upper margin of the conus elasticus inside the true vocal fold.
notes.E: The vestibular ligament forms the lower free edge of the quadrangular membrane inside the false vocal fold.

questions.stem: The vocal ligament is the free upper edge of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The vocal ligament is the upper free margin of the lateral cricothyroid membrane, or conus elasticus. It extends from thyroid cartilage to the vocal process of an arytenoid inside the true vocal fold.

notes.A: The lower free edge of the quadrangular membrane forms the vestibular ligament in the false vocal fold.
notes.C: The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid, outside the internal vocal fold attachments.
notes.D: The cricotracheal ligament joins the cricoid to the first tracheal ring, below the true vocal folds.
notes.E: The hyoepiglottic ligament joins the epiglottis to the hyoid near the inlet rather than supporting the vocal folds.

questions.stem: The part of the laryngeal cavity between the vestibular and vocal folds opens laterally into the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The ventricular recess extends laterally between the vestibular fold above and vocal fold below. Its saccule projects upwards and contains glands whose secretions help lubricate the vocal folds.

notes.A: The piriform recess lies outside the laryngeal cavity, beside the inlet in the laryngopharynx.
notes.B: The epiglottic vallecula is a depression between the tongue base and epiglottis, above the vocal folds.
notes.D: The infraglottic space lies below the vocal folds, rather than between the true and false folds.
notes.E: The laryngeal vestibule extends from the inlet down to the vestibular folds, above the ventricle.

questions.stem: The vocal ligament is attached posteriorly to which part of the arytenoid cartilage?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The vocal ligament extends from the inner surface of thyroid cartilage to the anteriorly projecting vocal process of the arytenoid. Arytenoid movements change this attachment's position and move the vocal fold.

notes.A: The muscular process projects laterally and gives attachment to intrinsic laryngeal muscles that move the arytenoid.
notes.B: The arytenoid apex supports a corniculate cartilage rather than receiving the posterior end of the vocal ligament.
notes.C: The arytenoid base carries the processes, but the ligament attaches specifically to its anterior projection.
notes.E: The articular facet is on the base where it forms a synovial joint with the cricoid cartilage.

questions.stem: The trachea begins at the lower border of the larynx at the level of:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The trachea begins below the cricoid cartilage at about C6 in an adult. It descends through the neck and superior mediastinum to divide into the main bronchi near the sternal angle.

notes.A: C4 lies near the thyroid cartilage, above the lower cricoid border marking the start of the trachea.
notes.B: By C7 the airway is usually already tracheal rather than at its junction with the larynx.
notes.C: T1 is near the thoracic inlet through which the already established cervical trachea descends.
notes.D: T2 is within the thorax below the usual starting level of the trachea in the neck.

questions.stem: The trachea is about:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The adult trachea is about 10 cm long and 2–2.5 cm wide, running from C6 to the sternal angle.

notes.B: A 5 cm length with a 1–1.5 cm diameter is smaller than the usual adult tracheal dimensions.
notes.C: The proposed width is close to the textbook estimate, but 20 cm is too long for the adult trachea.
notes.D: A 10 cm length is plausible, but a 4–4.5 cm width greatly exceeds the typical adult calibre.
notes.E: Both measurements are above the usual textbook dimensions, particularly the proposed diameter of 3–3.5 cm.

questions.stem: Compared with the adult, the trachea of a child is:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: D
options.text: the same size but more movable

questions.why: In a child the trachea is smaller, set more deeply and more mobile than in the adult, which makes airway procedures more difficult.

notes.A: The child's trachea is physically smaller and more mobile, while its deeper position can make it harder to expose.
notes.C: The lumen is smaller, but the paediatric trachea is comparatively mobile and can sit deeper in the neck.
notes.D: Greater mobility is characteristic, but the paediatric trachea has a smaller calibre and length than the adult airway.
notes.E: The paediatric trachea is shorter and narrower, with its deeper position making surface access more challenging.

questions.stem: An artery that, when present, lies in front of the trachea in the neck is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: A thyroidea ima artery can arise from a great vessel and ascend in front of the trachea to the thyroid isthmus. Its variable midline course makes it an important anterior tracheal relation.

notes.A: The usual inferior thyroid artery approaches the thyroid from the side rather than ascending in the anterior midline.
notes.B: The superior thyroid artery is usually an external carotid branch that descends towards the upper pole of the gland.
notes.D: The common carotid artery ascends laterally in its sheath and does not normally cross the front of the trachea.
notes.E: The vertebral artery passes posteriorly into cervical transverse foramina rather than ascending in front of the trachea.

questions.stem: In the thorax, the right side of the trachea is related to the pleura, the brachiocephalic artery and the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: On its right side the thoracic trachea is related to the right vagus nerve, the azygos vein, the brachiocephalic artery and the right pleura; the aortic arch is a left-sided relation.

notes.A: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve runs under the arch and ascends on the left in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.
notes.B: The aortic arch lies to the left of the trachea and curves over the left main bronchus.
notes.C: The left subclavian artery originates from the arch and passes superiorly on the left of the central airway.
notes.E: The thoracic duct passes behind the oesophagus and has a left-sided course in the upper thorax.

questions.stem: The mucous membrane of the trachea is supplied by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Tracheal mucosal sensation and much of its parasympathetic secretomotor supply travel in vagal branches, including recurrent laryngeal branches. These pathways help trigger protective reflexes and regulate secretion.

notes.A: Sympathetic fibres can influence vascular tone, while mucosal sensation and secretion also have important vagal pathways.
notes.B: Phrenic nerves provide diaphragmatic motor supply and sensation from selected serous surfaces rather than tracheal mucosal sensation.
notes.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides important sensation to the oropharynx, while tracheal sensation is chiefly vagal.
notes.D: Upper intercostal nerves serve the chest wall and costal pleura rather than the lining of the airway.

questions.stem: The thoracic cavity is divided into the mediastinum and the two:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The thorax has a central mediastinum flanked by right and left pleural compartments. Each pleural sac surrounds one lung, and its potential cavity lies between visceral and parietal pleura.

notes.B: The pericardial cavity is single, surrounds the heart and lies within the middle mediastinum.
notes.C: Intercostal spaces are the intervals between ribs in the wall rather than large compartments around the lungs.
notes.D: Intercostal spaces lie in the thoracic wall between ribs rather than forming the large lateral compartments.
notes.E: Thoracic apertures are the superior and inferior openings of the bony thorax, not spaces alongside the mediastinum.

questions.stem: The thoracic wall is closed superiorly by the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The suprapleural membrane spans each side of the inlet from the first rib to the C7 transverse process and reinforces the cervical pleura. The central inlet remains open for structures passing between neck and thorax.

notes.A: The diaphragm forms the muscular floor of the thorax and covers most of the inferior aperture.
notes.C: Clavipectoral fascia lies in the pectoral region and encloses subclavius and pectoralis minor rather than the pleural cupola.
notes.D: The pretracheal fascia surrounds cervical visceral structures and can descend into the thorax within the central inlet.
notes.E: Endothoracic fascia forms a lining inside the thoracic wall, with a local thickening that forms the suprapleural membrane.

questions.stem: Which is NOT listed as an extrinsic muscle of the thoracic wall?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Transversus thoracis arises inside the anterior chest wall and extends from sternum to costal cartilages. Both attachments are to the thoracic wall, making it part of the deepest intrinsic layer.

notes.A: Pectoralis major attaches the thorax to the humerus, placing it among the extrinsic muscles covering the chest wall.
notes.B: Serratus anterior runs between the outer ribs and scapula, linking the chest wall to the shoulder girdle.
notes.D: Subclavius runs between the first rib region and clavicle, giving it an extrinsic shoulder-girdle attachment.
notes.E: Sternocleidomastoid has an attachment to the sternum and can elevate it during forced inspiration, acting as an accessory muscle.

questions.stem: The inner layer of intercostal muscles consists of the innermost intercostal, the subcostal and the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The innermost layer of thoracic wall muscles comprises the innermost intercostals, the subcostals and, anteriorly, transversus thoracis.

notes.A: Serratus posterior inferior lies externally on the lower back rather than on the inner surfaces of the ribs.
notes.B: The internal intercostals form the middle layer, separated from the innermost layer by the main neurovascular plane.
notes.C: Levatores costarum are posterior muscles running from vertebral transverse processes to ribs, outside the anterior deep layer.
notes.E: External intercostals form the superficial muscular layer between the ribs.

questions.stem: The serratus posterior superior arises from the spinous processes of:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: the lower 2 thoracic and upper 2 lumbar vertebrae

options.label: E
options.text: the lowest 2 cervical and upper 2 thoracic vertebrae

questions.why: In the attachment scheme used here, serratus posterior superior arises from the lower nuchal region and the C6–T2 spinous processes. It runs downwards and outwards to attach to upper ribs.

notes.A: Lower thoracic and upper lumbar origins are features of serratus posterior inferior, well below the superior muscle.
notes.B: The origin has inferior cervical attachments in addition to the upper thoracic ones.
notes.C: The attachment includes upper thoracic spines as well as lower cervical ones, so it is not confined to the neck.
notes.D: The lowest thoracic processes contribute to the inferior member of the pair, not the muscle attached to the upper ribs.

questions.stem: The serratus posterior muscles are supplied by:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Serratus posterior muscles receive segmental branches of thoracic anterior rami through the intercostal or subcostal nerves. Their supply follows that of thoracic wall muscles despite their posterior position.

notes.B: Posterior rami supply intrinsic back muscles such as erector spinae rather than serratus posterior.
notes.C: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and commonly levator scapulae, not the usual supply of serratus posterior.
notes.D: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior on the lateral chest wall, a separate muscle.
notes.E: The accessory nerve provides motor supply to trapezius and sternocleidomastoid rather than the paired serratus posterior muscles.

questions.stem: The serratus posterior inferior acts in:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Serratus posterior inferior attaches to the lowest four ribs. Its traditional mechanical description is that it pulls the ribs down or stabilises them during expiration, although its active respiratory role is debated.

notes.A: The fibre direction is usually described as pulling the lower ribs down rather than elevating them during inspiration.
notes.C: Elevation of the upper ribs is the conventional action of serratus posterior superior, whose attachments are higher.
notes.D: The inferior muscle attaches to ribs 9–12 and acts on these rather than pulling down the upper ribs.
notes.E: The named muscle has rib attachments and is classically associated with rib movement or stabilisation, rather than axial rotation.

questions.stem: The left dome of the diaphragm reaches up to the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The right dome reaches the upper border of the 5th.

notes.A: Too high.
notes.B: Right dome.
notes.D: Too low.
notes.E: Not as taught.

questions.stem: The muscle fibres of the diaphragm are inserted into the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Diaphragmatic muscle fibres run inwards from sternal, costal and lumbar attachments to the central tendon. Their contraction pulls the tendon down and increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity.

notes.A: The xiphoid process provides an anterior origin for the sternal fibres rather than their shared insertion.
notes.B: The lower six ribs and cartilages provide peripheral origins for slips of the costal diaphragm.
notes.C: Lumbar vertebrae are the posterior anchors for the crura, whose fibres insert on the central tendon.
notes.E: Arcuate ligaments provide posterior origins for diaphragmatic fibres over the psoas and quadratus lumborum.

questions.stem: The lumbar part of the diaphragm consists of the arcuate ligaments and the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The lumbar diaphragm is anchored by the right and left crura on the lumbar vertebrae and by the arcuate ligaments. Fibres from these posterior attachments pass upwards to the central tendon.

notes.A: The central tendon receives fibres from the lumbar, costal and sternal regions rather than forming a lumbar origin.
notes.B: Sternal slips have an anterior origin at the xiphoid process, remote from the lumbar attachments.
notes.C: Costal slips have origins on the lower ribs and costal cartilages at the sides of the thorax.
notes.D: The suprapleural membrane supports the pleural apex at the superior thoracic aperture, far above the lumbar region.

questions.stem: The medial arcuate ligament arches over the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The medial arcuate ligament forms an arch over psoas major by thickening its fascia. It lies medial to the lateral arcuate ligament and provides a posterior origin for diaphragm fibres.

notes.B: Quadratus lumborum lies beneath the lateral arcuate ligament, which extends towards the twelfth rib.
notes.C: The aorta passes beneath the median arcuate ligament joining the two crura, closer to the midline.
notes.D: The oesophagus passes through a muscular hiatus formed chiefly by right-crural fibres rather than beneath a fascial arch.
notes.E: The inferior vena cava passes through the right part of the central tendon, anterior and superior to the lumbar arches.

questions.stem: The central tendon of the diaphragm is partially blended above with the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The fibrous pericardium is attached inferiorly to the superior surface of the central tendon. This attachment helps stabilise the cardiac sac and makes it move with the diaphragm.

notes.A: Diaphragmatic pleura lies over lateral parts of the diaphragm, while fibrous pericardium fuses centrally.
notes.C: The oesophagus passes through a muscular hiatus posterior to the main part of the central tendon.
notes.D: The liver is below the diaphragm and therefore cannot provide the superior attachment of the central tendon.
notes.E: The sternum is an anterior attachment for peripheral sternal muscle fibres rather than the covering fused above the tendon.

questions.stem: The central tendon of the diaphragm is shaped like:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: a trefoil leaf with three leaflets

options.label: D
options.text: a triangle with its apex behind

questions.why: The diaphragm's central tendon is a broad aponeurosis classically described as a trefoil. Its anterior, right and left leaflets receive converging muscle fibres from the surrounding rim.

notes.A: The arcuate ligaments arch posteriorly over related structures, while the central tendon has three distinct leaflets.
notes.B: The oesophageal opening is surrounded by crural muscle, separate from the broad three-part central tendon.
notes.D: A simple triangle omits the rounded lateral and anterior portions that make up the trefoil shape.
notes.E: Two leaflets omits the anterior portion, which lies between the right and left components.

questions.stem: The lowest and most posterior of the three large openings of the diaphragm is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The aortic hiatus lies between the crura near T12, behind the median arcuate ligament. It is lower and farther posterior than the oesophageal hiatus at T10 and caval opening at T8.

notes.A: The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening around T10 and lies anterior and superior to the aortic passage.
notes.B: The caval opening is at approximately T8 in the central tendon, the highest of the three principal openings.
notes.C: The sternocostal gap lies near the xiphoid process anteriorly rather than at the posterior midline.
notes.E: Small openings through a crus can transmit veins or nerves, but the lowest major opening is between the crura.

questions.stem: Besides the IVC, the vena caval foramen transmits branches of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The main caval opening lies on the right side of the central tendon at about T8. Small branches of the right phrenic nerve may pass through it alongside the inferior vena cava.

notes.A: The left phrenic nerve pierces the muscular left hemidiaphragm separately from the right-sided caval opening.
notes.B: Vagal trunks run with the oesophagus through the oesophageal hiatus rather than joining the vena cava.
notes.C: Greater splanchnic nerves usually pierce a diaphragmatic crus rather than passing with the vena cava.
notes.D: Sympathetic trunks pass posteriorly near the medial arcuate ligaments rather than entering at the central tendon.

questions.stem: The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves of the right side pass through the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The right greater and lesser splanchnic nerves descend in the posterior thorax and usually pierce the right crus to reach abdominal autonomic plexuses. They use separate passages from the major vascular openings.

notes.B: The aortic hiatus contains the aorta and thoracic duct in the midline between both crura.
notes.C: The oesophageal hiatus carries the oesophagus with vagal trunks rather than the thoracic splanchnic nerves.
notes.D: The caval opening transmits the inferior vena cava and can carry small right phrenic branches.
notes.E: The sympathetic trunk passes behind the medial arcuate ligament, while its splanchnic branches usually pierce the crus.

questions.stem: The superior epigastric vessels pass between which parts of the diaphragm?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The superior epigastric vessels continue onto the anterior abdominal wall through the sternocostal triangle between the diaphragmatic sternal and costal slips. This same gap is the site of a Morgagni hernia.

notes.A: The junction of costal and lumbar origins is posterolateral, away from the route of the vessels near the sternum.
notes.C: The area between the right and left crura is posterior and includes the aortic hiatus.
notes.D: Costal fibres insert on the central tendon, whereas these vessels pass near the anterior peripheral attachments.
notes.E: The medial and lateral arcuate ligaments lie posteriorly over psoas and quadratus lumborum, away from the epigastric route.

questions.stem: The musculophrenic and pericardiacophrenic arteries to the diaphragm are branches of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The internal thoracic artery gives off the pericardiacophrenic artery, which accompanies the phrenic nerve. It also divides inferiorly into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.

notes.A: The thoracic aorta provides paired superior phrenic branches distinct from the anterior internal thoracic system.
notes.B: The abdominal aorta commonly gives the inferior phrenic arteries supplying the diaphragm from below.
notes.D: The coeliac trunk may give a variant inferior phrenic branch, rather than these anterior thoracic branches.
notes.E: Posterior intercostal arteries supply the thoracic wall from behind and may anastomose with anterior branches.

questions.stem: The diaphragm develops from how many sources?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The classical model distinguishes four contributions: septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal folds, dorsal oesophageal mesentery and peripheral body wall. Migrating cervical somite cells supply diaphragm muscle, accounting for its phrenic innervation.

notes.A: A two-source model is incomplete because the classic scheme distinguishes separate tendon, crural, posterolateral and peripheral contributions.
notes.B: There are four structural contributions in the conventional model, so a count of three leaves one out.
notes.C: Five may result from counting migrating myoblasts separately from the four regions they populate and help form.
notes.E: Six is not the conventional count because the crura and peripheral muscle are grouped by developmental contribution.

questions.stem: The motor fibres to the diaphragm come from spinal segments:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The phrenic nerves arise from anterior rami of C3–C5, with C4 usually providing the largest contribution. Each supplies the diaphragm with motor fibres despite the muscle's descent into the thorax.

notes.A: C5 contributes, but the phrenic nerve receives higher cervical inputs rather than C6 and C7.
notes.B: C3 is part of the phrenic roots, while C1 and C2 do not normally provide their major motor fibres.
notes.C: Upper thoracic segments provide intercostal motor fibres, whereas the diaphragm's primary motor supply is cervical.
notes.D: C7, C8 and T1 contribute to upper limb innervation rather than forming the usual phrenic root combination.

questions.stem: The costovertebral and costotransverse joints are:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: At the upper ten ribs the rib tubercles articulate with thoracic transverse processes through synovial joints. Rib heads also have synovial articulations with vertebral bodies, allowing small gliding or rotational movements during breathing.

notes.B: A synchondrosis contains hyaline cartilage, as at the costochondral junction rather than the synovial rib-head articulation.
notes.C: A symphysis is a fibrocartilaginous joint, such as the one between adjacent vertebral bodies.
notes.D: Saddle joints have reciprocally concave and convex surfaces, unlike the small plane joints at the posterior rib attachments.
notes.E: Fibrous joints lack a synovial cavity, while the costovertebral articulations contain synovial surfaces and supporting ligaments.

questions.stem: The manubriosternal and xiphisternal joints are classed as:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Per the lecture slide.

notes.A: Sternocostal.
notes.C: Sternoclavicular.
notes.D: Many textbooks say this for the manubriosternal joint, but the lecture slide lists synchondrosis.
notes.E: Skull.

questions.stem: During inspiration, the upward and forward movement of the sternum is called the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: During the pump-handle movement, the upper ribs elevate and carry the sternum upwards and forwards. This increases the anteroposterior diameter of the chest during inspiration.

notes.A: Bucket-handle movement elevates the lateral rib shafts and increases the transverse diameter of the chest.
notes.B: The diaphragm moves down like a piston during inspiration, increasing the vertical diameter of the cavity.
notes.D: Rib articulation permits rotation, but the standard name for the forward sternal displacement is pump-handle movement.
notes.E: See-saw breathing describes abnormal opposing chest and abdominal movements rather than the normal forward sternal excursion.

questions.stem: The vein that arches over the right main bronchus from behind is the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The azygos vein ascends along the right posterior thorax and arches forward over the right lung root. It passes superior to the main bronchus before joining the superior vena cava.

notes.A: The hemiazygos ascends on the left before crossing to join the azygos, without arching over the right bronchus.
notes.B: The superior vena cava lies anteriorly and receives the azygos arch rather than forming that arch itself.
notes.C: The right brachiocephalic vein helps form the superior vena cava above the opening of the azygos vein.
notes.E: The right superior pulmonary vein lies anterior in the lung root and returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

questions.stem: The hyparterial part of the right main bronchus divides to supply the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: After giving the eparterial upper lobar branch, the right main bronchus continues below the pulmonary artery as the bronchus intermedius. It divides into the right middle and lower lobar bronchi.

notes.A: The upper lobe receives the separate eparterial bronchus, whereas the middle lobe receives a branch below the artery.
notes.B: The lower lobe receives a hyparterial branch, but the upper lobe is supplied by the eparterial bronchus.
notes.C: The lower lobar bronchus is one branch of the bronchus intermedius, which also supplies the middle lobe.
notes.D: The lingula is in the left lung and has no bronchial connection to the right bronchus intermedius.

questions.stem: The left main bronchus crosses in front of the oesophagus, the descending aorta and the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The left main bronchus passes beneath the aortic arch on its way to the hilum. Its posterior relations include the oesophagus, thoracic duct and descending thoracic aorta.

notes.B: The azygos arch passes over the right main bronchus rather than behind the left one.
notes.C: The left vagus runs behind the left lung root, but it is not the third structure in the classic oesophagus–duct–aorta group.
notes.D: The left phrenic nerve passes anterior to the root along the pericardium, rather than behind the bronchus.
notes.E: The pulmonary trunk is an anterior great vessel near the proximal pulmonary arteries and does not lie behind the left main bronchus.

questions.stem: The bronchial arteries arise from the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The bronchial arteries usually arise from the descending thoracic aorta or one of its branches. They provide oxygenated systemic blood to conducting airways and supporting lung tissues.

notes.A: The pulmonary trunk carries venous blood towards the alveolar capillaries through the pulmonary arteries, separately from the bronchial arteries.
notes.C: The internal thoracic artery mainly supplies the anterior chest wall and gives pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic branches.
notes.D: The subclavian artery supplies neck and upper limb structures, while its direct branches are not the usual bronchial origins.
notes.E: The arch gives the main arterial branches to the head and upper limbs, whereas bronchial arteries usually arise distal to it.

questions.stem: Branches of the pulmonary artery accompany every bronchus but supply the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Pulmonary arterial branches travel beside the bronchial tree to reach alveolar capillary networks. The capillaries bring venous blood next to the alveolar air for gas exchange.

notes.A: Bronchial walls receive nutrient blood chiefly from the systemic bronchial arteries running alongside the airways.
notes.B: The bronchial circulation supplies supporting pulmonary tissues, including much of the visceral pleura.
notes.D: Hilar lymph nodes receive lymph from lung and bronchial tissues rather than being the destination of the pulmonary gas-exchange vessels.
notes.E: Bronchial cartilage is supported through the surrounding tissues and their bronchial arterial supply, not by alveolar capillaries.

questions.stem: Bronchopulmonary lymph nodes are also called:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Bronchopulmonary lymph nodes are the hilar nodes clustered around the main bronchi and pulmonary vessels where they enter the lung. Their efferents continue towards tracheobronchial nodes.

notes.A: Paratracheal nodes lie alongside the trachea and receive lymph at a more central stage of drainage.
notes.B: Tracheobronchial nodes are near the tracheal division and receive lymph leaving the more peripheral hilar nodes.
notes.C: Pretracheal nodes are in front of the trachea, rather than at the entrance to the lung.
notes.E: Deep cervical nodes lie in the neck and can receive downstream drainage rather than directly occupying the lung root.

questions.stem: Each lung has how many segmental bronchi (as taught)?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Counting the usual segmental territories separately gives three upper, two middle and five lower on the right, and five upper and five lower on the left. Some left-sided bronchi share stems.

notes.A: Eight can describe a left-sided scheme combining common segments, while this teaching scheme counts their component territories separately.
notes.B: Five is the count for a typical lower lobe, while a whole lung has additional upper segmental territories.
notes.C: Twelve exceeds the standard anatomic count, which is ten when the specified segmental territories are counted separately.
notes.D: Eighteen can represent a total across both lungs in some schemes, rather than the number within one lung.

questions.stem: How many segmental bronchi supply the right middle lobe?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The right middle lobar bronchus divides into a lateral and a medial segmental bronchus. These supply the two bronchopulmonary segments on either side of the lobe's arterial branches.

notes.B: Three is typical for the right upper lobe, which has apical, posterior and anterior segmental bronchi.
notes.C: Five is the conventional right lower-lobe count, including a superior segment and four basal segments.
notes.D: Four is the usual count of basal segments in the right lower lobe, rather than all right middle-lobe segments.
notes.E: The right middle lobe receives one lobar bronchus, which then divides to form two distinct segmental branches.

questions.stem: The receptors for the cough reflex in the tracheobronchial tree are:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: E
options.text: free endings in the bronchial arteries

questions.why: Their fibres travel in the vagus.

notes.A: Not as taught.
notes.C: Not the cough receptors.
notes.D: Aortic arch.
notes.E: Not as taught.

questions.stem: The visceral pleura becomes continuous with the parietal pleura at the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The mediastinal parietal pleura turns onto the lung as visceral pleura around the root at the hilum. The inferior continuation of this double reflection forms the pulmonary ligament.

notes.A: Cervical parietal pleura overlies the apex, while the two layers remain separated by a potential space there.
notes.B: The costodiaphragmatic recess forms where two portions of the parietal pleura meet, without a visceral reflection.
notes.D: The cardiac notch is on the anterior lung edge and is covered by visceral pleura like other lung surfaces.
notes.E: The oblique fissure has visceral pleura on its two opposing surfaces rather than a parietal-to-visceral junction.

questions.stem: The cervical pleura is also called the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The pleural cupula is the dome of cervical parietal pleura covering the apex of the lung. It projects into the root of the neck through the superior thoracic aperture.

notes.A: The suprapleural membrane reinforces the outside of the dome but is a separate layer of fascia.
notes.B: The pulmonary ligament is a double pleural fold below the root rather than a dome at the top of the lung.
notes.C: Endothoracic fascia separates pleura from the chest wall and thickens apically to form the suprapleural membrane.
notes.E: Costal pleura lines the costal wall and is distinguished from the cervical dome above the first rib.

questions.stem: The two pleurae touch each other behind the sternum from the level of the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The anterior pleural reflections come close behind the sternum around the second to fourth costal cartilages. Below this region the left reflection deviates laterally to accommodate the cardiac notch.

notes.A: Around the first cartilage the pleural reflections are approaching one another, above the usual close parasternal region.
notes.B: Below the fourth cartilage the left pleura diverges, creating a bare pericardial area behind part of the lower sternum.
notes.C: Near the sixth cartilage the reflections continue into inferior costodiaphragmatic lines rather than remaining together centrally.
notes.D: This interval extends well below the leftward divergence, where the two anterior reflections are more widely separated.

questions.stem: The lower pleural reflection crosses the midaxillary line at the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The lower pleural border usually crosses the eighth rib at the midclavicular line, the tenth at the midaxillary line and the twelfth posteriorly. It extends below the lower edge of the lung.

notes.B: The eighth rib is the usual midclavicular pleural landmark and is closer to the midaxillary lower lung edge.
notes.C: The sixth rib is near the anterior lower lung border rather than the lateral lower pleural reflection.
notes.D: The twelfth rib locates the posterior end of the lower pleural reflection closer to the vertebral column.
notes.E: The conventional midaxillary surface marking is one rib lower, with individual variation according to position and respiration.

questions.stem: A useful rule for the surface marking of the pleura is that each change occurs at:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The usual teaching landmarks for pleural reflections follow an approximate even-numbered sequence. Anterior changes occur near the second, fourth and sixth cartilages, with the lower reflection reaching roughly ribs eight, ten and twelve.

notes.A: The standard surface marking uses even levels, including the second and fourth cartilages and the eighth and tenth ribs.
notes.C: The usual checkpoints advance in steps of two rib levels rather than a sequence spaced every third rib.
notes.D: Floating ribs are only relevant to the posterior region, whereas the pleural reflection also has more anterior landmarks.
notes.E: True ribs supply some anterior landmarks, but the lower pleura extends to levels of false and floating ribs.

questions.stem: Air in the pleural cavity is called:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax; blood there is a haemothorax and fluid a pleural effusion.

notes.A: A haemothorax is blood accumulating between visceral and parietal pleura, rather than air in that cavity.
notes.B: A pleural effusion contains liquid within the pleural space and can blunt the costophrenic angle on imaging.
notes.D: Pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, sometimes with sharp pain during inspiration.
notes.E: Emphysema involves enlargement of air spaces inside the lung, rather than free air in the pleural cavity.

questions.stem: The three borders of each lung are the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The anterior and posterior borders lie where the costal and mediastinal surfaces meet. The inferior border encloses the base where the diaphragmatic surface meets the costal and mediastinal surfaces.

notes.A: Medial describes the mediastinal surface and superior refers to the apex, rather than identifying a pair of lung borders.
notes.B: The costal and mediastinal aspects are surfaces, although inferior correctly describes the rim of the base.
notes.C: The anterior border is present, but the other named borders are posterior and inferior rather than lateral and superior.
notes.E: The posterior edge is a named border, whereas medial and lateral are directional descriptions of lung surfaces.

questions.stem: The cardiac impression is found on which surface of the lung?
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: The heart and pericardium indent the adjacent medial surfaces of the lungs, producing a cardiac impression. It is deeper on the left because most of the heart lies left of the midline.

notes.A: The costal surface is convex against the chest wall and may show impressions from ribs.
notes.B: The diaphragmatic surface is the concave lung base moulded by the dome below it.
notes.C: The apex extends upwards into the root of the neck, away from the heart and pericardium.
notes.D: Interlobar surfaces face adjacent lobes across fissures rather than lying next to the heart and its sac.

questions.stem: In each lung root, the two pulmonary veins lie:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm

options.label: A
options.text: anterior and inferior to the bronchus

options.label: B
options.text: posterior and superior to the bronchus

options.label: C
options.text: superior and lateral to the bronchus

options.label: D
options.text: posterior and inferior to the bronchus

questions.why: Pulmonary veins lie on the anterior and inferior sides of the hilar bronchial structures. The superior vein is usually anterior, and the inferior vein is the lowest principal hilar structure.

notes.B: Bronchial structures generally lie posterior to the veins, and the inferior pulmonary vein is below the other large components.
notes.C: On the left the pulmonary artery lies superior to the bronchus, while the main pulmonary veins are anterior or inferior.
notes.D: Inferior describes the lower vein correctly, but the superior vein is usually the most anterior large hilar structure.
notes.E: The pulmonary veins are large hilar vessels distinct from the small bronchial vessels that serve the bronchial wall.

questions.stem: The horizontal fissure is found in the:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: In usual anatomy the horizontal fissure separates the right upper lobe from the right middle lobe. The left lung has only the oblique fissure as its standard lobar boundary.

notes.A: The left lung usually has only an oblique fissure separating its upper and lower lobes.
notes.C: The oblique fissure is present on both sides, while the usual horizontal fissure is right-sided.
notes.D: The right lung normally has a horizontal fissure in addition to the oblique fissure.
notes.E: An accessory left fissure can occur, but the horizontal fissure is not a normal finding in most left lungs.

questions.stem: When a fresh lung is handled, it:
questions.subtopic: Respiratory system, thoracic wall and diaphragm
questions.why: A fresh aerated lung feels soft and spongy because it contains air within many small spaces. Pressure during handling displaces the air and produces fine crackling known as crepitation.

notes.A: The lung contains numerous air spaces and elastic tissue, which give it a spongy rather than solid feel.
notes.B: An aerated lung usually floats because the air in its alveoli lowers its overall density.
notes.D: The lung is highly vascular, but the characteristic palpable finding in aerated tissue is crackling from its air spaces.
notes.E: Lung tissue is elastic and spongy rather than having the dense parenchymal texture of the liver.

questions.stem: The digestive tube extends from the mouth to the anus and measures approximately:
questions.why: The adult alimentary canal runs from mouth to anus, with the small intestine providing much of its length. Approximately nine metres is a useful teaching estimate, with measurements varying with muscle tone and method.

notes.B: Three metres can approximate a contracted small intestine in some measurements, but it omits other portions of the entire tract.
notes.C: Five metres is shorter than the usual rough estimate for the complete alimentary canal, although individual lengths vary.
notes.D: Fifteen metres is considerably longer than the usual estimate, even with intestinal muscle relaxed.
notes.E: Twenty metres is far above the usual anatomical range for the adult mouth-to-anus tract.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the accessory organs of the digestive system?
questions.why: The stomach is a dilated part of the alimentary canal through which food passes. Accessory digestive structures aid digestion outside that continuous lumen or project into it, as the teeth do.

notes.A: Pancreatic ducts deliver digestive enzymes and bicarbonate to the duodenum, allowing the gland to act as an accessory organ.
notes.C: Teeth mechanically reduce food in the mouth without forming a segment of the digestive tube.
notes.D: The parotid produces saliva and delivers it through a duct into the oral vestibule.
notes.E: The liver produces bile that reaches the duodenum through bile ducts, so it supports digestion as an accessory organ.

questions.stem: The vestibule of the mouth is the space lying between the:

options.label: C
options.text: cheeks/lips and the teeth and gums

options.label: D
options.text: tongue and the floor of the mouth

options.label: E
options.text: hard palate and the soft palate

questions.why: The oral vestibule is the small space outside the dental arches but inside the cheeks and lips. It communicates with the oral cavity proper around or behind the teeth.

notes.A: The region behind the teeth towards the palatoglossal arch is part of the oral cavity proper.
notes.B: The fauces is the posterior opening from the oral cavity to the oropharynx, not the space in front of the teeth.
notes.D: The tongue overlies the muscular oral floor within the dental arches, rather than lying in the vestibule.
notes.E: The hard and soft palates form continuous portions of the roof of the oral cavity proper.

questions.stem: The oral cavity communicates posteriorly with the pharynx through the fauces, which is bordered by the:
questions.why: The passage from the mouth into the oropharynx is the oropharyngeal isthmus. Its lateral margins are the palatoglossal arches, which extend from the soft palate to the sides of the tongue.

notes.A: The palatopharyngeal arch is the posterior tonsillar pillar behind the palatoglossal arch, forming the other side of the tonsillar bed.
notes.B: The pharyngeal raphe is a posterior midline attachment for the constrictors and does not bound the mouth's opening.
notes.C: The salpingopharyngeal fold runs from the auditory tube region of the nasopharynx, higher than the fauces.
notes.E: The pterygomandibular raphe gives attachment to buccinator and superior constrictor, lateral to the mucosal isthmus.

questions.stem: The roof of the oral cavity is formed by the:
questions.why: The hard palate provides a bony anterior roof, while the muscular soft palate forms the mobile posterior part. Together they separate the mouth from the nasal cavity and nasopharyngeal region.

notes.A: The soft palate and uvula form the mobile posterior portion, leaving out the larger anterior hard palate.
notes.B: The hard palate forms the anterior roof, while the tongue lies on the floor of the mouth.
notes.C: The maxilla contributes to the hard palate, whereas the mandible forms the lower jaw and is not part of the roof.
notes.D: The palatine tonsils lie in the sides of the oropharynx rather than making up its anterior neighbour's roof.

questions.stem: The principal muscle in the substance of the cheek forming the lateral wall of the oral cavity is the:
questions.why: Buccinator forms the muscular basis of the cheek and compresses it against the teeth. This keeps food on the occlusal surfaces during chewing and supports the lateral oral vestibule.

notes.B: Masseter is a muscle of mastication lying lateral to the mandibular ramus and elevates the lower jaw.
notes.C: Risorius is a superficial facial muscle that retracts the corner of the mouth rather than forming the muscular cheek wall.
notes.D: Temporalis lies in the temporal fossa and inserts on the coronoid process to elevate and retract the mandible.
notes.E: Platysma is a superficial sheet in the neck and lower face rather than the deep muscular wall of the cheek.

questions.stem: The tongue is best described as a mass of:

options.label: B
options.text: skeletal muscle covered by mucous membrane

options.label: C
options.text: smooth muscle covered by mucous membrane

options.label: D
options.text: skeletal muscle covered by serous membrane

options.label: E
options.text: fibrous tissue covered by mucous membrane

questions.why: Interwoven intrinsic and extrinsic skeletal muscle fibres give the tongue its voluntary mobility and ability to change shape. Mucosa covers the surface and is specialised into papillae in parts of the dorsum.

notes.A: The tongue is a muscular organ, while cartilage supports distinct structures such as the larynx or external ear.
notes.C: Smooth muscle drives involuntary movement in digestive walls, whereas tongue movements largely use striated skeletal muscle.
notes.D: The tongue is covered by oral mucosa exposed to food and saliva, rather than by a mesothelial serosa.
notes.E: A median fibrous septum provides connective tissue support, but skeletal muscle makes up most of the tongue.

questions.stem: The oral (anterior two-thirds) and pharyngeal (posterior one-third) parts of the tongue are separated by the:
questions.why: The V-shaped sulcus terminalis separates the mobile oral part of the tongue from the posterior pharyngeal part. The foramen caecum sits at the midline apex of the sulcus.

notes.A: The palatoglossal arch runs from soft palate to tongue and marks a lateral boundary of the fauces.
notes.B: Vallate papillae form a V-shaped row immediately in front of the sulcus, while the groove itself marks the boundary.
notes.D: The median sulcus runs longitudinally on the oral dorsum, separating its surface into right and left halves.
notes.E: The pectinate line is an anal canal landmark rather than a groove dividing regions of the tongue.

questions.stem: At the apex of the sulcus terminalis lies a small pit that marks the embryological origin of the thyroid gland, the:
questions.why: The foramen caecum is a small midline depression at the apex of the sulcus terminalis. It marks the starting point from which the thyroid primordium descended through the thyroglossal duct.

notes.A: The foramen spinosum is an opening in the sphenoid for the middle meningeal vessels, not a lingual depression.
notes.B: The foramen lacerum lies at the skull base near the internal carotid canal and is filled largely by cartilage in life.
notes.C: The incisive foramen lies on the anterior hard palate and transmits the nasopalatine nerves and small vessels.
notes.E: The foramen ovale of the skull transmits the mandibular nerve, and the cardiac foramen ovale is a separate fetal opening.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an EXTRINSIC muscle of the tongue?
questions.why: Genioglossus originates from the mandible and enters the tongue, so its attachment outside the tongue makes it extrinsic. Bilateral action draws the tongue forwards.

notes.A: Superior longitudinal fibres lie within the tongue and can shorten it and curl its tip upwards.
notes.B: Transverse fibres run from the median septum laterally within the tongue to narrow and elongate it.
notes.C: Vertical fibres are intrinsic and flatten the tongue by drawing its dorsal and ventral aspects closer together.
notes.D: Inferior longitudinal fibres run along the underside and help curl the tip downwards as part of the intrinsic muscle group.

questions.stem: The most numerous papillae roughening the dorsum of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue are the:
questions.why: Filiform papillae are the numerous slender, often keratinised projections covering most of the anterior dorsum. They provide friction for manipulating food and lack the taste buds found in some other papillae.

notes.B: Fungiform papillae are rounded structures scattered among filiform papillae, especially near the tip and margins.
notes.C: Vallate papillae are a small number of large taste papillae arranged in a row immediately anterior to the terminal sulcus.
notes.D: Foliate papillae form folds along the posterolateral edges rather than carpeting the anterior dorsal surface.
notes.E: Conical describes the shape of many filiform projections, but filiform is the conventional class name in human tongue anatomy.

questions.stem: The lingual frenulum is a midline fold of mucosa found on the:

options.label: D
options.text: under surface of the soft palate

questions.why: The lingual frenulum is a midline mucosal fold linking the ventral tongue to the floor of the mouth. It becomes conspicuous when the tip of the tongue is elevated.

notes.A: The floor of the nasal cavity lies above the hard palate and has no continuation with the lingual frenulum.
notes.C: The dorsal tongue carries papillae and sulci, while the frenulum connects the smooth underside to the oral floor.
notes.D: The undersurface of the soft palate faces the mouth but is above the tongue and separate from its frenulum.
notes.E: The posterior pharyngeal wall is behind the tongue base, away from the fold under the mobile anterior tongue.

questions.stem: Paralysis of which nerve is responsible for deviation of the protruded tongue?
questions.why: A unilateral lower motor neuron hypoglossal lesion weakens the ipsilateral genioglossus. On protrusion, the intact genioglossus on the opposite side pushes the tongue towards the weak side.

notes.A: The facial nerve supplies facial expression muscles and anterior tongue taste, but not the genioglossus.
notes.B: The vagus supplies palatoglossus, while tongue protrusion mainly requires hypoglossal motor input to genioglossus.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation and taste to much of the posterior tongue, rather than its protrusion muscle.
notes.E: The lingual nerve carries anterior tongue sensation and accompanying taste fibres, rather than motor fibres for tongue protrusion.

questions.stem: Human beings possess two successive sets of teeth during life; this condition is termed:
questions.why: Humans are diphyodont because a deciduous dentition appears first and is replaced by a permanent dentition. Permanent molars erupt behind the primary teeth rather than replacing primary molars.

notes.A: Homodont describes teeth of similar shape, independent of how many generations of teeth develop.
notes.B: Polyphyodont describes repeated tooth replacement through more than two generations, as occurs in many reptiles.
notes.C: Monophyodont describes a single generation of teeth, whereas humans develop both primary and permanent dentitions.
notes.E: Heterodont describes different tooth forms such as canines and molars, rather than how often a dentition is replaced.

questions.stem: Teeth that differ in structure and are adapted to handle food in different ways describe a dentition that is:
questions.why: Heterodont dentition contains several tooth forms adapted for distinct tasks. Incisors cut, canines help tear, and premolars and molars crush or grind food.

notes.A: Diphyodont refers to the succession of a primary and a permanent dentition rather than diversity of tooth shape.
notes.B: Homodont describes teeth of broadly similar shape, lacking the range of specialised human tooth forms.
notes.C: Thecodont describes teeth rooted in bony sockets, independent of the functions and forms of individual teeth.
notes.D: Brachydont describes relatively low-crowned teeth, rather than a mixture of tooth forms adapted to different functions.

questions.stem: The total number of teeth in the full permanent (adult) dentition is:
questions.why: Each adult quadrant contains two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. Eight teeth in each of four quadrants give a full complement of 32, including the wisdom teeth.

notes.B: Twenty is the usual primary dentition, which lacks premolars and has fewer molars in each quadrant.
notes.C: Twenty-eight is the adult tooth count before including the four third molars, which belong to the full complement.
notes.D: Twenty-four is only six teeth per quadrant and excludes teeth from the normal complement of eight.
notes.E: Thirty-six would require nine teeth per quadrant, which exceeds the standard human permanent dental formula.

questions.stem: The full deciduous (milk) dentition consists of how many teeth?
questions.why: In each primary quadrant there are two incisors, one canine and two molars, with no premolars. Those five teeth across four quadrants give a total of 20.

notes.A: Twenty-eight is the permanent count when third molars are excluded, rather than the primary count.
notes.C: Thirty-two represents a full permanent dentition with third molars, including teeth absent from the primary set.
notes.D: Twenty-four would give six per quadrant, but the primary formula has five in each.
notes.E: Sixteen is four teeth per quadrant and leaves out one tooth in each quadrant of the full primary dentition.

questions.stem: Which class of tooth is absent from the deciduous dentition?
questions.why: Primary teeth include incisors, canines and two molars in each quadrant. Permanent premolars erupt later and take the positions previously occupied by the two primary molars.

notes.A: The primary dentition has two molars in each quadrant to help grind food during childhood.
notes.B: The primary formula does omit one class found in the adult set: premolars that succeed the primary molars.
notes.D: Each primary quadrant contains one canine between the incisors and the first primary molar.
notes.E: There are two primary incisors in each quadrant, at the front of the dental arch.

questions.stem: The gingivae are best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: loose fatty tissue deep to the cheek muscle

options.label: B
options.text: serous membrane covering the tongue dorsum

options.label: C
options.text: cartilage supporting the roots of the teeth

options.label: D
options.text: fibrous tissue bound to the alveolar margins

options.label: E
options.text: mucous glands lining the floor of the mouth

questions.why: Gingiva is masticatory mucosa with a tough connective tissue core around the tooth necks. The attached portion binds firmly to the periosteum over the alveolar process.

notes.A: Buccal fat cushions the cheek in a different compartment, whereas gingival tissue lies against alveolar bone.
notes.B: The tongue is covered by oral mucosa rather than serosa, and that lining is separate from the gingiva.
notes.C: Tooth roots are supported by alveolar bone and periodontal ligament rather than a cartilaginous gingival framework.
notes.E: Salivary tissue occurs in the floor of the mouth, while the gingiva consists of surface epithelium and connective tissue.

questions.stem: Which pair of glands is the LARGEST of the salivary glands?
questions.why: The parotids are the largest of the paired major salivary glands. Each lies below and anterior to the ear and sends a duct across the masseter to the cheek.

notes.A: The submandibular gland is a major salivary gland beneath the mandible and is normally smaller than the parotid.
notes.B: The sublingual is the smallest major salivary gland and lies in the anterior floor of the mouth.
notes.C: The palate contains groups of minor salivary glands, with small ducts that open locally onto the oral surface.
notes.D: Lingual salivary glands are small glands in the tongue, such as the serous glands near vallate papillae.

questions.stem: The parotid duct crosses the masseter and then pierces which muscle to open into the mouth?
questions.why: The parotid duct crosses superficially over masseter, then turns medially at its anterior margin to pierce buccinator. It opens into the oral vestibule opposite the second upper molar.

notes.B: The duct runs superficial to masseter before turning medially; masseter does not form the wall it penetrates.
notes.C: Orbicularis oris forms a muscular ring around the lips, while the parotid duct enters farther back through the cheek.
notes.D: Temporalis passes deep to the zygomatic arch to the mandible, away from the superficial duct's course.
notes.E: Risorius is a superficial facial muscle that retracts the mouth corner, whereas the duct passes through deeper buccinator.

questions.stem: The parotid duct opens into the oral cavity opposite the crown of the:
questions.why: The parotid papilla is on the cheek mucosa opposite the second maxillary molar. Saliva reaches the oral vestibule there after the parotid duct passes through buccinator.

notes.A: The upper third molar lies posterior to the usual papilla opposite the second molar.
notes.C: A mandibular molar is in the lower arch, while the parotid papilla is aligned to the upper arch.
notes.D: The first upper premolar is anterior to the site where the duct pierces the posterior cheek.
notes.E: The upper canine is near the front of the arch, well anterior to the molar-level opening.

questions.stem: Painful swelling of the parotid gland is the classic feature of which infection?
questions.why: Mumps is a viral illness classically associated with painful swelling of one or both parotid glands. Inflammation expands the gland and can make chewing uncomfortable.

notes.A: Diphtheria usually produces pharyngeal inflammation with a pseudomembrane rather than characteristic parotid gland swelling.
notes.B: Tetanus produces muscle rigidity and spasms, including trismus, rather than swelling from parotid inflammation.
notes.D: Measles commonly causes fever, rash and buccal Koplik spots, rather than classic painful parotitis.
notes.E: Rubella can enlarge posterior auricular and suboccipital lymph nodes, which is different from inflammation of the parotid.

questions.stem: The submandibular duct (of Wharton) opens into the floor of the mouth:

options.label: A
options.text: at the apex of the tongue

questions.why: The submandibular duct travels forward in the floor of the mouth and opens at the sublingual caruncle. One caruncle lies on each side of the lingual frenulum.

notes.A: The tongue tip is anterior to the paired papillae, which lie on the floor of the mouth.
notes.B: The palatoglossal arch forms a margin of the fauces posteriorly, far from the sublingual caruncle.
notes.C: The duct runs anteriorly from the gland and opens beside the frenulum rather than behind the last molar.
notes.E: The second upper molar is the landmark for the parotid duct opening in the cheek.

questions.stem: The submandibular gland is partially covered by which muscle?
questions.why: The submandibular gland curves around the free posterior border of mylohyoid. Its superficial part is below and lateral to the muscle, while a smaller deep part extends above it into the oral floor.

notes.A: Buccinator forms the cheek wall and is pierced by the parotid duct, rather than separating the submandibular parts.
notes.B: Masseter lies on the lateral mandibular ramus beside the parotid region and does not form the muscular oral floor.
notes.C: Hyoglossus lies medial to the deep part and duct, while mylohyoid separates the deep and superficial portions.
notes.D: The digastric bellies bound the submandibular triangle, while mylohyoid is the muscle around whose edge the gland curves.

questions.stem: Which salivary gland lies directly beneath the mucosa of the floor of the mouth and drains by several small ducts?
questions.why: The sublingual gland lies above mylohyoid immediately beneath the mucosa of the anterior oral floor. Numerous small ducts usually open along the raised sublingual fold over the gland.

notes.B: The parotid lies near the ear and drains through a single main duct to the cheek.
notes.C: The submandibular gland primarily drains through one main duct at the caruncle beside the frenulum.
notes.D: Palatine glands are minor salivary glands producing secretions in the palate rather than beneath the sublingual fold.
notes.E: Buccal glands lie in or near the cheek mucosa and open locally rather than forming an anterior oral-floor gland.

questions.stem: Saliva performs all the following functions; it is primarily secreted by two cell types, namely:
questions.why: Salivary secretory units contain serous cells that produce a watery, enzyme-rich secretion and mucous cells that produce more viscous, mucin-rich secretion. Their proportions differ between glands.

notes.A: Paneth cells are found in intestinal crypts, and endocrine cells release signalling molecules rather than forming the two salivary secretory types.
notes.C: Goblet cells secrete mucin in various epithelia, while gastric parietal cells secrete acid and intrinsic factor.
notes.D: Chief and oxyntic cells are gastric cells that produce pepsinogen and acid respectively, rather than the main components of saliva.
notes.E: Salivary acini do secrete fluid, but islet cells are pancreatic endocrine cells that release hormones into blood.

questions.stem: The pharynx is a fibromuscular tube extending from the base of the skull to become continuous below with the:
questions.why: The pharynx starts at the skull base and descends behind the nasal cavity, mouth and larynx. At the lower border of the cricoid cartilage near C6, it continues as the oesophagus.

notes.A: The nasal cavities open forward from the upper pharyngeal subdivision through the choanae rather than continuing inferiorly.
notes.B: The oral cavity communicates with the oropharynx through the fauces, anterior to the pharyngeal lumen.
notes.D: The trachea is the inferior continuation of the larynx, whereas the pharyngeal food passage continues as the oesophagus.
notes.E: The larynx has an opening into the pharynx anteriorly, but the pharynx continues to the oesophagus behind it.

questions.stem: How many parts does the pharynx have, based on its anterior communications?
questions.why: The pharynx has nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and laryngopharyngeal regions, named for the cavities that open into them anteriorly. The oesophagus below is a continuation, rather than a fourth part.

notes.A: The three anterior communications define three compartments, while the oesophagus is a separate structure below.
notes.B: Features such as tonsils and pharyngeal recesses are landmarks within the three named regions rather than extra regions.
notes.C: There are three regions associated with the nasal cavity, oral cavity and larynx, with no standard subdivision into six parts.
notes.E: Counting only two leaves out a named region, for example the laryngopharynx behind the larynx.

questions.stem: The lowest part of the pharynx, also called the hypopharynx, is the:
questions.why: The laryngopharynx lies behind the larynx and leads to the upper oesophagus at the lower cricoid border. It is called the hypopharynx because it is the lowest pharyngeal region.
