notes.A: The nasopharynx lies above the soft palate and receives airflow from the nasal cavities.
notes.B: The oropharynx lies behind the mouth between the soft palate and upper epiglottic region, above the hypopharynx.
notes.C: The piriform recess is a depression lateral to the laryngeal inlet within the hypopharynx, rather than the whole region.
notes.D: The pharyngeal isthmus is an opening between nasopharynx and oropharynx, not the inferior subdivision.

questions.stem: The posterolateral wall of the pharynx is supported mainly by the:

options.label: A
options.text: superior, middle and inferior constrictor muscles

options.label: D
options.text: the genioglossus and the hyoglossus muscles

options.label: E
options.text: the mylohyoid and the anterior digastric muscles

questions.why: The three pharyngeal constrictors overlap to form most of the posterior and lateral muscular wall. Their sequential contraction moves a swallowed bolus towards the oesophagus.

notes.B: Stylopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus run longitudinally and help elevate the pharynx rather than forming its main circular wall.
notes.C: Palatopharyngeus helps elevate the pharynx, and palatoglossus forms an oral arch at the opening of the fauces.
notes.D: Genioglossus and hyoglossus move the tongue, with their main bulk in the mouth rather than the posterior pharyngeal wall.
notes.E: Mylohyoid and the anterior digastric belly lie in the suprahyoid region and contribute to movement of the oral floor or hyoid.

questions.stem: The pharynx communicates anteriorly with all of the following cavities EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The nasal cavity, mouth and laryngeal inlet communicate with their corresponding pharyngeal regions. The pericardial cavity is a separate serous space in the thorax around the heart.

notes.A: The pericardial cavity is a clear exception, so it is possible to identify one listed cavity without an anterior pharyngeal opening.
notes.C: The nasal cavity communicates through the choanae with the anterior aspect of the nasopharynx.
notes.D: The oral cavity connects through the fauces to the oropharynx behind the tongue.
notes.E: The laryngeal inlet is the connection from the laryngopharynx forwards to the upper airway.

questions.stem: The superior boundary of the abdominal cavity is formed by the:
questions.why: The muscular diaphragm arches above the upper abdominal viscera and separates them from the thoracic cavity. It forms the superior abdominal boundary despite rising into the lower rib cage.

notes.B: The pelvic brim is the inferior transition between the abdominal cavity and the true pelvis.
notes.C: The lumbar vertebrae and their associated muscles contribute to the posterior abdominal wall rather than its roof.
notes.D: Transversalis fascia lines the deep surface of the anterolateral abdominal wall and is distinct from the muscular dome above the viscera.
notes.E: The costal margin forms part of the lower rib cage and gives muscle attachments, while the diaphragm spans the cavity above.

questions.stem: Inferiorly, the abdominal cavity has no distinct boundary because it is continuous with the pelvic cavity at the:
questions.why: The abdominal and pelvic cavities communicate through the pelvic inlet, outlined by the pelvic brim. It is a reference boundary rather than a tissue floor separating the two cavities.

notes.A: The ischioanal fossa lies below the pelvic diaphragm next to the anal canal, well below the abdominal transition.
notes.C: The perineum lies below the pelvic floor, separate from the inlet into the true pelvis.
notes.D: The arcuate line of the ilium forms one part of the pelvic brim, which as a whole marks the transition.
notes.E: The inguinal ligament runs across the anterior groin and marks the abdominal wall's lower edge rather than the pelvic inlet.

questions.stem: The four abdominal quadrants are produced by the intersection of the median plane and the:
questions.why: The transumbilical plane runs horizontally through the umbilicus and crosses the vertical median plane. Together they form the right and left upper and lower abdominal quadrants.

notes.A: The transtubercular plane passes through the iliac tubercles and is a boundary used in the nine-region scheme.
notes.B: The interspinous plane joins the anterior superior iliac spines and lies below the usual transumbilical plane.
notes.D: The transpyloric plane passes near L1 and is mainly used to describe the level of viscera and vessels.
notes.E: The subcostal plane joins the inferior costal margins and is commonly used to define the upper row of nine regions.

questions.stem: The transpyloric plane lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The transpyloric plane is a horizontal plane that passes near the L1 vertebral body in the usual surface marking. It approximates the pyloric level in a supine adult.

notes.A: L3 is near the subcostal plane and the typical inferior mesenteric origin, below the transpyloric level.
notes.B: L5 is near the transtubercular plane through the iliac tubercles, several vertebral levels below the pylorus.
notes.C: T10 is the approximate oesophageal hiatus level in the diaphragm, higher than the transpyloric plane.
notes.E: T12 is close to the aortic hiatus and coeliac origin, just above the conventional L1 plane.

questions.stem: The subcostal plane, used to define the nine regions, passes at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The subcostal plane joins the lowest points of the costal margin, typically at the tenth costal cartilages. It crosses near L3 and separates the upper from the middle abdominal regions.

notes.A: L1 is the approximation for the transpyloric plane, which sits above the lowest costal margin.
notes.B: L5 is the usual level of the transtubercular plane, which separates the middle and lower regional rows.
notes.C: T12 is near the posterior aortic hiatus, above the standard subcostal plane.
notes.D: T10 is near the oesophageal hiatus through the diaphragm, above the abdominal subcostal plane.

questions.stem: The transtubercular (intertubercular) plane passes at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The transtubercular plane crosses the iliac tubercles, palpable prominences on the outer iliac crests. It is near L5 and serves as the lower horizontal plane of the nine-region scheme.

notes.B: L3 is the usual level of the subcostal plane through inferior costal margins rather than the iliac tubercles.
notes.C: The transpyloric plane is near L1, several levels above the transtubercular plane through the iliac crests.
notes.D: S1 is around the sacral promontory, below the L5 level used to describe the transtubercular plane.
notes.E: T12 is at the lower end of the thoracic spine, clearly superior to the iliac tubercles.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the nine abdominal regions?
questions.why: The central lower region is called the hypogastric, pubic or suprapubic region. The standard four-quadrant scheme has right and left upper and lower quadrants, so there is no named suprapubic quadrant.

notes.A: The left lumbar region is the left-sided middle region, lateral to the umbilical region.
notes.C: The epigastric region is the central upper region between the two hypochondriac regions.
notes.D: The right hypochondriac region is one of the upper lateral regions, beneath the right costal margin.
notes.E: The umbilical region is the central middle region, bounded laterally by the reference lines through the abdomen.

questions.stem: McBurney's point, used in the diagnosis of appendicitis, lies one-third of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the:

options.label: A
options.text: the crest of the iliac bone

questions.why: McBurney's point is one-third along the line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus.

questions.stem: The linea semilunaris corresponds to the:

options.label: B
options.text: lower free border of external oblique

questions.why: The linea semilunaris is the curved lateral border of rectus abdominis, where aponeurotic layers turn to form the rectus sheath. It marks the boundary between the rectus and lateral abdominal muscles.

notes.A: Transversus abdominis has arching fibres near the inguinal region, a separate feature from the lateral rectus border.
notes.B: The lower free border of the external oblique aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament in the groin.
notes.C: Tendinous intersections cross the rectus muscle transversely, rather than tracing its curved lateral edge.
notes.E: The aponeuroses interweave at the linea alba, which is in the midline medial to both rectus muscles.

questions.stem: The midline fibrous band between the two rectus abdominis muscles, attached from xiphoid process to pubic symphysis, is the:
questions.why: The linea alba is formed where the abdominal muscle aponeuroses interweave between the two rectus muscles. It runs in the midline from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis.

notes.A: The linea semilunaris is curved and lies at the lateral margin of each rectus muscle rather than between them.
notes.B: The arcuate line forms the lower free edge of the posterior rectus sheath rather than a vertical midline seam.
notes.C: The iliopubic tract is a deep fascial band near the inguinal region and lies below and lateral to much of the linea alba.
notes.D: Tendinous intersections span individual rectus bellies transversely and separate their muscular segments rather than separating right from left.

questions.stem: Below the umbilicus the superficial fascia splits into a superficial fatty layer and a deep membranous layer; the fatty layer is called:
questions.why: Camper's fascia is the superficial, fat-rich layer of subcutaneous tissue on the lower anterior abdominal wall. The deeper Scarpa layer is more membranous and continues towards the perineum.

notes.B: Scarpa's fascia is the deeper membranous layer, beneath the fatty subcutaneous layer in the lower abdomen.
notes.C: Colles' fascia is superficial membranous fascia of the perineum, continuous with the deeper abdominal subcutaneous layer.
notes.D: Buck's fascia is a deep layer surrounding the erectile tissues of the penis below the superficial penile fascia.
notes.E: Gallaudet's fascia is deep investing fascia of superficial perineal muscles, rather than fatty tissue of the anterior abdomen.

questions.stem: The membranous layer of superficial fascia (Scarpa's fascia) continues into the perineum as:
questions.why: Scarpa's fascia continues into the superficial perineum as the membranous layer called Colles' fascia. Its fascial attachments help determine where fluid can spread between the perineum and lower anterior abdominal wall.

notes.A: Fascia lata is deep fascia of the thigh, to which Scarpa's fascia is attached below the inguinal ligament.
notes.C: Buck's fascia is deep penile fascia, lying below the superficial layer continuous with the abdominal membranous fascia.
notes.D: Camper's fascia is the superficial fatty layer of abdominal subcutaneous tissue rather than the named perineal membrane.
notes.E: The dartos layer is the specialised superficial tissue of the scrotum, whereas Colles' fascia names the layer in the perineum.

questions.stem: Over the scrotum, the fatty layer of superficial fascia is replaced by:
questions.why: The scrotal superficial fascia contains smooth dartos muscle and has little or no subcutaneous fat. When dartos contracts it wrinkles the scrotal skin, changing its exposed surface area.

notes.A: Cremasteric fascia accompanies cremaster muscle around the spermatic cord and lies deeper than the scrotal superficial fascia.
notes.B: The tunica vaginalis is a serous sac derived from peritoneum and lies deep around the testis.
notes.D: Colles' fascia is the membranous superficial fascia of the perineum, while the scrotal layer incorporates smooth muscle.
notes.E: Buck's fascia invests the deep tissues of the penis and is separate from the scrotum's subcutaneous layer.

questions.stem: A characteristic feature of the anterior abdominal wall compared with the limbs is that it has:
questions.why: There is no deep fascia over the anterior abdominal wall muscles.

questions.stem: The external oblique muscle arises from the outer surfaces of which ribs?
questions.why: External oblique has slips arising from the outer surfaces of the fifth to twelfth ribs. They descend into the lateral abdominal wall and continue anteriorly as a broad aponeurosis.

notes.A: The first through sixth ribs are too high overall, as the origin begins at the fifth and continues to the twelfth.
notes.B: The seventh through twelfth ribs are included, but the fifth and sixth ribs also give origin to slips.
notes.C: The ninth through twelfth ribs represent only the lowest part of the origin, which spans eight ribs.
notes.D: The second through eighth ribs include some upper slips but leave out the lower attachments extending to rib 12.

questions.stem: The fibres of the external oblique muscle run in which direction?
questions.why: Most fibres of external oblique slope downwards and medially from the ribs, like the direction of hands inserted into front pockets. This orientation helps the muscle flex and rotate the trunk.

notes.B: A generally superomedial direction is characteristic of much of the internal oblique, whose fibres cross external oblique.
notes.C: Transverse fibres are most characteristic of transversus abdominis, the deeper circumferential muscle layer.
notes.D: Vertical fibres are characteristic of rectus abdominis, the paired muscle beside the midline.
notes.E: Some posterior fibres descend towards the iliac crest, but the predominant anterior direction is towards the midline.

questions.stem: The fibres of the internal oblique muscle are generally directed:
questions.why: Most internal oblique fibres fan upwards and medially from the iliac crest and thoracolumbar region. Their orientation generally crosses that of external oblique, while the lowest fibres arch more horizontally.

notes.A: Some lower fibres curve towards the groin, but the predominant direction of the muscle is upwards and medially.
notes.C: Inferomedial fibres are the characteristic direction of external oblique, the more superficial layer.
notes.D: Transverse fibres are most characteristic of transversus abdominis, although the lowest internal oblique fibres also arch across.
notes.E: Rectus abdominis is the mainly vertical muscle adjacent to the linea alba.

questions.stem: Which muscle of the anterolateral abdominal wall has horizontally running fibres and is the main muscle for compressing the abdominal viscera?
questions.why: Transversus abdominis wraps around the abdominal cavity with predominantly horizontal fibres. Contraction draws the wall inward, compressing the viscera and helping increase intra-abdominal pressure with the other abdominal muscles.

notes.A: Internal oblique helps compress the contents, but most of its fibres have a more oblique, superomedial direction.
notes.B: Rectus abdominis runs vertically and chiefly flexes the trunk while also contributing to compression.
notes.D: Quadratus lumborum belongs to the posterior wall and helps stabilise the twelfth rib and flex the trunk laterally.
notes.E: External oblique contributes to compression and rotation but has mainly inferomedial fibres rather than a horizontal course.

questions.stem: The rectus abdominis muscle arises from the pubic symphysis and crest and inserts on the:

options.label: B
options.text: anterior iliac crest and inguinal ligament

questions.why: Rectus abdominis runs from the pubic crest and symphysis to the xiphoid process and fifth to seventh costal cartilages. Its longitudinal course allows it to flex the trunk.

notes.A: The linea alba forms the medial seam of the rectus sheath, while the pubic attachments are at the muscle's lower end.
notes.B: The iliac crest and inguinal ligament provide attachments for lower fibres of lateral abdominal muscles such as internal oblique.
notes.C: The thoracolumbar fascia and twelfth rib are posterior or lateral attachments, separate from the anterior upper rectus attachments.
notes.E: Rectus abdominis has more superior attachments at cartilages five to seven and the xiphoid rather than the ninth cartilage.

questions.stem: The small triangular muscle that lies within the rectus sheath anterior to the lower rectus abdominis and is absent in about 20% of people is the:
questions.why: Pyramidalis is a small triangular muscle in front of lower rectus abdominis inside the sheath. It runs from pubis to linea alba and tenses the latter when present.

notes.A: Plantaris is a small muscle in the posterior leg with a long tendon, well away from the abdominal wall.
notes.B: Palmaris longus is a variable superficial forearm muscle that tenses the palmar aponeurosis rather than the linea alba.
notes.C: Cremaster is associated with the spermatic cord and elevates the testis rather than lying in the rectus sheath.
notes.D: Psoas minor is a variable muscle on the posterior abdominal wall, anterior to psoas major.

questions.stem: The anterolateral abdominal wall muscles are chiefly supplied by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.why: Lower thoracic anterior rami continue between internal oblique and transversus abdominis to supply the wall. The usual pattern includes T7–T11, the T12 subcostal nerve and L1 through the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

notes.B: T1–T6 chiefly supply higher thoracic territories, while the main segmental abdominal wall supply travels in lower thoracic nerves.
notes.C: L1 contributes through the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves, but this range omits the major lower thoracic supply.
notes.D: T12 and L1 contribute, but this range wrongly omits the thoracoabdominal nerves arising above T12.
notes.E: C5–T1 are principal roots of the brachial plexus, which supplies the upper limb rather than the abdominal wall.

questions.stem: Below the arcuate line, the rectus sheath has:
questions.why: Below the arcuate line, the aponeuroses of all three lateral abdominal muscles pass in front of rectus abdominis. Transversalis fascia remains behind it but does not form a posterior aponeurotic sheath.

notes.A: Below this level the aponeuroses contribute to the anterior layer rather than doubling behind the muscle.
notes.C: The anterior aponeurotic layer remains below the arcuate line, with transversalis fascia alone covering the rectus posteriorly.
notes.D: Both aponeurotic walls are present higher up, while the posterior wall ends at the arcuate line.
notes.E: The anterior sheath is substantial below the line because it receives aponeuroses from all three lateral muscles.

questions.stem: The arcuate line of the rectus sheath is located approximately:

options.label: A
options.text: a little above the pubic symphysis

options.label: B
options.text: just below the anterior costal margin

options.label: C
options.text: a third of the way from umbilicus to pubis

options.label: D
options.text: midway between the xiphoid and umbilicus

options.label: E
options.text: exactly at the level of the umbilicus

questions.why: In a common teaching approximation the arcuate line is one-third of the way from the umbilicus towards the pubis, although its level varies. It is the lower edge of the posterior aponeurotic rectus sheath.

notes.A: The line can be low in some people, but the standard landmark is a short distance below the umbilicus.
notes.B: The anterior costal margin is well above the usual lower-rectus transition from a posterior sheath to transversalis fascia.
notes.D: The xiphoid-to-umbilicus interval is in the upper anterior wall, whereas the arcuate line is usually below the umbilicus.
notes.E: The umbilicus is a reference point above the standard location, and the line has no fixed relation to it.

questions.stem: A defect in which layer is the fundamental basis of an abdominal wall hernia?
questions.why: The transversalis fascia gives the wall its structural integrity; a hernia results from a defect in it.

questions.stem: The external spermatic fascia covering the spermatic cord is derived from the:
questions.why: At the superficial inguinal ring the external oblique aponeurosis forms the outermost spermatic fascial covering. The cord has already acquired its two deeper coverings on the way through the canal.

notes.A: Internal oblique fibres and fascia contribute to the cremasteric layer, which lies deep to the external spermatic fascia.
notes.B: Transversalis fascia contributes the internal spermatic fascia at the deep inguinal ring.
notes.C: The processus vaginalis is a peritoneal extension that gives rise to the tunica vaginalis, rather than external spermatic fascia.
notes.D: Cremaster muscle belongs to the middle cord covering with its fascia, while the outer covering is aponeurotic.

questions.stem: The cremasteric muscle and fascia of the spermatic cord are derived from the:
questions.why: The cord receives cremasteric muscle and fascia as it passes through the inguinal canal next to internal oblique. The striated fibres can contract to elevate the testis.

notes.B: External oblique aponeurosis forms the external spermatic fascia at the superficial inguinal ring.
notes.C: Transversalis fascia provides the innermost spermatic fascia where the cord enters the deep inguinal ring.
notes.D: Transversus abdominis usually arches above the canal without giving a separate covering to the cord.
notes.E: Peritoneum extends as the processus vaginalis, whose distal part persists as the serous tunica vaginalis.

questions.stem: The internal spermatic fascia of the spermatic cord is derived from the:
questions.why: The spermatic cord acquires its internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring. This is the innermost of the three fascial and muscular coverings gained in the inguinal passage.

notes.A: Scarpa's fascia is membranous subcutaneous tissue and remains superficial to the coverings gained from the canal walls.
notes.C: External oblique aponeurosis forms the most superficial spermatic fascial covering at the superficial ring.
notes.D: Internal oblique provides the cremasteric layer, between the external and internal spermatic fascias.
notes.E: Peritoneum forms the serous tunica vaginalis around the testis via the processus vaginalis, separate from internal spermatic fascia.

questions.stem: The superior epigastric artery, supplying the upper rectus abdominis, is a continuation of the:
questions.why: The internal thoracic artery divides into superior epigastric and musculophrenic branches near the lower thoracic wall. The superior epigastric enters the rectus sheath and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery.

notes.A: The abdominal aorta gives branches to the abdominal wall but is not the direct parent of the superior epigastric artery.
notes.B: The subcostal artery runs below the twelfth rib and supplies a different part of the thoracoabdominal wall.
notes.D: The external iliac artery gives the inferior epigastric artery, which reaches the sheath from below.
notes.E: The femoral artery gives superficial epigastric branches below the inguinal ligament, separate from the deep superior epigastric route.

questions.stem: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the:
questions.why: The inferior epigastric artery branches from external iliac just above the inguinal ligament. It ascends on the deep surface of the anterior abdominal wall and joins superior epigastric branches within the rectus sheath.

notes.A: The femoral artery begins below the inguinal ligament and gives the superficial rather than the deep inferior epigastric artery.
notes.B: The internal iliac mainly supplies the pelvis and gives separate branches such as the obturator artery.
notes.C: The abdominal aorta supplies the external iliac indirectly via the common iliac, rather than giving a direct inferior epigastric branch.
notes.E: The internal thoracic artery gives the superior epigastric artery, which approaches the rectus muscle from above.

questions.stem: Dilated subcutaneous veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae) result from anastomoses carried by the paraumbilical veins to the:
questions.why: Paraumbilical veins link the left portal vein to veins in the anterior abdominal wall. In portal hypertension they can divert blood into superficial veins, whose enlargement produces the caput medusae pattern.

notes.A: Inferior caval tributaries can receive blood through systemic abdominal-wall channels, while paraumbilical veins connect those channels to the portal system.
notes.B: Superior caval tributaries can receive some collateral flow, but the direct paraumbilical connection to the liver is portal.
notes.C: Renal veins drain the kidneys into the inferior vena cava and do not form the usual direct periumbilical portal link.
notes.D: The splenic vein helps form the portal vein, but paraumbilical veins connect more directly with its left portal branch.

questions.stem: The dermatome overlying the umbilicus is supplied by which spinal nerve?
questions.why: The skin around the umbilicus corresponds roughly to the T10 dermatome. The T10 anterior ramus reaches the anterior wall as a thoracoabdominal nerve and supplies skin near this level.

notes.B: T7 supplies a higher band of skin nearer the upper anterior abdominal wall.
notes.C: T12 is the subcostal nerve and typically supplies skin in a lower band than the umbilicus.
notes.D: L1 supplies skin near the groin through branches such as the ilioinguinal nerve.
notes.E: T6 is higher, near the xiphoid region, and supplies skin above the usual umbilical level.

questions.stem: The neurovascular plane of the anterolateral abdominal wall lies between the:

options.label: A
options.text: the rectus abdominis and its own sheath

options.label: C
options.text: the external and the internal oblique layers

options.label: D
options.text: the skin and the external oblique muscle

questions.why: Segmental nerves and accompanying vessels run in the transversus abdominis plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis. They supply the abdominal muscles and continue towards the skin.

notes.A: Rectus receives branches within its sheath, but the main lateral segmental pathway lies between the two deeper flat muscles.
notes.C: External oblique is superficial to internal oblique, while the main neurovascular plane lies deep to internal oblique.
notes.D: The subcutaneous plane has superficial vessels and skin branches, rather than carrying the major segmental bundles between muscles.
notes.E: The extraperitoneal plane lies deeper than the transversalis fascia and is separate from the intermuscular neurovascular plane.

questions.stem: The median umbilical fold on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall is raised by the:

options.label: A
options.text: remnant of the round ligament of liver

questions.why: The median umbilical ligament is the closed urachus between the bladder apex and umbilicus. It raises a single midline fold of peritoneum on the posterior surface of the anterior abdominal wall.

notes.A: The round ligament of the liver is the remnant of the left umbilical vein and runs in the falciform ligament.
notes.B: The vitelline duct connected the midgut to the yolk sac, and persistence can produce an ileal diverticulum.
notes.D: The paired obliterated umbilical arteries raise the medial umbilical folds, one on each side of the midline.
notes.E: Functional inferior epigastric vessels elevate the lateral umbilical folds, outside the obliterated arterial folds.

questions.stem: The lateral umbilical folds are raised by the:
questions.why: Each inferior epigastric artery and vein elevates the overlying parietal peritoneum as a lateral umbilical fold. These folds are landmarks separating the medial and lateral inguinal fossae.

notes.A: The urachus is a single midline remnant raising the median umbilical fold rather than the paired lateral folds.
notes.B: Superior epigastric vessels enter the rectus sheath from above rather than forming the inferior peritoneal ridges.
notes.C: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal, not along the ridge made by the inferior epigastric vessels.
notes.E: Obliterated umbilical arteries raise the two medial folds, lying between the lateral folds and the midline urachus.

questions.stem: The inguinal ligament is formed by the rolled-under inferior border of the aponeurosis of the:
questions.why: The inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis rolls under and thickens between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle. This folded border forms the inguinal ligament.

notes.A: Internal oblique has attachments near the ligament, and its lowest arching fibres contribute to the canal roof.
notes.B: Transversus abdominis contributes to the canal roof and may join internal oblique in forming the conjoint tendon.
notes.C: Rectus abdominis is a vertical muscle near the midline, with an attachment on the pubic crest and symphysis.
notes.D: Transversalis fascia forms the deep inguinal ring and much of the posterior canal wall rather than its external aponeurotic ligament.

questions.stem: The inguinal canal is approximately how long in the adult?
questions.why: The adult inguinal canal is an oblique passage about 4 cm long. It runs inferomedially from the deep ring in transversalis fascia to the superficial ring in the external oblique aponeurosis.

notes.B: A one-centimetre estimate is too short for the full oblique distance between the adult inguinal rings.
notes.C: Eight centimetres is roughly twice the usual canal length and overstates the separation of its openings.
notes.D: Twelve centimetres is much longer than the distance from the deep ring to the superficial ring.
notes.E: Two centimetres is about half the conventional length of the full adult passage.

questions.stem: The deep (internal) inguinal ring is an opening in the:
questions.why: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in transversalis fascia just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. The fascia continues onto the spermatic cord as its internal covering.

notes.A: Parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity deep to the ring and can protrude through it in an indirect hernia.
notes.C: External oblique aponeurosis contains the superficial inguinal ring, which is the more anterior and medial exit.
notes.D: Internal oblique forms part of the canal roof and reinforces the anterior wall laterally rather than forming the deep opening.
notes.E: The conjoint tendon reinforces the medial posterior wall, while the deep ring lies farther laterally.

questions.stem: The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to which vessels?
questions.why: The inferior epigastric vessels ascend medial to the deep inguinal ring. An indirect inguinal hernia enters through the ring lateral to them, whereas a direct hernia emerges medial to them.

notes.A: Deep circumflex iliac vessels run laterally near the iliac crest and do not mark the medial edge of the deep ring.
notes.B: Superficial epigastric vessels ascend in the subcutaneous tissues and are too superficial to define the deep ring.
notes.D: The superior epigastric vessels run into the rectus sheath from above, separate from the lower inguinal landmarks.
notes.E: Inferior epigastric vessels branch from the external iliac vessels, whose main course is towards the lower limb.

questions.stem: The superficial (external) inguinal ring is a defect in the:
questions.why: The superficial ring is a triangular opening in external oblique aponeurosis near the pubic tubercle. Its edges form crura and give fascia to structures passing out of the canal.

notes.A: Internal oblique contributes arching roof fibres, while the superficial opening lies in the aponeurosis in front of it.
notes.B: The conjoint tendon reinforces the medial posterior wall rather than forming the superficial exit in the anterior wall.
notes.C: The rectus sheath encloses the medial vertical muscle and is separate from the ring in external oblique.
notes.E: Transversalis fascia contains the deep ring, at the opposite end of the inguinal canal.

questions.stem: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching fibres of the:

options.label: A
options.text: the external and the internal oblique muscles

options.label: B
options.text: the transversalis fascia and the peritoneum

options.label: C
options.text: the inguinal and the lacunar ligaments

options.label: D
options.text: the rectus abdominis and the pyramidalis

questions.why: Inferior fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis arch over the inguinal canal. Medially their aponeurotic portions can unite in the conjoint tendon to reinforce the posterior wall.

notes.A: Internal oblique contributes to the roof, but external oblique aponeurosis principally forms the anterior wall.
notes.B: Transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall, with peritoneum lying still deeper away from the muscular arch.
notes.C: The inguinal ligament forms the floor and the lacunar ligament reinforces it medially.
notes.D: Rectus and pyramidalis are within the rectus sheath medial to most of the canal, rather than spanning its roof.

questions.stem: The anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed mainly by the:
questions.why: External oblique aponeurosis spans the length of the canal anteriorly and forms the superficial inguinal ring at its medial end. Internal oblique adds reinforcement in the lateral part.

notes.B: Transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall of the canal and contains the deep inguinal ring.
notes.C: The conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially rather than extending along the front of the canal.
notes.D: Internal oblique gives lateral reinforcement, while external oblique aponeurosis remains the principal continuous anterior layer.
notes.E: The rolled lower edge of external oblique forms the inguinal ligament, which contributes to the canal floor.

questions.stem: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the transversalis fascia reinforced medially by the:
questions.why: The conjoint tendon brings together aponeurotic fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis near the pubic crest and pecten. There it reinforces transversalis fascia in the medial posterior canal wall.

notes.A: The pectineal ligament lies on the superior pubic ramus and helps bound the femoral ring posteriorly.
notes.C: The inguinal ligament forms the floor of the canal rather than the medial reinforcement behind it.
notes.D: The lacunar ligament reflects medially from the inguinal ligament and supports the medial floor of the canal.
notes.E: External oblique aponeurosis forms the principal anterior wall and contains the superficial ring.

questions.stem: Which structure passes through the inguinal canal in BOTH sexes?
questions.why: The ilioinguinal nerve enters the canal by piercing internal oblique, bypassing the deep ring. It emerges from the superficial ring to supply parts of the upper medial thigh and external genitalia in both sexes.

notes.A: The genital branch may use the deep ring, but the genitofemoral trunk itself divides before reaching the inguinal canal.
notes.B: The vas deferens is carried in the spermatic cord, which is present only in males.
notes.D: The spermatic cord carries vessels and the vas deferens to the testis, so it is a male canal content.
notes.E: The round ligament of the uterus is the corresponding female canal content, rather than a structure present in both.

questions.stem: The conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) is formed by the lower fibres of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis and inserts on the pubic crest and the:
questions.why: Fibres from the lower internal oblique and transversus abdominis form the conjoint tendinous region. It attaches to the pubic crest and pectineal line on the superior pubic ramus, supporting the medial posterior canal wall.

notes.A: The anterior superior iliac spine is the lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament, far from the conjoint insertion.
notes.B: The pubic tubercle is a key inguinal ligament attachment, whereas the conjoint tendon is classically described on the crest and pecten.
notes.C: The arcuate line marks the inferior edge of the posterior rectus sheath and is not a bony attachment.
notes.E: The iliac crest provides origins for lateral abdominal muscles rather than the medial insertion of their lowest conjoint fibres.

questions.stem: The medial boundary of the femoral canal is formed by the:
questions.why: At the femoral ring, the lacunar ligament curves medially from the inguinal ligament onto the superior pubic ramus. It forms the medial limit of the femoral canal's entrance.

notes.A: The inguinal ligament lies anterior to the femoral ring and forms its anterior boundary.
notes.B: The pectineal ligament lies posteriorly on the superior pubic ramus and contributes to the posterior boundary of the ring.
notes.C: The femoral vein is immediately lateral to the canal within the femoral sheath.
notes.D: The femoral artery is farther lateral than the vein and lies in a separate sheath compartment.

questions.stem: The lateral boundary of the femoral canal is the:
questions.why: The femoral canal is the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath. The femoral vein occupies the adjacent compartment and lies immediately lateral to the canal and its upper opening.

notes.B: The femoral artery is lateral to the vein and occupies the lateral compartment of the sheath.
notes.C: The femoral nerve lies still farther laterally and is outside the femoral sheath.
notes.D: The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring rather than its lateral border.
notes.E: The pectineal ligament lies along the superior pubic ramus and contributes to the posterior boundary of the ring.

questions.stem: The boundaries of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle include the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, the inguinal ligament inferiorly, and medially the:

options.label: C
options.text: medial border of the psoas major

questions.why: The rectus abdominis margin is the medial side of Hesselbach's triangle. With the inferior epigastric vessels and inguinal ligament it outlines the posterior inguinal wall region through which direct hernias can emerge.

notes.A: The pectineal ligament is a landmark behind the femoral ring, below the inguinal triangle.
notes.C: Psoas major lies on the posterior abdominal wall, far from the medial boundary of this anterior triangle.
notes.D: The conjoint tendon can strengthen the triangle's posterior wall medially, but its named medial boundary is the rectus margin.
notes.E: The rolled lower edge of external oblique forms the inguinal ligament, which is the triangle's inferior boundary.

questions.stem: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring, lying which way in relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
questions.why: An indirect hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring, which is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. This vascular landmark helps distinguish it from a direct hernia.

notes.A: The hernial sac approaches from the abdominal side, but its diagnostic relation to the vessels at the ring is lateral.
notes.B: The deep ring lies above the inguinal ligament, while the distinction from a direct hernia uses its position lateral to the ascending vessels.
notes.D: A medial relation to the inferior epigastric vessels is characteristic of a direct hernia through Hesselbach's triangle.
notes.E: The sac may proceed forwards along the canal, but its neck is classed by the lateral vascular relation.

questions.stem: A direct inguinal hernia bulges through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, lying which way in relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
questions.why: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through the posterior wall in Hesselbach's triangle. The inferior epigastric vessels lie lateral to the triangle, so they also lie lateral to the hernial neck.

notes.A: Superior position does not distinguish these hernias, because the useful landmark is the medial or lateral relationship to the vessels.
notes.B: The sac may project anteriorly as it bulges through the wall, but its neck lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
notes.C: The sac starts behind the posterior wall, but a direct hernia's characteristic relation to the vessels is medial.
notes.E: A hernia lateral to the vessels can enter through the deep ring and is typical of an indirect route.

questions.stem: A congenital indirect inguinal hernia results from persistence of the:
questions.why: The processus vaginalis is a peritoneal diverticulum that extends through the inguinal canal during testicular descent. If its proximal part remains patent, abdominal contents can enter it as an indirect hernia.

notes.A: The gubernaculum guides gonadal descent, while patency of a peritoneal tract provides the route for this hernia.
notes.B: A patent urachus can connect the bladder and umbilicus in the midline rather than opening into the inguinal canal.
notes.C: The vitelline duct once linked the midgut and yolk sac and can persist as a Meckel diverticulum.
notes.D: The left umbilical vein becomes the round ligament of the liver and is separate from the inguinal canal.

questions.stem: Compared with an indirect hernia, the neck of a direct inguinal hernia sac is:

options.label: A
options.text: wide, so less likely to strangulate

options.label: B
options.text: narrow, so more likely to strangulate

questions.why: A direct inguinal hernia often pushes through a broad weak area of the posterior wall, producing a wider neck. It is generally less likely to strangulate than a sac with a tight neck.

notes.B: A narrow neck is more characteristic of an indirect hernia that has entered through the deep ring.
notes.C: A direct hernia has a neck at its wall defect, although that opening is often relatively broad.
notes.D: Direct sacs usually present in the groin, while an indirect sac may extend down the canal into the scrotum.
notes.E: The direct sac emerges medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, whereas the deep ring is lateral to those vessels.

questions.stem: A femoral hernia, which passes through the femoral canal, is more common in:
questions.why: Femoral hernias occur disproportionately in women, particularly in older adulthood. They enter the femoral canal beneath the inguinal ligament and typically present inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.

notes.A: Athletic groin symptoms may involve muscle or tendon injury, while femoral hernia is more frequent among women.
notes.C: Men account for many inguinal hernias, but femoral hernias occur more often in women.
notes.D: In male infants a patent processus vaginalis can cause indirect inguinal hernia rather than the typical adult femoral hernia.
notes.E: Femoral hernia can occur at other ages but is chiefly associated with adults, particularly older women.

questions.stem: The testis is drawn down into the scrotum during fetal life by the:
questions.why: The gubernaculum is a fetal connective tissue structure that anchors and guides the testis towards the scrotum as the surrounding anatomy develops. Testicular descent also depends on hormonal and mechanical factors.

notes.A: Dartos smooth muscle wrinkles the scrotal skin and is involved in temperature regulation rather than guiding fetal descent.
notes.B: The round ligament of the uterus is a female derivative of the gubernaculum, not the structure accompanying a descending testis.
notes.D: The processus vaginalis is a peritoneal outpouching that precedes the testis along the route and later contributes to the tunica vaginalis.
notes.E: The cremaster elevates the testis after descent and is involved in the cremasteric reflex.

questions.stem: The quadratus lumborum muscle inserts onto the:

options.label: A
options.text: internal lip of the iliac crest

options.label: C
options.text: tips of the lumbar transverse processes

options.label: D
options.text: body of the twelfth thoracic vertebra

questions.why: QL arises from the lumbar transverse processes and 12th rib and inserts on the internal lip of the iliac crest.

questions.stem: During inspiration the quadratus lumborum assists breathing by:

options.label: A
options.text: expanding the lower costal cartilages outward

options.label: B
options.text: anchoring the 12th rib against the diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: actively elevating the first and second ribs

options.label: D
options.text: depressing the sternum and the manubrium

options.label: E
options.text: flexing the whole thoracic vertebral column

questions.why: Quadratus lumborum attaches to the twelfth rib and can stabilise it during inspiration. This provides a steadier attachment for the diaphragm as its contraction enlarges the thoracic cavity.

notes.A: Widening the costal margins is related to diaphragm and rib movements rather than the specific stabilising action of quadratus lumborum.
notes.C: Elevating the first two ribs is an action associated with scalene muscles, far above the quadratus lumborum attachment.
notes.D: The sternum moves mainly through movements of the ribs and costal cartilages, without a direct quadratus lumborum attachment.
notes.E: Quadratus lumborum can laterally flex the lumbar trunk but assists inspiration through stabilisation of the lowest rib.

questions.stem: The psoas major muscle unites with the iliacus to insert, as the iliopsoas, onto the:

options.label: E
options.text: internal lip of the iliac crest

questions.why: Psoas major and iliacus pass beneath the inguinal ligament and converge as iliopsoas. Their tendon attaches to the lesser trochanter on the proximal femur, allowing hip flexion.

notes.A: The iliopubic eminence is a pelvic landmark near the course of iliopsoas rather than its distal attachment.
notes.B: The intertrochanteric crest joins the greater and lesser trochanters posteriorly and receives other hip muscle attachments.
notes.D: The greater trochanter provides attachments for muscles such as gluteus medius, whereas iliopsoas inserts on the smaller medial projection.
notes.E: The iliac crest is a pelvic attachment for other posterior and lateral wall muscles rather than the insertion of iliopsoas.

questions.stem: The psoas major muscle is innervated by the anterior rami of which nerves?
questions.why: Direct branches from upper lumbar anterior rami, usually described as L1–L3, enter psoas major. Despite acting with iliacus as iliopsoas, psoas major receives its own segmental supply.

notes.A: T12 continues as the subcostal nerve and is not among the usual principal rami supplying psoas major.
notes.B: L4 and L5 are too low as a pair, leaving out the usual upper lumbar inputs to psoas major.
notes.C: Upper sacral rami contribute to the sacral plexus rather than directly supplying this upper lumbar muscle.
notes.E: L2–L4 is the classic root range of the femoral nerve, whereas psoas major typically receives more cranial direct branches.

questions.stem: The iliacus muscle is innervated by the:
questions.why: Iliacus receives muscular branches of the femoral nerve, which contains fibres from L2–L4. Its partner psoas major has a separate supply from direct upper lumbar branches.

notes.A: The obturator nerve chiefly supplies adductors of the medial thigh and does not supply iliacus.
notes.B: The subcostal nerve supplies parts of the abdominal wall and skin, rather than the main iliacus motor fibres.
notes.C: The genitofemoral nerve lies on psoas and supplies the cremaster and small skin territories, rather than iliacus.
notes.D: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae outside the iliac fossa.

questions.stem: The psoas minor muscle, absent in about 40% of people, inserts onto the:
questions.why: When present, psoas minor lies anterior to psoas major and ends in a slender tendon near the iliopubic eminence and adjoining fascia. Its line of pull can weakly flex the lumbar region.

notes.B: The lesser trochanter receives the iliopsoas tendon formed by psoas major and iliacus, rather than psoas minor.
notes.C: The iliac crest provides attachments for muscles such as quadratus lumborum, separate from the psoas minor insertion.
notes.D: The twelfth rib receives a posterior attachment of quadratus lumborum, above the pelvic insertion of psoas minor.
notes.E: The greater trochanter receives insertions of gluteal muscles rather than the tendon of psoas minor.

questions.stem: Which posterior abdominal wall muscle is reported to be absent in roughly 40% of people?
questions.why: Psoas minor is a variable slender muscle lying in front of psoas major when present. Roughly 40% absence is a commonly cited estimate, although prevalence varies by the group studied.

notes.A: Transversus abdominis is a standard flat muscle of the anterolateral wall that also arises from thoracolumbar fascia.
notes.C: Psoas major is normally present and forms a principal hip flexor with iliacus.
notes.D: Iliacus normally occupies the iliac fossa and joins psoas major distally to help flex the hip.
notes.E: Quadratus lumborum is normally present between the iliac crest, lumbar transverse processes and twelfth rib.

questions.stem: The right dome of the diaphragm sits higher than the left mainly because of the:
questions.why: The right liver lobe fills the space below the right hemidiaphragm and supports its higher position. The dome levels also change as the diaphragm moves during breathing.

notes.A: The stomach lies mainly below the left dome and does not account for elevation of the right.
notes.B: The right lung lies above the diaphragm and conforms to its dome rather than raising it from underneath.
notes.D: The spleen lies beneath the left dome in the left upper quadrant, away from the elevated right side.
notes.E: Most of the heart lies above the central and left diaphragm, whereas the right-sided rise is associated with the liver below.

questions.stem: The muscular fibres of the diaphragm converge to insert onto the:
questions.why: Diaphragm fibres arise around the lower thoracic aperture and converge into a broad, three-part central tendon. Their contraction draws this tendon down, increasing the vertical dimension of the chest.

notes.A: The costal margin provides peripheral attachments for the costal fibres, rather than their central insertion.
notes.B: The upper lumbar vertebrae are posterior attachments of the crura, whose fibres converge on the tendon.
notes.C: The twelfth rib and nearby arcuate ligament provide peripheral lumbar and costal attachments rather than the principal insertion.
notes.E: The xiphoid process gives origin to anterior sternal slips, which then insert on the central tendon.

questions.stem: The motor nerve supply to the diaphragm is the:
questions.why: Motor fibres from the C3–C5 anterior rami descend in each phrenic nerve to the diaphragm. They activate its skeletal muscle to expand the thorax during inspiration.

notes.A: The vagus supplies thoracic and abdominal viscera and is not the main somatic motor nerve to respiratory diaphragm muscle.
notes.B: Lower intercostal nerves supply chest wall muscles and carry peripheral diaphragmatic sensation rather than providing phrenic motor supply.
notes.C: The T12 subcostal nerve supplies parts of the abdominal wall, while diaphragm motor fibres arise in the cervical region.
notes.D: The greater splanchnic nerve carries autonomic fibres to abdominal plexuses rather than motor fibres to the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Sensation from the peripheral part of the diaphragm is carried by the:
questions.why: Lower intercostal nerves provide sensory innervation to peripheral diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum. The central region instead sends sensory fibres through the phrenic nerves, explaining the difference in referred pain.

notes.B: Phrenic nerves provide diaphragm motor supply and central sensation, while the periphery also receives segmental intercostal sensation.
notes.C: The vagus carries visceral afferents and accompanies the oesophagus through the diaphragm, rather than supplying its peripheral serosa.
notes.D: The greater splanchnic nerve connects thoracic sympathetic pathways to abdominal plexuses and does not convey the main peripheral diaphragmatic sensation.
notes.E: The sympathetic trunk runs along the vertebral column and is distinct from the lower thoracic segmental sensory nerves.

questions.stem: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the bodies of vertebrae:
questions.why: The right crus usually has the longer lumbar attachment, arising from the upper three lumbar vertebral bodies and adjacent discs. Its fibres help form the muscular sling of the oesophageal hiatus.

notes.A: T12 is near the aortic hiatus above the usual lumbar vertebral attachments of the right crus.
notes.C: L1–L2 describes the typical shorter left crus, while the right usually reaches one segment lower.
notes.D: The lower thoracic levels are above the lumbar vertebral bodies anchoring the right crus.
notes.E: L3 can be its lowest usual attachment, but this range omits the more superior attachments at L1 and L2.

questions.stem: The medial arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arches over the:
questions.why: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of fascia that forms an arch over psoas major. It provides a posterior diaphragmatic attachment between the lumbar vertebral body and transverse process.

notes.A: The inferior vena cava traverses a higher opening in the central tendon, rather than an arcuate ligament posteriorly.
notes.B: The oesophagus passes through a muscular hiatus formed mainly by the right crus, not under the medial fascial arch.
notes.D: Quadratus lumborum lies beneath the lateral arcuate ligament, which is farther from the midline.
notes.E: The aorta passes under the median arcuate ligament that joins the two crura in the midline.

questions.stem: The lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arches over the:

options.label: B
options.text: the head of the twelfth rib

options.label: E
options.text: the belly of the psoas major

questions.why: The lateral arcuate ligament runs from the L1 transverse process to the twelfth rib as a thickening of fascia over quadratus lumborum. Diaphragm muscle fibres attach along its superior aspect.

notes.A: The aorta passes beneath the median arcuate ligament in the midline, medial to the arch over quadratus lumborum.
notes.B: The twelfth rib provides the lateral attachment, but the ligament arches over the muscle along the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.C: The lumbar sympathetic trunk is related to the medial arcuate ligament and lies farther medially.
notes.E: Psoas major lies beneath the medial arcuate ligament, while quadratus lumborum is under the lateral arch.

questions.stem: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The aorta enters the abdomen at the T12 level behind the median arcuate ligament between the diaphragmatic crura. Its posterior position distinguishes it from the two higher openings.

notes.A: The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon near T8, substantially above the aortic hiatus.
notes.B: The oesophagus travels through a muscular diaphragmatic opening around T10, anterior and superior to the aorta.
notes.C: By L1 the aorta is already in the abdomen, near the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
notes.D: T6 is within the thoracic course of the descending aorta, well before its passage behind the diaphragm.

questions.stem: In addition to the aorta, the aortic hiatus transmits the:
questions.why: The aortic hiatus carries the aorta and thoracic duct behind the diaphragm at about T12. The azygos vein can also use this passage, although it may enter through the right crus separately.

notes.B: The inferior vena cava passes through the right portion of the central tendon near T8.
notes.C: The oesophagus and accompanying vagal trunks pass through a separate muscular opening at about T10.
notes.D: Small right phrenic branches may accompany the inferior vena cava through the caval opening instead.
notes.E: The oesophageal hiatus contains oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels rather than the aortic hiatus.

questions.stem: The caval opening of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The inferior vena cava enters the thorax through a right-sided aperture in the central tendon at about T8. This is the highest of the three principal diaphragmatic openings.

notes.A: T6 is above the usual caval crossing and is near the level of the left lung root.
notes.C: T10 is the approximate level of the oesophageal hiatus in the muscular portion of the diaphragm.
notes.D: T12 is the level of the posterior aortic opening rather than the more anterior passage through the tendon.
notes.E: L1 lies below the major diaphragmatic apertures and is near the superior mesenteric artery origin.

questions.stem: The caval opening of the diaphragm is located within the:
questions.why: The inferior vena cava crosses a gap in the right part of the diaphragm's central tendon near T8. The tendon is attached to the vein, helping keep the opening patent during breathing.

notes.A: The median arcuate ligament arches anterior to the aorta near T12, leaving a passage posterior to it.
notes.B: The costal muscle fibres arise at the chest wall, as opposed to the tendinous region containing the caval opening.
notes.D: The right crus forms much of the muscular sling around the oesophageal hiatus rather than the caval opening.
notes.E: The left crus is a lumbar muscle attachment and lies well posterior and left of the caval passage.

questions.stem: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The oesophageal hiatus usually lies at T10 within a muscular sling formed mainly by the right crus. It transmits the oesophagus with anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

notes.A: T12 is the level of the aorta and thoracic duct passing behind the diaphragm.
notes.B: L1 lies below the oesophageal hiatus and close to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
notes.C: At T6 the oesophagus lies within the thorax, still above its passage through the diaphragm.
notes.E: T8 is the usual level of the inferior vena cava's opening in the central tendon.

questions.stem: Besides the oesophagus, the oesophageal hiatus transmits the:

options.label: A
options.text: the thoracic duct and azygos vein

options.label: C
options.text: the aorta and the thoracic duct

questions.why: The oesophageal plexus reforms into anterior and posterior vagal trunks on the lower oesophagus. Both travel with it through the hiatus around T10, along with small oesophageal vessels and lymphatics.

notes.A: The thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos vein use the posterior aortic opening rather than the muscular oesophageal hiatus.
notes.B: The inferior vena cava passes through a separate aperture in the central tendon near T8.
notes.C: The aortic hiatus carries the aorta and thoracic duct together at approximately T12.
notes.D: Branches of the right phrenic nerve can pass with the inferior vena cava rather than with the oesophagus.

questions.stem: The most common type of hiatus hernia is the:
questions.why: In the most common hiatus hernia, the gastro-oesophageal junction slides above the diaphragm with the proximal stomach. That displacement defines a type I hernia and can compromise the anti-reflux barrier.

notes.B: A type II hernia allows the fundus to herniate beside the oesophagus while the junction remains below the diaphragm.
notes.C: A type III hernia has both upward displacement of the junction and paraoesophageal herniation of stomach.
notes.D: A type IV hernia contains an abdominal structure other than the stomach, such as colon or omentum.
notes.E: A Bochdalek hernia is a congenital posterolateral diaphragmatic defect, separate from the oesophageal hiatus.

questions.stem: In a type IV hiatus hernia, the characteristic finding is that the:

options.label: B
options.text: entire stomach lies within the thorax

options.label: E
options.text: defect lies within the central tendon

questions.why: A type IV hernia has the entire stomach (and sometimes other organs) in the thorax.

questions.stem: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of nerves and lies within the substance of the:
questions.why: The lumbar plexus forms from anterior rami of the upper lumbar nerves within the posterior part of psoas major. Its branches emerge from the muscle's medial, lateral or anterior surfaces.

notes.A: Erector spinae lies posterior to the spine and receives posterior rami, separate from the lumbar plexus.
notes.B: Transversus abdominis carries some distal abdominal nerve branches but does not contain the root plexus.
notes.D: Quadratus lumborum lies lateral to psoas; some lumbar branches cross its anterior surface after leaving psoas.
notes.E: Iliacus shares the femoral nerve's course distally, while the plexus itself forms within the adjacent psoas major.

questions.stem: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.why: The lumbar plexus is principally formed by anterior rami of L1–L4 within psoas major. T12 can contribute to its upper part, and part of L4 continues towards the sacral plexus.

notes.A: T12 may contribute, but stopping at L3 omits the L4 input to several important branches.
notes.B: L2–S1 omits L1, while S1 is a sacral plexus contribution rather than one of the primary lumbar roots.
notes.C: L4–S4 describes the main span of the sacral plexus when its lumbosacral contribution is included.
notes.E: The full L5 anterior ramus passes into the lumbosacral trunk rather than helping form most lumbar plexus branches.

questions.stem: The lumbosacral trunk, which joins the sacral plexus, is formed from part of L4 and the whole of:
questions.why: A descending branch from L4 joins the whole anterior ramus of L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk. This trunk crosses the pelvic brim and joins the upper sacral rami.

notes.A: S1 joins lower down as part of the sacral plexus rather than forming the lumbar portion of the trunk.
notes.B: L3 contributes to lumbar plexus branches such as femoral and obturator nerves, while the lumbosacral trunk has lower inputs.
notes.C: S2 is a sacral plexus contribution below the point where the trunk enters the pelvis.
notes.D: L2 supplies branches from the upper lumbar plexus, while the trunk specifically carries L4 and L5 fibres.

questions.stem: The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves both arise mainly from which spinal level?
questions.why: The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves arise mainly from the L1 anterior ramus and cross the posterior wall towards the abdominal muscle planes. The iliohypogastric nerve may also receive T12 fibres.

notes.B: L2 is a major contributor to other branches such as the genitofemoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves.
notes.C: T12 forms the subcostal nerve and can contribute fibres, but L1 is the principal root for the two named nerves.
notes.D: L3 contributes to larger nerves such as femoral and obturator, rather than chiefly supplying these upper abdominal branches.
notes.E: L4 contributes to lower lumbar plexus branches and the lumbosacral trunk, not normally to the named pair.

questions.stem: Within the inguinal canal, the ilioinguinal nerve accompanies the:
questions.why: In males the ilioinguinal nerve runs for part of the inguinal canal alongside the spermatic cord, outside its coverings. It enters through muscle rather than the deep ring and exits at the superficial ring.

notes.A: The lumbar sympathetic trunk lies against the vertebral bodies, well posterior to the inguinal canal.
notes.C: The inferior epigastric artery ascends in the abdominal wall medial to the deep ring instead of running through the canal.
notes.D: Femoral vessels travel beneath the inguinal ligament, separated from the canal above it.
notes.E: The vas deferens is only one component of the cord, alongside which the nerve travels outside the cord coverings.

questions.stem: The genitofemoral nerve emerges from and pierces the anterior surface of which muscle?
questions.why: The genitofemoral nerve forms from L1–L2 within psoas major and pierces its anterior surface. It descends over the muscle before dividing into genital and femoral branches.

notes.A: Transversus abdominis is a wall muscle traversed by some abdominal nerves farther laterally, not the site of genitofemoral emergence.
notes.B: Obturator internus lies against the lateral pelvic wall, inferior to the psoas origin of the genitofemoral nerve.
notes.D: Iliacus lies lateral to psoas and is related to the femoral nerve and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
notes.E: Quadratus lumborum has upper lumbar nerve branches passing in front of it, while the genitofemoral nerve emerges from psoas.

questions.stem: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies motor fibres to the:
questions.why: In males the genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring and supplies cremaster muscle around the spermatic cord. Stimulation can elevate the testis as the motor limb of the cremasteric reflex.

notes.A: External oblique receives segmental thoracoabdominal branches rather than motor fibres from the genital branch.
notes.B: The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle controlled by autonomic pathways rather than by the genitofemoral nerve.
notes.C: Bulbospongiosus is a superficial perineal muscle supplied through the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve.
notes.E: Dartos is smooth muscle in scrotal superficial fascia and receives autonomic input, unlike striated cremaster.

questions.stem: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is derived from which spinal levels?
questions.why: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve receives fibres from L2 and L3 and crosses iliacus towards the anterior superior iliac spine. It carries sensation from the anterolateral thigh.

notes.A: L1–L2 is the usual root combination for the genitofemoral nerve rather than the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
notes.B: L3 contributes, but the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve also receives L2 rather than normally including L4.
notes.C: L4 and L5 help form the lumbosacral trunk and are below the roots of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
notes.D: T12 and L1 can contribute to abdominal wall nerves, while the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve arises farther caudally.

questions.stem: The femoral nerve emerges at the lateral border of the psoas major and is formed from which spinal levels?
questions.why: Posterior divisions of the L2–L4 anterior rami form the femoral nerve within psoas major. It emerges laterally and travels between psoas and iliacus towards the anterior thigh.

notes.B: The femoral nerve contains L4 rather than L1, so the proposed range is shifted cranially.
notes.C: L4 contributes to the femoral nerve, while L5 and S1 are lower inputs to lumbosacral and sacral plexus pathways.
notes.D: L2 and L3 contribute, but L4 also provides fibres important for the quadriceps and patellar reflex.
notes.E: T12 and L1 supply chiefly upper lumbar and abdominal wall territories and are not principal femoral nerve roots.

questions.stem: The femoral nerve gives rise to a long cutaneous branch that accompanies the great saphenous vein, the:
questions.why: The saphenous nerve is the long sensory branch of the femoral nerve. It leaves the adductor canal and accompanies the great saphenous vein in the medial leg, supplying skin towards the foot.

notes.A: The iliohypogastric nerve supplies skin around the lower anterior abdomen and upper lateral gluteal region rather than the medial leg.
notes.C: The sural nerve mainly supplies the posterolateral leg and lateral foot and can accompany the small saphenous vein.
notes.D: The obturator nerve chiefly supplies the medial thigh and does not give the long medial leg branch.
notes.E: The genitofemoral nerve supplies small skin areas near the groin and has a separate origin from the femoral nerve.

questions.stem: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of the psoas major?
questions.why: The obturator nerve forms within psoas major and emerges at its medial border to cross the pelvis. It reaches the medial thigh via the obturator canal.

notes.A: The lumbar roots form the plexus in the posterior part of psoas, but the obturator nerve emerges medially.
notes.B: The obturator nerve has already emerged along the medial border before descending towards the pelvic obturator canal.
notes.D: The femoral nerve typically emerges from the lateral border and passes between psoas and iliacus.
notes.E: The genitofemoral nerve runs through psoas major and descends on its anterior surface.

questions.stem: The obturator nerve provides motor supply mainly to the:
questions.why: The obturator nerve enters the medial thigh and supplies most adductor muscles, including adductor longus, brevis and much of magnus. Some muscles in the region have additional or variable supply.

notes.A: Hamstrings receive branches of the sciatic nerve, chiefly its tibial division, rather than the obturator nerve.
notes.B: Gluteal muscles are principally supplied by superior and inferior gluteal nerves from the sacral plexus.
notes.C: The anterior compartment of the leg receives the deep fibular nerve, well distal to the obturator motor territory.
notes.E: Quadriceps is in the anterior thigh and receives branches of the femoral nerve to extend the knee.

questions.stem: Because the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, disease of the hip may produce referred pain in the:
questions.why: Articular branches of the obturator nerve can convey sensation from the hip and knee. Their shared spinal segments help explain why hip pathology can be perceived as pain around the knee.

notes.A: Shoulder pain commonly involves cervical sensory pathways rather than the lumbar segments supplying the hip and knee.
notes.B: Lower back pain can coexist with hip disease, but the shared articular distribution in this question explains pain in another joint.
notes.C: Periumbilical skin corresponds to T10, rather than the upper lumbar segments carrying the articular inputs.
notes.D: The hip can cause groin pain locally, but its shared sensory pathways can also produce pain at the knee.

questions.stem: The subcostal nerve that runs on the posterior abdominal wall is the anterior ramus of which nerve?
questions.why: The subcostal nerve is the anterior ramus of T12 and runs below the twelfth rib. It then crosses the posterior abdominal wall and contributes to its muscular and cutaneous supply.

notes.B: T11 is an intercostal nerve that runs in the eleventh intercostal space before continuing onto the abdominal wall.
notes.C: L1 is the main source of the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves below the subcostal nerve.
notes.D: T10 is a thoracoabdominal nerve associated with the skin near the umbilical level.
notes.E: L2 contributes to lumbar plexus branches and does not form the nerve lying immediately beneath the twelfth rib.

questions.stem: The abdominal oesophagus pierces the diaphragm through the right crus at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The oesophagus crosses the diaphragm at about T10 through a muscular opening formed predominantly by right-crural fibres. The segment below the hiatus is the short abdominal oesophagus.

notes.B: The central tendon contains the caval opening near T8, above and anterior to the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.C: T12 is the usual level of the aortic hiatus behind the median arcuate ligament.
notes.D: T11 approximates the level of entry into the stomach, rather than the passage through the diaphragm itself.
notes.E: L1 lies below the hiatus and is near the transpyloric plane and superior mesenteric artery origin.

questions.stem: The abdominal oesophagus terminates in the cardiac part of the stomach at approximately the level of:
questions.why: After passing through the oesophageal hiatus near T10, the oesophagus descends for a short distance to the cardia. The gastro-oesophageal junction is usually projected near T11 to the left of midline.

notes.A: T12 is around the posterior aortic hiatus and below the usual projection of the cardia.
notes.C: T8 is the usual level of the caval opening, superior to both the oesophageal hiatus and cardia.
notes.D: T10 is the usual level where the oesophagus passes the diaphragm, just above its opening into the stomach.
notes.E: L1 is the approximate transpyloric level and marks a lower, more distal part of the stomach.

questions.stem: At the lower oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks lie respectively on its:
questions.why: As vagal fibres regroup on the lower oesophagus, they form trunks on its anterior and posterior surfaces. The anterior trunk derives mainly from the left vagus and the posterior mainly from the right.

notes.A: The two trunks run along the lower oesophagus at overlapping levels and cross the hiatus together.
notes.B: Both trunks lie against the external surface of the oesophagus, one in front and one behind it.
notes.D: The vagal nerves may initially approach on the sides, but their lower trunks are positioned anteriorly and posteriorly.
notes.E: Medial and lateral describe positions beside a structure, whereas these trunks lie on its front and back.

questions.stem: Which of the following contributes to the lower oesophageal (physiological) sphincter mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: the left crus gripping the aorta

options.label: C
options.text: tone of the external anal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: the right crus acting as a pinch-cock

questions.why: Right-crural fibres form a muscular sling around the oesophageal hiatus and help tighten the gastro-oesophageal junction, especially during inspiration. This external pinch complements the intrinsic lower oesophageal smooth-muscle barrier.

notes.A: The aorta passes behind the diaphragm and is not surrounded by the crural sling controlling the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.B: The ileocaecal valve regulates passage between ileum and caecum, far downstream from the gastro-oesophageal junction.
notes.C: The external anal sphincter is striated muscle involved in continence at the distal end of the tract.
notes.E: The pyloric sphincter controls gastric emptying at the distal stomach rather than guarding its oesophageal entrance.

questions.stem: The widest and most dilated part of the alimentary tract is the:
questions.why: The stomach expands as a reservoir between the oesophagus and duodenum. Its fundus and body accept a meal through relaxation and distension, making it the broadest region of the alimentary canal.

notes.A: The caecum is the blind initial part of the large bowel and usually has less capacity than the stomach.
notes.B: The rectal ampulla provides temporary storage before defaecation, but it is a smaller local dilatation.
notes.C: The duodenal cap is only the expanded proximal duodenum immediately after the pyloric sphincter.
notes.D: The sigmoid colon is a mobile S-shaped distal bowel segment rather than the largest reservoir of the tract.

questions.stem: The cardiac orifice of the stomach lies to the left of the midline at the level of:
questions.why: The cardia (gastro-oesophageal junction) lies left of the T10 vertebra.

questions.stem: The pylorus of the stomach lies to the right of the midline at the level of:
questions.why: In a supine adult the pylorus typically lies just right of the midline near the L1 transpyloric plane. This region controls passage from the stomach into the first part of the duodenum.

notes.A: L5 is near the transtubercular plane, well below the usual projection of the gastric outlet.
notes.C: T10 is near the oesophageal hiatus, higher than the usual transpyloric plane.
notes.D: T12 is near the aortic hiatus and lies above the conventional projection of the pylorus.
notes.E: L3 approximates the subcostal plane and is below the usual supine pyloric level, although stomach position can change.

questions.stem: The longitudinal mucosal folds seen in the empty stomach are called:
questions.why: Gastric rugae are ridges of mucosa and submucosa prominent in the empty stomach. The folds flatten during distension, allowing the wall to accommodate a larger meal.

notes.A: Villi are projections of small-intestinal mucosa that enlarge the absorptive surface area rather than forming gastric folds.
notes.B: Taeniae are longitudinal bands of colonic smooth muscle rather than ridges in the gastric lining.
notes.D: Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds in the small intestine, unlike expandable folds of the empty stomach.
notes.E: Haustra are sacculations of the colon associated with the taeniae, not folds of the gastric mucosa.

questions.stem: The pyloric sphincter is a thickening of which muscle layer of the stomach wall?
questions.why: The middle circular smooth muscle layer thickens at the pylorus to form a sphincter around the gastric outlet. Changing its tone regulates the passage of chyme into the duodenum.

notes.A: The inner oblique layer helps mix gastric contents, while a circular band is best arranged to narrow the outlet.
notes.B: Submucosa is a connective tissue layer carrying vessels and nerves rather than a contractile sphincter.
notes.C: Serosa is the external mesothelial covering of the stomach rather than the muscular ring in its wall.
notes.E: The longitudinal muscle layer can shorten the wall but does not form the main circumferential pyloric thickening.

questions.stem: Which structure is part of the posterior relations ('stomach bed') of the stomach?
questions.why: The body of the pancreas lies behind the stomach, separated from it by the lesser sac. It forms part of the stomach bed together with neighbouring posterior structures such as the splenic artery.

notes.A: The left hepatic lobe is chiefly an anterior relation overlying part of the stomach.
notes.B: The anterior abdominal wall lies in front of the stomach and cannot form its posterior bed.
notes.C: The stomach lies against the left diaphragmatic dome in the left upper abdomen.
notes.D: The gallbladder fundus is in the right upper abdomen near the inferior liver surface, apart from the stomach bed.

questions.stem: A posterior gastric ulcer eroding backwards may cause torrential haemorrhage by involving the:
questions.why: The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas in the stomach bed behind the lesser sac. An ulcer penetrating the posterior gastric wall can reach it and cause major arterial bleeding.

notes.B: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas and lies farther right than the usual posterior gastric arterial relation.
notes.C: The superior mesenteric vein drains the midgut and approaches the portal confluence from below the pancreatic neck.
notes.D: The left gastric vein drains the lesser curvature, whereas the classic major vessel in the posterior stomach bed is arterial.
notes.E: The inferior vena cava lies deeper and to the right of the midline, away from the typical posterior gastric ulcer relation.

questions.stem: The total length of the duodenum is approximately:
questions.why: The duodenum runs for about 25 cm from the pylorus to the duodenojejunal flexure. Its four segments form a curve around the head of the pancreas.

notes.A: Five centimetres is about the length of the first segment, not the whole four-part duodenum.
notes.C: Fifty centimetres is about twice the usual anatomical length of the duodenum.
notes.D: Ten denotes the approximate length in inches, while 10 cm is shorter than the full duodenal curve.
